unit: ACU Library (Faculty Guide: AI and ChatGPT)
title: Faculty Guide: AI and ChatGPT: Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Library-hosted faculty guide on academic integrity that tells instructors to define acceptable AI use in each class and lists elements a syllabus statement should include. It provides three example statements (AI required, prohibited, use-with-permission) and citation formats for AI output. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Academic Integrity Policy
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Short school-level academic integrity statement for computer science. It frames programming assignments as learning opportunities, defines submitting code one did not write (including AI-generated code from tools such as Copilot or ChatGPT) as plagiarism, and makes this the school default unless a syllabus or assignment allows generated code.

title: Algoma University: Guidelines for the Responsible Use of Generative AI by Students
date_or_term: Approved by Algoma University Senate May 2, 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Senate-approved student guidelines that prohibit generative AI in all coursework unless the instructor explicitly permits it, and require written permission before use. Where AI is allowed, students must cite it, verify outputs and protect their privacy; instructors may use AI detectors, and sanctions range from a zero on the assignment or course to suspension or expulsion.

title: OAI's Guidance for Fall 2024: AI & Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Academic Integrity Office guidance for faculty writing course AI policies. It notes there is no university-wide AI policy, assigns faculty responsibility for deciding appropriate use, offers five steps and sample language across strict, conditional and open stances, requires suspected misuse to go to OAI rather than unilateral grade penalties, and states OAI does not treat detector scores as evidence.

unit: AI at Amherst (Academic Technology Services / Information Technology)
title: Updated AI Usage Guidelines
analyst_summary: Tier 4. College-wide guidelines for students, faculty and staff that encourage responsible exploration of generative AI under conditions. Users stay responsible for the accuracy of AI-assisted material, including code, and must keep sensitive data out of unapproved tools and follow data-classification rules. Use must also align with the Student Code of Conduct, and transparency about significant AI contributions is encouraged.

title: CS 3435: Data Collection and Visualization
analyst_summary: Course website for an App State Python data collection and visualization course. Its AI-based Assistance section permits university-licensed AI tools (Copilot, Gemini, NotebookLM) within the academic integrity policy, and adopts Georgia Tech's collaboration analogy with two heuristics: never copy between the AI conversation and the assignment, and do not keep the AI and the assignment open at once, including avoiding IDE-integrated AI. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: School of Computing and Augmented Intelligence (offered through ASU Learning Enterprise / Universal Learner Courses)
title: CSE 110: Principles of Programming (Summer C 2025) - Artificial Intelligence Policy: Use of Generative AI
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus (Universal Learner Courses section) that welcomes and encourages AI tools, citing workplace adoption, while requiring that submissions be authored by the student. AI may be used for debugging, concept clarification, and tutoring; unattributed AI-generated content is an integrity violation. The page is JavaScript-rendered, so the text was captured from a browser rendering rather than curl.

unit: Artificial Intelligence Policy Committee (A-State knowledge base)
title: Guidelines and Considerations for the Ethical Use of Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Campus committee guidelines that keep AI-use decisions with faculty, colleges and departments, advise putting AI policies in syllabi, and describe four approaches (prohibited, with permission, with acknowledgement, freely permitted). They also promote AI literacy and recommend campus AI-detection platforms while cautioning that detector results are a guide, not proof. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of the Provost and Vice-President Academic
title: What students need to know about generative AI tools like ChatGPT
analyst_summary: Tier 4: University-published notice in which the provost gives interim generative-AI guidance until a committee issues formal principles. Students must ask before using AI unless course guidance says otherwise, must cite permitted use, and remain the sole author. The notice was issued in news format; no later formal AU guidelines were found publicly.

unit: Biggio Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning
title: Syllabus Language for Generative Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Auburn's teaching-centre page offering four syllabus statements chosen by the instructor's desired level of GenAI use: open use with attribution, use only when assigned, not permitted, and not permitted for assignments but allowed for study. The permissive options require disclosure through a standard acknowledgement sentence and warn against entering sensitive data; all technology must go through Auburn's vetting process.

title: Artificial Intelligence at Augusta University
analyst_summary: Institution-wide AI guidelines covering data classification and approved tools, risks (including flawed generated code), a student do/don't table and faculty guidance on course policies. Students must follow syllabus-specific AI rules, disclose use, and avoid AI on exams unless allowed. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Computer Science and Information Technology (CSIT) department
title: COSC-1336 Programming Fundamentals I, Faculty Syllabus, Fall 2023
analyst_summary: Tier 1. An intro programming syllabus that lets students consult ChatGPT or other AI assistants on assignments. Students who do must add a note to the per-assignment originality certification describing the help they received. The instructor asks them to use AI in ways that support their learning and to share their views on the tools.

unit: Computer Science and Information Technology (CSIT) department
title: COSC-1436 Programming Fundamentals I, Faculty Syllabus, Fall 2025 (CSIT Generative AI (GAI) Policy)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. An intro programming syllabus that reproduces the CSIT department's generative AI policy. AI is allowed and encouraged as a learning aid, including for coding, as long as students disclose which tool they used and which part of the work it touched. Undisclosed AI content, including code, counts as plagiarism, and misuse can bring penalties up to course failure. The course also includes a Problem Solving with AI microcredential.

unit: Computer Science and Information Technology (CSIT) department
title: ITSE-1302 Computer Programming: Scientific Python, Faculty Syllabus, Spring 2024
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A Python programming syllabus that allows AI help on assignments if students disclose it in the submission certification. It also requires comments in any AI-produced code that show the student understands it and explain any corrections made to meet the specifications.

title: Artificial Intelligence (A.I.) Classroom Use Policies: A Syllabus Resource for Instructors
analyst_summary: APU's curricular-support office notes that the revised academic integrity policy requires prior instructor permission for any AI use, and gives three syllabus options (no AI use, partial use with citation, full use with an appendix of tools, reflection and transcript). It also offers three levels of assignment makeover and strategies, including recommending Canvas's SimCheck AI detector. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of the Vice Provost for Academic Affairs
title: AI Use Guidelines
analyst_summary: Vice Provost hub page for Ball State's living GenAI guidelines, linking separate guidelines for instructors, research, administrative tasks, suspected misuse and students (the linked PDFs require a Ball State login). The public page tells students to work through two self-check tools before using GenAI and to follow the GenAI statement their instructor chose for the course. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Department of Computer Science (School of Engineering and Computer Science)
title: CSI 3334 — Data Structures — Fall 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 1. The course page for a data structures class includes an AI-tools rule in its academic-honesty section. All assignments must be the student's original work, with no help from AI tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly or Gemini. Using AI without the instructor's explicit permission is treated as an Honor Code violation.

title: AI for Students
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Short college statement on student AI use: Bellevue College has rules and guidelines for responsible AI use in coursework, each class and instructor defines whether AI is allowed, why, and the consequences of misuse, and students must review and clarify their instructor's AI policy. The fuller 'AI Syllabus Policy Guidance for BC Instructors' document is on a login-only SharePoint site. Captured from an Internet Archive snapshot because the live site blocks automated access.

unit: Binghamton University Policies (Information Technology and Information Security; approved by Senior Officers Group)
title: Generative AI Policy (Policy 312)
date_or_term: Approved by Senior Officers Group on 4/22/2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Short university-wide policy supporting responsible GenAI use by faculty, staff and students. It bans entering protected information without Information Security approval and sets principles of disclosure, consistency with academic integrity policies, verification of outputs for accuracy and bias, and human review of AI-informed decisions.

unit: Senate / University Regulations (Academic Code of Conduct), Academic Calendar
title: Academic Calendar 2025/2026 — University Regulations: Academic Integrity and Academic Misconduct
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): The university regulations in the academic calendar define AI and list, among forms of cheating and academic misconduct, using AI to source answers and using AI tools to generate submissions or complete assignments without explicit authorization. No Computer Science department or course AI policy was publicly available, so this is the university-wide fallback.

title: An approach to discussing AI in your department
analyst_summary: CS department post (URL dated March 2026) reporting its faculty committee's recommendations: a student-facing summary and syllabus blurb, faculty experimentation with AI, and five GenAI integration scenarios (no AI to full integration) assigned per course. It recommends redesigning lower-division assessment so at least half of points come from proctored demonstrations of understanding, and details a CS 321 plan with Copilot logs and a tutoring-mode AI prompt.

unit: University Catalog (Office of the Provost academic integrity policy)
title: Academic Integrity - University Catalog
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Boston College's university academic integrity policy. It lists work produced with unsanctioned or undocumented AI as cheating, defines plagiarism to include using AI text generators for central assignment tasks (explicitly including coding and programming) without both instructor permission and full attribution, and asks instructors to state in the syllabus when AI tools may be used.

unit: Department of Computer Science (College of Arts & Sciences)
course: CAS CS 111 Introduction to Computer Science I
title: CAS CS 111: Introduction to Computer Science I (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Intro CS syllabus whose list of prohibited behaviors includes using ChatGPT, Copilot or other generative AI for homework code or problem solving and requires all devices (including smart glasses) to be powered off during exams, with misconduct referred to the Academic Conduct Committee.

course: CAS CS 112 Introduction to Computer Science II
title: CAS CS 112: Introduction to Computer Science II Syllabus, Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Second-semester CS syllabus whose Academic Misconduct list bans tools that automate or assist code writing (ChatGPT is the example) and bans ChatGPT on exams. Suspected violations get an automatic zero on the problem set, and repeat cases go to the Academic Conduct Committee.

title: CS 391B: Responsible AI, Fall 2025
analyst_summary: Course site for a Responsible AI course. Its collaboration policy lets students use ChatGPT for general research, like a search engine, but not to answer specific homework problems or to pass off its output as their own.

title: CDS Generative AI Assistance (GAIA) Policy
analyst_summary: Unit-wide policy (originating in a student case study in DS 380 and endorsed by the CDS Academic Policy Committee) that embraces AI tools for writing and coding with limits. Students must credit AI and append full transcripts plus what, how and why; instructors grade AI-declared work against a lower baseline, use detection tools, penalize unreflective reuse, and may impose stricter rules; the policy also flags subscription-access inequity.

title: Foundations of Computer Systems (CSCI 2330) course page
analyst_summary: Course page with 'Guidelines on Generative AI' that fold AI into the department collaboration policy: AI use must be cited, asking AI to explain concepts is fine, but students must never have AI write their code. Live host returned HTTP 503, so the Wayback Machine snapshot (March 2026) was fetched.

unit: Academic Affairs (University Catalog, Academic Policies and Procedures)
title: Academic Policies and Procedures
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Catalog academic-policy page whose plagiarism section adds one AI rule: AI used in the research process must be described and cited according to the field's publishing conventions. Plagiarism penalties range from failing the assignment to dismissal, with the instructor setting the sanction.

title: AI Resources
analyst_summary: ITS page for students, faculty and staff describing AI tools available at BGSU and their privacy, security, ethical and IP risks. It permits ChatGPT with memory settings changed, forbids sharing personal or confidential data, and advises instructors to address AI data-privacy risks in syllabi. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Brandeis CTL page requiring that every syllabus state acceptable and unacceptable generative-AI uses and offering four university template policies from most restrictive (A) through situational B1/B2 to permissive. The templates explicitly address refining code (e.g., Claude Code) as well as writing, require citation where use is allowed, and hold students responsible for AI output.

title: Course Outline Policy
analyst_summary: Tier 3: Faculty of Science policy, covering Computer Science courses, on what course outlines must contain. Its only AI provision recommends, but does not require, that outlines reference a statement on AI use for coursework, leaving the stance to each instructor. The substantive AI rules are in the university-wide Senate Academic Integrity Policy (Tier 4, superseded here).

title: Syllabus & Course Policies :: BYU CS 111
analyst_summary: The intro-programming syllabus allows LLMs for understanding topics and provides a course ChatGPT-powered 'rubber duck' virtual TA for concept questions, but forbids AI-assisted autocompletion and any use of AI to write or debug assignment code. Proctored progress checks and exams permit an IDE without AI assistance, and TAs check that students can explain their own code.

title: CSE Generative AI Usage Policy
analyst_summary: A department-wide policy for a teaching-focused regional private university that actively encourages students to use generative AI for coding, debugging, ideation and learning, framed by analogy to pair programming and tutoring. It requires an AI-use statement (with an IEEE-style citation example) on all work and asks students to flag portions done without AI, while stressing that AI should complement rather than replace personal learning.

title: Introduction to Computer Science Course Information (COSC1P02)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2024 course outline for Brock's intro CS course, retrieved from an Internet Archive snapshot of the department PDF. Its only generative-AI provision concerns student communication: it tells students not to send the instructor AI-written or AI-polished emails, framing this as unprofessional. It also warns that misconduct-detection tools and scripts may be used and that FMS standard penalties apply.

course: CSCI 0190 Accelerated Introduction to Computer Science
title: Syllabus and Course Policies (AI Policy)
analyst_summary: Accelerated intro course AI policy that discloses staff use of AI to redesign the course, promises not to use AI for grading, and takes a 'balanced' approach: AI is disallowed for many tasks, optional or required for some, and limited to prescribed tools. AI for writing prose is banned except spelling and grammar checkers, and unpermitted use counts as an integrity violation; coarse assignment grading is meant to reduce the incentive to cheat.

title: CSCI 1377: Tools for Thought - S26
analyst_summary: The course academic integrity policy applies one rule to every resource: getting help with a problem is fine, getting a solution is not. AI coding tools are allowed for search-like help and small snippets students could write themselves, but not for skipping the parts of an assignment tied to its learning goals.

title: CSCI 2952-C: Learning with Limited Labeled Data
analyst_summary: A graduate seminar's short AI policy that adopts the ACL Rolling Review guidelines on generative assistance in authorship. Undisclosed use of AI assistants counts as academic dishonesty; spelling and grammar tools are exempt.

title: CS 109 - Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Intro computing course page. Its Collaboration/AI section encourages discussing material together but bars AI tools from completing programming assignments. Exams must be individual work.

title: CSCI 203: Introduction to Computer Science Syllabus (Fall 2026)
analyst_summary: A multi-section intro syllabus (linked from the department's course page) allowing online resources, including chatbots, for understanding topics if cited in code comments, but prohibiting searching for or generating solutions with chatbots and assistants; submissions across sections may go through a similarity checker.

unit: CUNY Board of Trustees (system-wide Academic Integrity Policy governing CCNY)
title: Academic Integrity Policy 2024
analyst_summary: CUNY's 2024 academic integrity policy, which applies at City College. It defines unauthorized AI use (including language models and code generators) as cheating, uncited AI-generated content as plagiarism, defers permitted use to each course's syllabus or instructor, and lists generating whole assignments or exam answers with AI as a substantial violation that can warrant disciplinary sanctions. Its rationale also stresses preparing students for AI-assisted careers. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

university: CUNY Graduate School and University Center
unit: CUNY Board of Trustees (system policy applying to the Graduate Center)
title: Academic Integrity Policy (rev. June 2024)
analyst_summary: CUNY-wide academic integrity policy revised in 2024 to cover AI. Unauthorized use of AI systems is cheating, generating assignment or exam content (explicitly including code generators) needs written instructor authorization, and uncited AI words count as plagiarism. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Syllabus, CSci 127, Hunter College
analyst_summary: Intro CS (Python) syllabus whose academic-integrity rules allow LLMs such as ChatGPT or Copilot only for explanations and suggestions. It bars using them to generate answers to graded work, uploading assignment questions as prompts, or AI chat/suggestions, and treats submitting such output as cheating and plagiarism. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: Center for the Advancement of Faculty Excellence (CAFE)
title: Faculty Samples (AI in the Classroom)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. CAFE's AI page for Cal Poly Pomona faculty, which notes elsewhere that no official university gAI policy exists yet. Its 'Sample Policy Statements from CAFE' give four graded options, from no use through allowed-unless-stated to full use with citation, each tying unauthorized or undisclosed use to a failing assignment grade and possible referral to Student Conduct. Faculty examples (music, mechanical engineering) are also shown; excerpts here come from the CAFE sample statements.

unit: Center for Effective Teaching and Learning (CETL)
title: Recommendations for Teaching & Learning with AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. CETL guidance for Cal State LA faculty. AI misuse falls under existing plagiarism standards, but instructors are urged to write their own policy, whether a ban, full use or a middle path, covering examples, rationale, citation and consequences, and possibly co-created with students. The page explains that the campus switched off Turnitin's AI detector and notes detector bias against non-native English writers.

title: Guidance on the Use of Generative AI and Large Language Model Tools
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Institute-wide memo from the Provost and COO supporting measured use of GenAI under four principles: disclosure, data and information protection, content responsibility, and the honor code. It defers to course instructors on writing and use, bars entering confidential or FERPA data into open tools, and says the guidance will evolve.

university: California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo
unit: Computer Science and Software Engineering Department
title: cpe453 Syllabus 30 March 2026
analyst_summary: Operating systems syllabus whose collaboration policy counts generative AI output as 'someone else's work'. Students may not refer to it while writing their own code. Uncredited collaboration counts as cheating.

university: California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo
unit: Computer Science and Software Engineering Department
title: Discrete Structures Winter 2025 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Discrete structures syllabus that bans ChatGPT and similar tools for graded work and calls their use academic dishonesty. It notes that most of the grade comes from in-class assessments, so skipping homework practice will show up on exams.

unit: Technology Services (ChatGPT Edu for Fresno State)
title: AI Guidelines - ChatGPT Edu for Fresno State
analyst_summary: Campus AI guidelines issued with the ChatGPT Edu rollout, setting general principles (ethical use, integrity, transparency, accountability, privacy) and separate guidance for faculty and students. Faculty are told not to use ChatGPT for grading and to set clear expectations; students must follow syllabus rules and cite AI content. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Creating a Generative AI Policy
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Teaching-center guidance that lets each faculty member set AI rules for the class and for individual assignments, and lists what a syllabus policy should cover: permitted and forbidden uses, citation, hallucination warnings, and how work will be authenticated under UPS 300.004. It provides sample statements (no AI, minor use, use by assignment) and a five-level continuum from No AI to AI Exploration. In the minor-use template, generating code for an assignment is one example of a banned use.

title: Optional Syllabus Statements for the Acceptable or Unacceptable Use of AI Tools in Your Course
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Campus guidance with four optional syllabus statements adapted from Temple University: broad acceptable use with documentation and citation, use only for listed activities, no use, and bans on specific activities. It asks instructors to be specific about permitted activities and to set penalties for first-time and repeat violations of a prohibition.

unit: Center for Teaching and Learning (Academic Affairs)
title: Course Preparation
analyst_summary: Sac State's teaching-center course-preparation checklist. Under promoting academic honesty, it asks instructors to decide whether and how AI is allowed and to state it explicitly in the syllabus in consultation with their department, to meet students one-on-one about suspected misconduct, and to use frequent and alternative assessments. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of the Associate Vice President Academic & Research / Chief Information Officer (AI with Purpose strategy)
title: Artificial Intelligence at Cape Breton University: AI With a Purpose
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Institution-wide, principle-based AI strategy (People First, Prudence, Accountability) rather than a rulebook. It declines universal rules, ties AI in teaching to existing academic integrity standards and the priority on critical thinking, and flags privacy, bias, copyright and environmental concerns; it is a living document overseen by an accountability committee.

title: Generative AI and Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Teaching-centre recommendations for instructors on generative AI and academic integrity. It urges explicit course policies, alternative assessment design, two-way disclosure of AI use, and states that the centre does not support AI detection tools. It closes with tiered sample syllabus language ranging from full prohibition to permitted use with citation.

title: CS 111.01 Introduction to Computer Science Winter 2024 General Course Info (syllabus PDF)
analyst_summary: The intro syllabus limits online help to the course site and official Python docs, names generative AI and Copilot as unacceptable sources, and calls AI code generation an integrity violation reported to the Academic Standing Committee; quizzes are closed-book on paper. (Newer CS 111 syllabi sit behind Moodle.)

title: COMP 1405/1005 A/B/C (Fall 2026) – "Introduction to Computer Science I" Course Outline
analyst_summary: Intro CS outline stating that course activities were designed for individual work without AI. Unless explicitly allowed, using any AI-based tool (chatbots, research assistants, image generators) counts as academic misconduct.

title: COMP 1406Z (Fall 2026) Introduction to Computer Science II
analyst_summary: Second intro CS outline banning AI tools (including Copilot-style autocomplete) on the midterm and final and strongly discouraging AI on other programming work. It explicitly allows AI as a tutor, as tech support and for explaining error messages, and treats unpermitted ChatGPT use as an academic-integrity breach.

title: COMP2401 A/B/C Fall 2026 Introduction to Systems Programming
analyst_summary: Systems-programming outline with rules that vary by assessment type. On assignments and exercises AI may be used for concepts and small code snippets, must be cited, and may not be given the spec; tests and the final project ban it, and resubmission changelogs cannot be AI-generated. A separate section lists ethical concerns (energy, data, IP, equity, labour) and gives tips for using AI to support learning.

unit: Machine Learning Department (School of Computer Science)
title: Introduction to Machine Learning | 10-301 + 10-601 | Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Each homework has two submissions. Slot A is human work only, with no AI (including AI-enabled IDEs and code agents). Slot B, opened after Slot A feedback, allows AI and full collaboration, but only to fix questions missed in Slot A. AI is banned in coding labs, and passing AI-assisted work off as Slot A work is an academic integrity violation that can mean failing the course.

unit: Machine Learning Department (School of Computer Science)
title: 10-315, Spring 2025
analyst_summary: The 'AI Assistance' policy asks students to complete all graded work without generative AI, so that the learning is their own, and to avoid producing any AI content for assessments. Passing off or paraphrasing AI output counts as a CMU academic integrity violation, and course-policy violations carry a -100% score on the affected work.

course: 15-112 Fundamentals of Programming and Computer Science
title: 15-112: Fundamentals of Programming - Syllabus (AI Policy)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that allows and encourages AI on preps, homework, labs and projects but forbids all AI on comps, quizzes and exams. Credit depends on earnest effort and on understanding and explaining any submitted code; citations of AI collaboration are not required up front but may be requested, and staff may respond to irresponsible AI use with warnings or deductions.

title: CS 15-122: Principles of Imperative Computation (Fall 2026)
analyst_summary: Course page requiring students to disable AI extensions and not use AI tools for any submitted work, including explaining tasks, formatting, commenting or generating tests. Referring to ChatGPT or other AI for solutions is forbidden even to double-check, use on assignments is reported as an integrity violation, and MOSS is used to detect plagiarism.

unit: Heinz College of Information Systems and Public Policy
title: 95-865: Unstructured Data Analytics
analyst_summary: A short note on the course page treats GenAI tools as external collaborators that may be used on homework if cited. Exams are electronics-free so students show their own understanding, which the instructor links to being able to judge AI-provided analyses in future work.

unit: Office of the Provost (AI Task Force)
title: Example AI Policies, Suitable for Course Syllabi
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost page offering four sample syllabus policies drafted by the university AI Task Force, ranging from no AI use through restricted, encouraged, and unrestricted use. It frames the samples as starting points that respect faculty academic freedom while signalling that CWRU embraces AI in education.

unit: Office of Curriculum and Instructional Support
title: Sample Statements for Teaching Syllabi
analyst_summary: CMU's official sample syllabus statements include an AI-referencing academic integrity statement and an 'Artificial intelligence-generated materials' statement. Submitting AI-generated work as one's own is prohibited, and where a course allows AI, the instructor provides guidance and citation methods, including for code. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Office of the Provost (Provost's Taskforce on Syllabus Policy Guidelines for AI Tools)
title: Chapman Considerations for Syllabus Policy on the Use of AI Generative Tools
analyst_summary: Provost taskforce guide that lets instructors set their own AI syllabus statement within a university position and ties AI use to the Academic Integrity Committee. It offers sample statements by permission level (broad use, some use with permission, no use) and cautions against choosing a no-use position. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

course: CS 110A (Introduction to Programming and Computer Science)
title: Introduction to Programming and Computer Science CS 110A
analyst_summary: Community-college intro programming syllabus whose academic honesty section counts submitting work written by AI as cheating and requires all submitted code to be the student's own. AI is addressed only inside the general cheating definition (borderline inclusion).

unit: Claremont Graduate University (MyCGU AI guidance; Office of Information Technology)
title: Guidance for Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the application of AI to CGU
analyst_summary: Institution-wide AI guidance page stating six guiding principles (people at the center, accessibility, digital literacy, AI enhancing teaching and learning, lifelong learning, responsible R&D). It announces a ChatGPT EDU license and permits free AI tools when used within CGU data-privacy policies; it contains no course-level rules. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Clark Atlanta University (official sample syllabus template)
title: Clark Atlanta University Sample Syllabus Template
analyst_summary: CAU's sample syllabus template includes a required 'Use of Artificial Intelligence' section that tells faculty to consult the university's AI guidelines and state their own AI-use expectations, alongside the general academic integrity statement. The template does not itself set substantive AI rules. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Syllabus, Intro to Societal Computing (CSCI 103)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus whose academic-integrity section counts using AI systems to answer writing assignments as plagiarism, while allowing AI help on programming assignments as long as it supports learning. It warns that AI will not be available on exams and that assignments are run through plagiarism detection. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: The AI Lab Notebook (Clarkson Documentation Library) / Faculty Senate
title: AI Course Policies
analyst_summary: Short internal documentation page advising instructors to include a paragraph on student AI use in their syllabi, and quoting the institutional syllabus template's note that the Faculty Senate recommended (but did not mandate) syllabus AI statements from Fall 2023. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Division of Undergraduate Learning (Undergraduate Academic Processes Team)
title: Guidance: Addressing Artificial Intelligence and Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Undergraduate academic-integrity office guidance for instructors. It notes that a course AI policy is a required syllabus component, recommends communicating and repeating expectations, designing AI-resistant or AI-integrated assessments (process work, oral defense, proctored work), and reducing pressures to cheat; for suspected misuse it explains that AI detector results alone cannot support a charge and suggests other evidence and a constructive conversation.

unit: Center for Faculty Excellence (AI Faculty Learning Community)
title: Example Policy Statements for AI in Higher Education
analyst_summary: A chapter of Cleveland State's Teaching and Learning open book, linked from the university AI hub, collecting AI syllabus statements written by faculty learning community members. It frames AI policy as set by instructors, departments and programs; sample statements require acknowledging and citing AI use, permit limited uses, warn about accuracy, and one lab-based statement requires students to write their own code. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: CS 151 Fall 2026 (course website, Generative AI section)
analyst_summary: AI-generated code or text may never be submitted and running Copilot counts as dishonesty, but other AI assistance is discouraged rather than banned, with a mandatory AI usage statement (including prompts and a reflection) in every project report and verification of AI answers as the student's responsibility.

unit: AI at Colgate (Office of the Provost and Dean of the Faculty, with CLTR and ITS)
title: Teaching and AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Colgate's official 'Teaching and AI' page. It leaves the role of AI in teaching to each faculty member, asks instructors to state clearly in the syllabus and in class whether and how students may use generative AI, links a CLTR sample syllabus statement and the Academic Honor Code, and warns against entering confidential data into AI tools.

title: CSCI-561: Theory of Computation (Theory)
analyst_summary: Graduate theory syllabus that applies the CS collaboration policy to GenAI: allowed as a resource (explanations, practice problems, grammar, translation) and banned for producing graded solutions. Any AI content must be cited. An appendix covers transparency and accountability and states how the instructor will and will not use AI, including protecting student data.

title: Computer Vision — Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Cross-listed computer vision syllabus that allows generative AI outside class but bans it during in-class coding sessions and exams. It points to the Provost's encouragement to explore generative AI.

title: Syllabus – CS-152
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that bans AI tools for writing or improving code or prose at any stage and treats AI-written work as plagiarism. It gives learning-based reasons, including in-person exams without the tools and the value of expertise before using AI. Misconduct earns a negative assignment score or an F for exam misconduct.

course: CS 220 Discrete Structures and their Applications
title: Syllabus – CS-220
analyst_summary: Discrete-structures syllabus that tells students to treat AI assistants like a person outside the class. AI may be used to understand lecture and book content but not to get homework solutions or hints, and exams allow no AI.

title: Syllabus, Activities and Policies – CS-312
analyst_summary: Web-development course policy that forbids generative AI on graded work unless explicitly allowed. It names AI coding assistants (ChatGPT, Grok, Copilot including the VS Code add-on) as misconduct, with an F and a misconduct report as the penalty. Suspected cases go through an investigation in which the student can present evidence.

title: W4111 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Database course syllabus requiring citation of anything not written by the student, including GenAI. LLMs are not permitted on homework by default, but GenAI may be used for designated project parts provided students document the AI-derived code and the prompts and edits involved.

title: Syllabus - CPSC 1302K Section 01
analyst_summary: A CS2 syllabus at a regional public university that lists learning-support uses of AI (brainstorming, studying, explaining examples, understanding compiler errors) as acceptable, with a templated disclosure statement for graded work. It forbids using AI for solution generation or pasting assignment, quiz or exam instructions into AI, and states that projects matching AI output earn zero points and may be reported.

title: Guidelines for Teaching with Generative Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Concordia's teaching centre guidelines ask every instructor to state a GenAI position in the syllabus and discuss it in class, and supply sample statements for encouraged, limited and prohibited use (several mention coding assistants and computer code). They recommend documentation by appendix, reflection or citation, instructor transparency statements, privacy safeguards, and note that AI detectors are not permitted at Concordia.

title: Instructor Guide to Generative AI & Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Institution-wide instructor guide linking generative AI to academic integrity. It asks instructors to state a course AI position, recommending the AI Assessment Scale. It warns that AI detectors are unreliable and gives FAQ advice on instructors using AI for grading, including privacy of student work and instructor accountability.

unit: Department of Computer Science (Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science)
course: CS 1110 Introduction to Computing using Python
title: Academic Integrity Policy
analyst_summary: Intro course integrity policy built on one principle: do not submit others' work (including AI output) as your own without disclosure. Assignments may not receive AI aid, but disclosed outside help is graded down rather than treated as a violation; AI is allowed for non-submitted practice, discussion sections are a no-AI zone, phones are banned in exams, and the course promises not to use AI detectors.

unit: Department of Information Science (Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science)
title: INFO 2950 – Syllabus
analyst_summary: Citing Cornell's report on generative AI in education, the syllabus allows GAI as a reference tool, much like documentation or a web search. It bars using GAI to complete substantive parts of assignments (for example, uploading data and having it build charts or models) and, unless instructed otherwise, to write narrative. Students remain responsible for submitted work.

unit: Department of Information Science (Cornell Ann S. Bowers College of Computing and Information Science)
course: INFO 5001 (Fundamental Programming for Data Science, graduate)
title: INFO 5001 – Syllabus
analyst_summary: The graduate version of the same instructor's policy is more permissive about code: students may use GAI to help write code, but any use beyond reference requires a written self-reflection, and all GenAI-produced work must be described and attributed. The instructor provides a course AI assistant, says AI use is not policed (in-person assessments catch over-reliance), reserves the right to oral checks with up to 100% penalties, and keeps the ban on AI-written narrative.

unit: Office of the Provost / Center for Teaching Innovation (CU Committee on Generative AI in Education)
title: CU Committee Report: Generative Artificial Intelligence for Education and Pedagogy
analyst_summary: University committee report proposing that instructors choose among three policy levels (prohibit, allow with attribution, encourage) for courses or individual assignments. It includes a dedicated section on courses in programming that recommends AI as a tutor or helper in advanced courses but not as sole code author, and it covers detection limits, attribution and equity of access.

unit: Office of the General Counsel / University Policies (Academic Misconduct Policy 4.1.7)
title: Policies and Procedures — POLICY: Academic Misconduct Policy
analyst_summary: Creighton's university academic misconduct policy lists unauthorized use of artificial intelligence as a form of cheating, alongside unapproved collaboration and unauthorized materials. Violations are handled by the school or college, with suspension or dismissal possible and appealable to the Provost. This is the only official university AI rule that could be retrieved; no public CS or provost AI guidance page was found. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Faculty of Computer Science (statement reproduced in the Centre for Learning and Teaching GenAI book)
title: Classroom Policies and Syllabus Statements: Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools (CSCI4177 Advanced Web Services and CSCI5709 Advanced Topics in Web Development)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus statement from two Dalhousie computer science web-development courses, published as an exemplar in the Centre for Learning and Teaching's GenAI book. AI tools may support learning, but some assessments forbid them; allowed use must be acknowledged with chat logs, and a README template asks students to record the tool, prompt, generated code and how it was modified.

course: CS 10 Problem Solving via Object-Oriented Programming
title: CS 10 | Problem solving | Fall 2025
analyst_summary: Course page with a 'special note' on AI code generators: using them to create or debug assignment solutions is not an honor-code violation, but the instructor urges students to write code themselves because exams are tool-free. Users must cite the tool and prompts per function, be able to explain every line, not share prompts or outputs, and be aware of privacy risks; submissions carry a sources/disclosure statement.

unit: Technology & Innovation / Vice President for Academic Affairs
title: Artificial Intelligence Policy
analyst_summary: Tier 4. College-wide AI policy covering recording/wearable AI tools, which data classifications may be entered into which AI platforms, academic uses and procurement. For courses, faculty set AI rules course by course, are urged to put an AI statement on the syllabus, and violations go through the academic integrity/Honor Council process.

unit: Academic Senate (published on college Rules and Policies page)
title: Academic Integrity: Use of Artificial Intelligence
date_or_term: Adopted by the Academic Senate March 17, 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4. De Anza's college academic integrity page includes a short Academic Senate statement on AI: students follow any course-specific AI policy, otherwise use AI consistently with the district student conduct standards so that submitted work reflects their own knowledge and skills, and ask the instructor when unsure. Text was captured from an Internet Archive snapshot because the live site blocks automated access.

unit: Jarvis College of Computing and Digital Media (School of Computing)
title: Course Syllabus: Database Systems (CSC 355 - 602), Spring 2023-2024
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Public CDM syllabus for a computing database course. Its academic-integrity section lists submitting chatbot, generative-AI or code-generator solutions, even after modification, as plagiarism, treats such output as another person's work, and warns of penalties up to an automatic F.

unit: College of Computing & Informatics, Department of Computer Science
title: CS 172 - Department of Computer Science - Drexel University
analyst_summary: Second-term programming course page. It requires students to turn off IDE code completion, and all graded code must be written without AI help. Using LLM services such as ChatGPT, Copilot or DeepSeek to write or debug solutions is listed as academic dishonesty.

unit: College of Computing & Informatics, Department of Computer Science
title: Computer Graphics Class Page (Fall 2025)
analyst_summary: Computer graphics course page whose academic honesty section bans generative tools for producing programs. Using them for any part of an assignment is listed as unacceptable. Honesty violations lead to an F in the course.

title: SE310 - Software Design Fall 2026 Drexel University
analyst_summary: Software design syllabus with a section on AI and code generation tools. Using ChatGPT, Copilot or similar tools for any part of graded work is prohibited unless the instructor explicitly allows it. Unauthorized use counts as a violation of the University's Academic Integrity Policy.

title: CompSci 101, Fall 2026, Syllabus (Can I use AI (LLMs) in this course?)
analyst_summary: Intro Python course FAQ-style statement that bars using LLMs to solve problems or write code, justified by the need to practice problem solving in a beginning course, while allowing informational questions about syntax and concepts.

title: Syllabus for Compsci 201, Fall 2026 (Collaboration, LLMs, Behavior, and More)
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that lists using LLMs to explore algorithms as a learning objective and encourages LLMs for understanding, but not for assignment-specific code, and asks students to note LLM use in a README. All AI is banned on in-class exams and APT quizzes, with similarity checks against LLM-generated solutions, possible screen recording, and grade penalties; students are asked to disable Copilot.

unit: Office of the Provost (with the faculty Artificial Intelligence Committee)
title: Artificial Intelligence at Duquesne
analyst_summary: Provost guidance for faculty and students on AI. Faculty should write course AI policies that align with school/department policies, disclose their own AI use, avoid unapproved AI in grading and treat detectors cautiously; the page offers open, moderate and restrictive syllabus templates plus a detailed AI citation prompt. Students follow course syllabi, use AI to support rather than replace learning, cite AI use and remain responsible for accuracy. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office for Faculty Excellence / ECU Libraries (Generative AI in the Classroom & Research LibGuide)
title: Generative AI in the Classroom & Research: Classroom Best Practices
analyst_summary: ECU's recommended syllabus language for generative AI (the Office for Faculty Excellence points instructors to this LibGuide). It affirms faculty discretion under academic freedom, ties prohibited AI use and uncited AI use to the academic integrity policy, and offers three adaptable syllabus scenarios: use prohibited, use only with prior permission, and use with acknowledgement. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: ETSU Board of Trustees (Academic, Research, and Student Success Committee)
title: Use of Artificial Intelligence Technologies for Instructional and Assignment Purposes
analyst_summary: Board policy covering faculty, staff and student use of AI for instruction and assignments. It bans AI-based fabrication or falsification, lets departments or instructors set written course policies, and lists user duties such as disclosure, accuracy checking, bias awareness, no malicious code and no confidential data. It also requires de-identifying student data when AI is used for grading and routes violations to academic misconduct or HR discipline. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Information Systems
title: Syllabus AI 500.1W Foundations of Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Graduate introductory AI course syllabus that rewrites the university's boilerplate AI statement to cover code generation and bans any use of AI chatbots or code generators as plagiarism; programming assignments are to be done individually. The AI provision is brief. Tier 1 (CS department course; the AI program sits in the CS & Information Systems department).

unit: Macon & Joan Brock Virginia Health Sciences at Old Dominion University
title: Brock Virginia Health Sciences AI Guidelines
analyst_summary: Landing page for the AI guidelines of the former EVMS (now Brock Virginia Health Sciences at ODU). It sets a stance of responsible integration under ODU's Board of Visitors AI policy and introduces role-specific guidance for faculty, medical students and others; the role pages themselves were not retrievable. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Embry-Riddle Student Code of Conduct (published on the Worldwide campus student handbook page)
title: Student Code of Conduct — Academic Integrity: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
analyst_summary: Embry-Riddle's Student Code of Conduct treats AI use that breaks university, program, course or instructor requirements as an academic integrity violation, while encouraging AI fluency. Students may use AI to support learning, including practising coding, when consistent with course rules, must verify outputs, and must follow course disclosure and labelling expectations. The page is hosted on the Worldwide site but is written as university-wide policy; no Daytona Beach CS/SE-specific AI policy was found. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Emory College of Arts and Sciences (Academic Affairs and Faculty Partnerships)
title: Emory College Syllabus Additions (Artificial Intelligence statement)
analyst_summary: Tier 3. Required syllabus additions for Emory College courses, which include computer science. Instructors decide whether students may use AI and must say so in the syllabus. Honor Council model language for courses that ban AI treats AI-generated content as plagiarism and unpermitted use as unauthorized assistance, with suspected cases reported to the Honor Council.

unit: Department of Computer and Information Sciences
title: COP 3014C C01 Fundamentals of Programming (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for FAMU's intro programming course (instructors Edward Jones and Michael Parrish). Its AI Policy treats AI as an assistive professional tool, requires it for some assignments, and lists appropriate uses (brainstorming, grammar, debugging help when noted) and inappropriate ones (whole coding solutions, unedited output). Students must acknowledge and describe any AI use and be able to explain their work; undisclosed AI-generated work counts as plagiarism under a graduated penalty scheme. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Department of Computer and Information Sciences
title: COP 3014C C04 Fundamentals of Programming (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Another Fall 2026 section of FAMU's intro programming course (instructors Idongesit Mkpong-Ruffin and Michael Parrish). Under 'College/School Policies and Standards' it limits AI to assistive tasks such as brainstorming and grammar, forbids using it for coding or other core programming work, requires disclosure, and says the instructor will monitor AI use. An allowed/prohibited table permits concept learning, explaining compiler errors and proofreading code, but bars generating project code or test cases and any AI use during exams. The same AI text appears in other FAMU programming sections, suggesting a shared standard. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: AI @ FAU (university AI hub; Faculty AI Hub)
title: AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: University-wide syllabus preamble stating that AI use is not allowed unless an instructor explicitly permits it for a specific assignment, with citation required when permitted and violations tied to the academic integrity regulation. It also offers faculty three short syllabus options (encouraged, flexible, prohibited) and asks faculty to state tolerance and penalties per assignment. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Responsible Use of Generative AI in Academic Work
analyst_summary: Provost guideline for students and instructors: AI use without instructor approval is an integrity violation, permitted use must be disclosed, and instructors must include a GenAI syllabus statement. Provides open, restricted and prohibited sample statements plus task-specific disclosure templates, including one for code generation. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Knight Foundation School of Computing and Information Sciences
title: CAP 4104 Human-Computer Interaction (course syllabus, AI-Assisted Interface Evaluation and Redesign assignment)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. School-hosted master syllabus for FIU's HCI course. Its sample assessment has students deliberately use generative AI for heuristic evaluation and redesign ideas, while keeping responsibility for analysis and final design, documenting how and why they used AI, and reflecting on its limits and biases; the rubric penalises unvalidated AI output.

course: COP 3330 Data Structures, Algorithms, and Generic Programming I
title: COP 3330 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Course syllabus whose honor-policy section lists inappropriate behaviours, including using AI tools such as ChatGPT to write assignment code, alongside bans on solution sites and code sharing. All work is individual and MOSS is used in grading.

unit: Office of the Provost (AI Vision Committee)
title: Policies and Principles on Using Generative AI Tools in Education
analyst_summary: Provost-commissioned committee proposal (co-chaired by a CIS professor) setting out Fordham's principles for generative AI in teaching. It supplies No-AI, Limited-AI and Full-AI syllabus statements requiring students to mark AI-generated sections and record prompts and software versions, suggests assignment and assessment designs (oral presentations, in-class work, prompt submission), warns that detectors are imperfect and may flag non-native writers, and asks faculty to include an explicit AI statement and revisit learning goals. It notes AI's role in creating and debugging programs. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Honor Code | Department of Computer Science
date_or_term: Wayback snapshot 2026-01-24 (live URL compsci.sitemasonry.gmu.edu no longer resolves)
analyst_summary: The CS department's supplemental honor code, applying to all work in CS-major courses, adds to a list of default prohibitions the use of AI or other tools that generate, translate or correct code or answers unless the instructor grants permission. It frames instructor permission as course- and assignment-specific and places the burden on students to ask when unsure. Text was captured from an archived copy because the department site moved.

unit: Department of Computer Science (School of Engineering and Applied Science)
title: GWU CSCI 1012 - Collaboration Policy (Introduction to Python Programming)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Collaboration policy for GW's introductory Python course. Students must write homework solutions themselves; copying code from AI tools and using AI for anything are listed among always-prohibited behaviours, students are told to switch off AI in web searches, and getting unstuck is routed to TAs and the professor.

unit: Department of Computer Science (School of Engineering and Applied Science)
title: CSCI 2113 Spring 2026 (Software Engineering) course syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course site for GW's second-year software development course. Its academic honesty list forbids using any LLM to generate code or code skeletons and bars LLM use for any other purpose in the course, with penalties up to failing the course.

title: COSC-3450: Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: AI course page that allows generative AI (ChatGPT, Bard, Copilot) on homeworks and projects for this offering. Students must follow tool terms and the university acceptable-use policy and submit a link or transcript, so tools without transcripts are barred. The general can/cannot list of allowed help includes generative AI under these conditions.

unit: School of Computer Science, College of Computing
title: CS1301 Syllabus (Artificial Intelligence Policy)
analyst_summary: Intro CS syllabus that allows AI for brainstorming and clarifying concepts but treats submitting AI-generated content as misconduct. It gives practical guidelines: no copy-paste, keep AI sessions separate from working on the assignment, and avoid in-editor code-generating assistants.

unit: School of Computer Science, College of Computing
title: CS 1331 - Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming, Fall 2026 (Musaev sections A/B/G/R)
analyst_summary: Section syllabus for the second programming course that bans ChatGPT and other AI and code-generation tools on all graded work. AI-influenced submissions receive a zero and a referral to the Office of Student Integrity, and TAs may screen submissions for AI use.

unit: School of Computer Science, College of Computing
title: CS 1331 Syllabus, Objects and Design, Section C/FAC, Fall 2026: Collaboration, Group Work, and Use of Generative AI
analyst_summary: Another CS 1331 section that does not permit generative AI for completing assignments and equates it to plagiarism, while acknowledging AI as useful for self-testing, practice problems, and documentation search. It frames homework as low-stakes learning and moves individual assessment to in-class exams.

unit: School of Interactive Computing (Online MS in Computer Science)
title: OMS CS7637 | Knowledge-Based AI — Summer 2024
analyst_summary: KBAI's 'AI Collaboration Policy' applies the course's human-collaboration rules to AI. Students may consult AI the way they would consult classmates, but may not copy AI output into their work or keep AI integrated in their editors and IDEs (anything beyond a grammar checker). A FAQ on the same page gives practical heuristics: never copy from the AI conversation, and don't have the AI and the assignment open at once. This is the most recent term posted on the public course site.

unit: Office of the Provost and Executive Vice-President for Academic Affairs
title: Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Academic Contexts
analyst_summary: University policy (implementing USG BOR Policy 6.28) leaving AI use to faculty but requiring every syllabus to carry an AI statement that defines AI, sets forbidden/restricted/permitted uses per activity, and states citation expectations, any process-tracking or detection tools (it names CodeGrade and Codio among them) and consequences. Students must complete AI training, follow course rules and disclose AI help; unpermitted or unattributed AI content is plagiarism and agentic completion of assessments is cheating; faculty may assess work only with approved tools and should tell students. Verbatim text taken from a September 2026 Wayback snapshot because the Digital Commons PDF is bot-protected. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Information Systems, Robinson College of Business
title: Memorandum of Understanding: Artificial Intelligence Course Usage Guidelines (CIS 3001 Managing IT Projects)
analyst_summary: Tier 2. Class AI agreement for an IT project management course in GSU's Computer Information Systems department, co-written with students in the first class meeting and linked from a CETLOE teaching blog post. It lists encouraged uses (study aids, explanations, brainstorming, planning), prohibited uses (AI on exams, graded homework answers, passing off AI work, AI-done group work), what AI use must be documented, and the penalties for violations.

unit: Instructional Design and Delivery (AI in Higher Education site)
title: AI Guides and Resources for Students: Asking the Right Questions: A Student Guide to Responsible AI Use in College
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Gonzaga's university student guide to AI use. It stresses that each instructor sets AI expectations for their course, tells students not to assume any AI use is acceptable and to ask the instructor, lists questions to clarify allowed uses (writing, studying for exams, disclosure), and frames responsible use around learning rather than replacing it. Captured from an Internet Archive snapshot because the live site blocks automated access.

title: CSC 151 (Fall 2026) - Functional Problem Solving: Syllabus
analyst_summary: The intro course bans AI programming assistants, discourages AI writing assistants, and asks students to avoid web search, while requiring citation of any of these if used anyway (noting the apparent paradox is driven by college citation expectations). It also asks students to disable AI summaries in web search.

title: CSC-151 (Functional Problem Solving, Fall 2025): Syllabus
analyst_summary: A different section of the same intro course takes a permissive-but-discouraged approach: outside resources including generative AI are allowed but 'not recommended', and any GenAI use for code or text must be cited with the model, exact prompt, and exact output. Quizzes are individual and in class.

unit: Direction de l’apprentissage et de l’innovation pédagogique (DAIP)
title: Intelligence artificielle générative en contexte d’évaluation
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): Teaching-centre guidance stating that instructors decide, assessment by assessment, whether generative AI is allowed, using standardized permission labels selected in ZoneCours, with unauthorized use sanctionable under the student integrity regulation. It also offers assessment-design options (oral, authentic, triangulation), notes detectors are unreliable, and suggests requiring prompts. No computing-specific (TI / data science) AI document was public, so this is the institution-wide fallback.

title: ChatGPT/Artificial Intelligence Task Force Midyear Report (Directing the Ethical Landscape)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Midyear slide report from Hampton's university AI task force, the only published university-level AI guidance found. It recommends against banning GenAI, proposes integrity training and a Code of Conduct addendum treating AI substitution for a student's own work as plagiarism, aims further AI policy at instructors and assessment redesign, and lets each department set GenAI policy with its Dean's approval. These are recommendations, not adopted policy.

unit: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (Computer Science)
course: CS 61 Systems Programming and Machine Organization
title: Course Description – CS 61
analyst_summary: Systems programming course description. Students may ask generative AI tools questions during problem sets, but they must understand and explain their code, may be quizzed orally, and must disclose AI use with transcripts. Because AI is allowed on psets, grading leans on exams, and AI is banned during tests.

unit: John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences (Computer Science)
title: Syllabus - CS50 (Academic Honesty)
analyst_summary: The CS50 syllabus frames academic honesty as 'be reasonable' and lists reasonable and unreasonable acts. The course's own AI tool (the CS50 Duck) is allowed and even used for graded completion quizzes, while other AI software that suggests or completes answers or code is not reasonable; a regret clause lets students self-report within 72 hours.

course: CS 70: Data Structures and Program Development
title: Course Syllabus - CS 70 (AI Usage Policy)
analyst_summary: CS 70 treats AI like a friend who already took the course: conceptual explanations and help interpreting compiler/runtime errors are allowed, but code generation (including autocomplete), use on take-home exams, and uncited use are prohibited. The course switched to an editor without AI completion and even supplies a suggested tutoring-style prompt for debugging help.

unit: Harvey Mudd College (faculty pilot; authors listed in the document)
title: Pilot Program: HMC AI-Use Course Policies (DRAFT)
analyst_summary: College-wide pilot syllabus language defining four AI Use Levels (0: no AI; 1: time-saving only; 2: augmentative only; 3: open use), applied per course or per assignment, with tips for instructors. Included as an influential source document: Pomona College's CS AI Policy Tier System is modeled on it. Added by PI decision on 2026-10-05.

title: Haverford CMSC H360 Machine Learning (Spring 2024)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course site for Haverford's machine learning course. Code generation tools such as GitHub Copilot are banned for regular assignments because generated code is often poorly understood and breaks in context, but are allowed on the final project with a required reflection; help from permitted sources must be documented in comments.

title: Resources for Generative AI in Teaching and Learning
analyst_summary: Provost EdTech page giving faculty background on generative AI, stating that student use must follow the instructor's course policy, and listing assessment-redesign ideas from Hofstra faculty, including having students evaluate AI-produced code. It links to separate syllabus-wording pages (prohibited, with acknowledgement, with permission and acknowledgement). Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Policy 100-022: Howard University Artificial Intelligence (AI)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Howard's formal university-wide AI policy, owned by the Provost. It sets general rules (accountability for verifying outputs, context-appropriate disclosure, no confidential data in AI tools) and a teaching-and-learning section requiring faculty to state permissible and impermissible AI use in syllabi, students to follow course rules and ask when guidance is absent, and AI use to respect integrity, accessibility and privacy. It is to be reviewed annually.

title: Best Practice Suggestions
analyst_summary: Idaho State's Academic Integrity Center gives faculty best practices on plagiarism, cheating and AI. It leaves AI permission to individual instructors, asks for a syllabus AI statement discussed in the first week that is specific per assignment type, and suggests talking with students about AI, teaching ethical use, staged assignments and planning for misuse. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Syllabus & Overview CS 442: Mobile App Development
analyst_summary: The honor-code slide warns against using Copilot or ChatGPT to blindly generate most of the code. It calls AI assistants useful as long as students understand the generated code, and the instructor models AI-assisted coding in demos. Suspected plagiarism or heavy AI use leads to a code review where students must explain their code.

title: CS536: Science of Programming, Fall 2023
analyst_summary: A graduate course that bans generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for homework and exams, penalizing violations with a zero and a report. A dedicated note explains why: language models lack a model of formal logic, and students must learn proofs themselves before they can check tool output.

title: Generative AI in the Classroom
analyst_summary: Teaching-center guide for Illinois State instructors. It says the existing academic integrity policy already covers unauthorized AI use (explicitly including using AI to develop code), advises against AI detectors without student consent, and offers assignment designs that either discourage or integrate AI-generated content. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

title: Policies and Guidance: Generative AI
analyst_summary: IU-wide teaching resource noting the university has no specific generative AI policy beyond data security, and offering least- and most-restrictive sample syllabus statements. It also advises instructors to repeat AI policies on assignments and to favour an ethics of practice over bans. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Types of Violations
analyst_summary: Academic Affairs list of academic integrity violation types. It states that plagiarism covers AI-generated sources and adds a specific violation for AI-generated work that is not authorized by the instructor. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of Student Conduct (Dean of Students Office)
title: Know the Code Resources: Faculty and Staff (Artificial Intelligence section)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Academic-integrity guidance for instructors from ISU's Office of Student Conduct. It says AI may be permitted, restricted or prohibited by course and asks instructors to state expectations in syllabi and assignment instructions. It frames misconduct as use that violates course expectations, warns against relying on AI-detection tools alone, and suggests assessment designs that show the student's process.

unit: THEE Pathway (General Education) common syllabus links
title: Common Syllabus Links for Students: AI Policy
analyst_summary: Tier 4. JSU's common syllabus AI policy for students. With instructor approval it allows AI for listed tasks such as brainstorming, outlining, summarizing and revising, but no graded work may be fully AI-generated. Such work can receive a zero, all use must be cited, departments may add their own criteria, and protected personal data must not be entered into AI tools.

title: Syllabus - CS 149 Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that makes learning to use AI in support of understanding a course-wide goal. AI is encouraged as a study aid outside class and is strictly banned on quizzes and exams. Students must be able to explain and defend all project code.

title: Data Structures And Algorithms: Syllabus
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that forbids AI code generators for labs and programming assignments, explaining that they short-circuit the learning goals. AI may not generate solutions or hints. It may be used to understand concepts. Quizzes allow no AI.

title: CS 470 - Syllabus
analyst_summary: Parallel and distributed systems syllabus that allows AI code-generation tools such as GitHub Copilot on labs and projects. Every project needs an 'AI-Assist Statement', including when no AI was used. The policy is labeled experimental, and changes will be announced at least 72 hours before deadlines.

unit: Department of Computer Science (Whiting School of Engineering)
title: EN.601.220: Syllabus
analyst_summary: Intermediate programming syllabus permitting limited AI assistance on homework (snippets, not whole solutions) with inline begin/end comments marking AI-derived code and a ten-line cap per collaborative segment. Students bear full responsibility for reviewing, testing and explaining AI-generated code; generating full solutions or uncritical reliance on AI output is penalized.

title: Fall 2026 Info :: CIS 598 Textbook
analyst_summary: A stoplight policy labels each assignment RED (no GenAI), YELLOW (limited use, cited, no direct pasting of output) or GREEN (unlimited use, cited). Each level comes with citation rules, an 'understand your work' clause and honor-code sanctions. A companion disclosure applies the same scale to instructors: GenAI is never used for grades or student communication, and only in limited ways for code-review feedback and course content. The page notes that official syllabi are in Coursedog.

unit: Office of Academic Affairs (Instructional Faculty Academic Policy Manual; Academic Integrity Policy)
title: Kean University Instructional Faculty Academic Policy Manual and Resource Guide, Fall 2025: Expectations of Generative AI
date_or_term: Fall 2025 (quotes Academic Integrity Policy, Fall 2024 revision)
analyst_summary: Faculty manual section reproducing Kean's academic integrity rules for generative AI: instructors set course-level AI rules in the syllabus, while university-wide rules require originality, citation of permitted AI use, and student accountability for accuracy. It lists evidence faculty may use (comparisons, Canvas AI detectors, oral demonstration), integrity consequences, and principles for deciding how much AI to allow, including disclosure and a cautious, experimental start. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: College of Computing and Software Engineering (CCSE), First Year Experience
title: CCSE FYE Policies
analyst_summary: College-level policies for the first-year programming sequence at a large regional public university, stating that all submitted labs, assignments, quizzes and tests must be written without AI. AI-aided completion is listed alongside other forms of academic misconduct, and the standard exam rules read at the start of each test forbid AI, with penalties up to an F and referral to student conduct.

unit: University Policy Register (Office of General Counsel / Provost)
title: 3 - 01.8 Administrative policy regarding student cheating and plagiarism
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Kent State's official academic-integrity rule, revised to name generative AI. Using GAI on exams or to produce coursework counts as cheating unless the instructor expressly allows it in the syllabus or assignment, and presenting GAI-produced ideas or words as one's own counts as plagiarism. Autocomplete and grammar tools are excluded from the GAI definition, and the rule lists sanctions from a zero on the work to an F in the course.

title: Constructive Uses of Generative AI at KPU: A Student Guide
analyst_summary: Tier 4: A three-page student guide that defers course-level rules to each instructor's syllabus and sets cross-cutting expectations on original work, citation, copyright of course materials, privacy, and social and environmental impact. It then gives advice for when AI is allowed (verify output, ask for guidance rather than answers, document prompts) and restates KPU's rule that personal study use is not a breach if outputs are not submitted or used in exams.

title: CS150 Data Structures and Algorithms (Fall 2023)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course page for Lafayette's required data structures course (instructor Jia Tao). Its academic integrity section bans AI and machine-learning tools such as ChatGPT on assignments, treats prohibited AI use as plagiarism, and asks students to check with the instructor when unsure. The live page now returns 404, so the Internet Archive capture from December 2023 is the source.

title: Can students use ChatGPT and other AI tools at Lakehead?
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Student-facing academic integrity FAQ with a stop-look-ask checklist. Whether AI is allowed depends on each instructor, and the page maps unauthorized use, unacknowledged use and passing off AI work as one's own to specific offences in the Academic Integrity Code. It also warns about fabricated sources, bias and harm to learning.

unit: Department of Computer Science, College of Arts and Sciences
title: UNIX/C++ > Syllabus
analyst_summary: C++/UNIX programming syllabus with an Academic Integrity, AI and Digital Tools section: generative AI and similar tools (including automated problem-solvers) are allowed only with explicit prior authorization per assignment. Permitted use must be disclosed, the university bars instructor use of AI detectors but students may be asked for evidence of their work, and violations carry academic penalties up to course failure. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: Artificial Intelligence at Lehigh (Provost / Library & Technology Services)
title: Policies and Best Practices
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Lehigh's university AI hub page restating existing policies that apply to generative AI. It focuses on data classification and approved tools, says students follow instructor course rules plus the Student Code of Conduct, asks users to check outputs and cite AI assistance, and advises instructors to give clear coursework guidance using the LU Syllabus Template.

title: Use of Artificial Intelligence Statement
analyst_summary: One-page Academic Affairs statement placing generative AI under existing university policies. Students are responsible for what they submit, must document AI use, face conduct procedures for unauthorized use, and should ask instructors when unsure. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Faculty Senate Generative AI Committee Guidelines on the Use of Generative AI in Curriculum
date_or_term: Endorsed by Faculty Senate on Dec 4, 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Senate-endorsed guidelines that set obligations, permitted and prohibited uses for both students and faculty, including a note that GAI can generate code and a ban on using GAI for malicious code. Every syllabus must say whether and how GAI may be used. Faculty may not use GAI to assign grades or feed student work into it without consent, and may not rely on detectors alone. The document ends with three syllabus options: prohibited, permitted with full disclosure and reflection, and permitted with specific limitations.

title: Academic Misconduct
analyst_summary: LSU New Orleans' student-conduct page on academic misconduct sets a campus default: any AI-generated content in coursework counts as academic misconduct unless the instructor authorizes it, and authorized use must be cited. Instructors must report suspected misconduct, and students are pointed to each syllabus for course expectations. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science (Seaver College of Science and Engineering)
title: CMSI 3300 Artificial Intelligence: Syllabus
analyst_summary: Course syllabus with a 'Generative AI and Your Learning' section that limits GenAI in programming assignments to specific learning-support uses (docstrings, syntax examples, error messages, unit tests, reviewing own code). It requires understanding every line, citing nontrivial agent-generated code for experienced students, and acknowledging chatbot help. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: Office of the Provost, Division of Academic Affairs
title: Statement on Academic Integrity and Use of Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Short provost statement making non-use the default: students may not use AI in graded work unless a faculty member authorizes it. Whether to allow GenAI is left to faculty, who must put their expectations in the syllabus, and the statement says the university will keep reviewing its approach.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Your Class: Recommended practices
