analyst_summary: Tier 4: Teaching-centre guide for instructors covering syllabus statements, assessment design, communicating with students, and academic misconduct. It defines when AI use is misconduct under the Student Academic Integrity Policy and discourages relying on AI detectors. It also addresses equity of access and alternative assessments for students who object to AI.

unit: Department of Mathematics, Statistics, and Computer Science
course: COMP 123: Core Concepts in Computer Science
title: COMP 123: Core Concepts in Computer Science, spring 2026 (syllabus)
analyst_summary: The intro course uses a weightlifting metaphor to argue that AI coding help removes the thinking that builds skill, and treats any AI-generated solution as a prohibited source, including AI features in the course IDE (PyCharm).

title: COSC 3250 Operating Systems — Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: OS syllabus that assumes students will use generative AI coding assistants on projects and requires listing them in each assignment's authorship comment block. Unattributed AI help is an integrity violation, and AI is not allowed on written or lab practical exams.

title: COSC 3410 Programming Languages — Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Programming languages syllabus with an 'Artificial Intelligence' section expecting many students to use LLMs for coding. It requires comment-block attribution of non-original passages, forbids presenting LLM output as one's own, and warns that relying on LLMs leaves students unprepared for exams.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Syllabus Guidance
analyst_summary: Academic Affairs requires every Marshall instructor to include a generative AI policy in the syllabus, leaving the degree of use to instructors' academic freedom while tying it to discipline and industry norms. A sample policy treats AI as a source to critique and cite, varies permission by assignment, and asks departments to supply sample assignments showing ethical, disclosed AI use. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
course: 6.100A Introduction to Computer Science Programming in Python
title: 6.100A Course Information (Course Policies for Fall 2025)
analyst_summary: Intro programming course policy that treats generative AI like any other collaborator: students may use it as a tutor to understand concepts and to discuss approaches, but may not have it generate code. Quizzes are in person with no Internet, code-similarity checks are run, and violations carry a zero and possible referral.

unit: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
title: Collaboration, Sharing, and AI Tools
analyst_summary: Collaboration page for an intermediate software-construction course, with a summary table that marks generative AI for writing text or code as forbidden. It bars code or text from code-authoring tools and chatbots and asks students to check with staff before using any code-generation tool.

unit: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
title: Syllabus | 6.110 Spring 2025
analyst_summary: Compiler-project course syllabus that explicitly allows and encourages LLM-generated code, stating it has no effect on grades. Teams must describe their LLM approach in project reports and complete an LLM code-usage survey after each phase.

course: COMP 480 Advanced algorithms, data structures, and techniques for competitive programming
title: McGill University School of Computer Science COMP 480 Course Outline - Draft
analyst_summary: Course outline for a competitive-programming course. It discourages AI tools, including generative AI, for assignments unless stated otherwise, and gives a learning rationale. Students remain accountable for their submissions, and any AI-produced content must be cited.

title: COMPSCI 2LC3 Logical Reasoning for Computer Science, Fall 2024 Outline
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course outline for a second-year logic course for CS students. It bans generative AI outright using McMaster's 'Use Prohibited' template, which treats AI-produced work as acquired from another source and as contract cheating, and adds the instructor's own explanation that assessments are meant to test understanding needed in later courses.

title: CS 2C03 Data Structures and Algorithms (Fall 2024)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course web outline for the second-year data structures and algorithms course. It states in the assignment rules that generative AI is strictly prohibited and repeats McMaster's 'Use Prohibited' template, which frames AI-generated work as contract cheating referred to the Office of Academic Integrity.

unit: Office of Educational Improvement, Faculty Development (Teaching Toolbox)
title: AI Digest | Teaching Toolbox
analyst_summary: MCW's faculty-development digest on AI in health sciences education. Beyond curated external resources, it summarizes MCW's April 2024 Guiding Principles for Responsible Use of AI, which apply to all faculty, staff and students: treat uncontracted tools as public, never enter protected data, verify and cite AI outputs, and keep human judgment central; program and course policies are expected to follow these principles. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Center for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning (CATL), Office of Education
title: MUSC AI Acceptable Use Framework for Academic Tasks
analyst_summary: MUSC's teaching-center page presenting its AI Acceptable Use Framework, approved by the Education Advisory Council, Student Affairs Advisory Council and Provost Council and embedded in the Plagiarism and AI Guideline. Instructors designate one of five categories (No AI, AI Planning, AI Limited, AI Extensive, AI Exploration) for each academic task, students must follow the category and provide any required documentation, and documentation such as AI logs is framed as a learning artifact rather than surveillance. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Centre for Innovation in Teaching and Learning (CITL)
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Tier 4. CITL resource giving instructors sample syllabus statements for generative AI, ranging from full prohibition through permission in some assessments or a specific assignment to permission throughout the course. The prohibition templates explicitly list computer code; permissive templates require citing AI and appending the prompt sequence. Instructors are told to check whether their unit has a standard statement.

title: Sample Syllabus and Assignment Guidance for AI Use
analyst_summary: Teaching-center guidance built on the Mercer AI Policy: faculty decide AI use, set a course baseline in the syllabus and restate rules per assignment using Red/Yellow/Green labels. It provides sample statements (including debugging student-written code as a limited use), a disclosure template, privacy and equity rules, and a warning that AI-detector scores are not proof of misconduct. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering
title: CSE Academic Integrity Guidelines
analyst_summary: Department integrity guidelines for problem-solving assignments (programming, math, proofs) stressing that students must build solutions independently. Lists acceptable and unacceptable behaviours: generative AI tools are acceptable only within limits the instructor sets for each assignment, and unapproved use is unacceptable. Tier 1 (CS department).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSE 231 Syllabus (Fall Semester, 2026)
analyst_summary: Intro Python syllabus that makes AI coding tools an opt-in choice for projects, available only after Project 4/Exam 1 and only for students working alone. Code is still plagiarism-checked, AI generation is not an excuse for similarity, staff will not help debug code students do not understand, and exams are taken unaided.

unit: Office of the Provost / Academic Affairs (AI Working Group)
title: Michigan Tech Syllabus Guidance
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Three tiered syllabus templates from Michigan Tech's AI Working Group: general permission, conditional permission for listed assignments, and prohibition. Templates require transparency about AI use, keep students responsible for AI-caused errors, and treat unauthorized use as cheating.

unit: Office of the University Provost (MTSU Policies)
title: 323 Instructional and Assignment Use of Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: MTSU's formal university policy on instructional and assignment use of AI. Faculty set course-level GAI rules in the syllabus; without explicit faculty permission GAI may not be used for any graded work; students must not outsource intended learning; permissions must be granted equitably; faculty may use GAI but not to build entire courses; confidential data may not be entered into training-retaining tools; violations fall under the academic misconduct policy. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

course: CSCI 1010 (Winter 2026; machine learning and generative AI)
title: CSCI1010 Winter 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: A hands-on ML/generative-AI course that permits and encourages AI use as a form of collaboration, provided students never copy solutions, can explain everything they submit, and attribute all AI contributions; mastery is checked through paper quizzes, an oral exam and oral project presentations without AI. Instructors disclose that parts of the course materials were AI-generated.

title: CSCI 201 (course website)
analyst_summary: Generative AI may only be used to learn theoretical concepts, never to write code or directly complete assignments; any theoretical question asked of an AI during labs/homework must be disclosed with tool, prompt and response, and AI is banned on exams.

title: Syllabus – CSCI 451: Machine Learning S26
analyst_summary: Rather than enumerating rules, the syllabus reviews research evidence that LLM answer-seeking can harm learning and self-assessment, then supports AI uses that build reasoning while discouraging outsourcing. Enforcement relies on assessments (quizzes, exams, oral exams) taken without external aids.

unit: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering
title: ECE 1013 Foundations in ECE Lecture and Lab, Starkville (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. First-year ECE course syllabus (MATLAB/Simulink and Arduino programming labs; corequisite CSE 1284) with an 'AI Policy: Permitted for Select Assignments' section. Generative AI is barred except where an assignment allows it, unauthorized use is an Honor Code matter, and all work is screened with Turnitin's AI detector. Where allowed, students must cite AI material (e.g., IEEE style), respect any allowed percentage, and add an acknowledgment statement.

university: Missouri University of Science and Technology
unit: Teaching and Learning Center (GAI task force)
title: GAI Guidelines
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Campus guidance from a spring 2024 faculty task force that set three traffic-light levels of generative AI use (green, yellow, red) for syllabi and assignments, with official icons added to syllabus materials and Simple Syllabus. It stresses instructor academic freedom, asks faculty to write their own policy, advises against AI checkers, and gives optional statements on verifying and citing AI output.

course: CSCI 132 Basic Data Structures and Algorithms
title: Syllabus - CSCI 132: Basic Data Structures and Algorithms, Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A short 'Bots and AI' rule in a second-semester programming syllabus. Students may not use bots or AI to develop their lab, program or exam solutions, and a student found using such a tool gets a zero on that assignment.

title: Syllabus - CSCI 232: Data Structures and Algorithms, Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1. The academic-integrity part of a data structures syllabus has a dedicated generative AI section. Students may not use AI tools or chatbots to develop solutions for labs, programs or exams, and an AI-written solution earns a zero. The instructor justifies the ban by saying students need to learn the material organically in an introductory course.

title: AI Course Policies and Assignment Guidelines
analyst_summary: Faculty-development page explaining Montclair's institutional AI framework. From Fall 2026 the university syllabus template has an AI-policy field with preset no-use, some-use and unrestricted-use options; the academic integrity policy treats unauthorized generative AI as dishonesty and requires students to cite or acknowledge AI use; instructors are urged to disclose their own AI use. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Academic Affairs (Vice Provost for Academic Innovation and Learning)
title: Guidelines for the Academic Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI Academic Guidelines 2.0)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. College-wide academic AI guidelines. They require every instructor to adopt one of three syllabus statements (little, average, or full AI use), classify teaching uses into open use, use with disclosure, use with oversight and prohibited use, set disclosure and citation expectations, keep faculty and students accountable for grading and originality, and define a warning-then-referral process for misconduct.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Information Systems
title: COMP 3309 Winter 2024 Course Outline
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Outline for a computing-and-society writing course, hosted on the instructor's site, with a 'please read' section warning against using ChatGPT-style tools to write assessments. It cites past zero grades and conduct records, argues AI writing lacks specificity and honest attribution, appeals to professional ethics and employability, and requires drafts in Google Docs or tracked-changes Word as evidence of authorship.

unit: Ying Wu College of Computing, Department of Computer Science
title: CS 485-007: Selected Topics In CS - Usable Security and Privacy (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for an upper-level NJIT computer science topics course. It discourages AI tools as harmful to the course goals but allows them with full disclosure of tools, prompts, responses and outputs. Students must check for hallucinations, violations bring a zero and a Dean of Students report, non-disclosure is punished more harshly, and work may be run through AI detectors.

unit: Ying Wu College of Computing, Department of Computer Science
title: CS 490-001: Guided Design in Software Engineering (Au24) syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Software engineering course syllabus from NJIT's Digital Commons. Its collaboration policy lists acceptable and unacceptable code reuse: code from a generative AI tool the student prompted is allowed if a link to the chat is left as a code comment, but uncited AI code or AI output prompted by someone else is not. The rules are framed as copying industry norms.

unit: Ying Wu College of Computing, Department of Computer Science
title: CS 698-004: Machine Learning for Time Series Analysis and Forecasting (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Graduate machine learning syllabus from NJIT's Digital Commons. Students may usually build code or text from online sources or LLMs into their solutions, but must credit them. LLM users must hand in the full conversation transcript, which must be their own, and failing to give credit counts as plagiarism under NJIT's academic integrity policy.

title: Required Sections: Artificial Intelligence Statements
analyst_summary: NMSU's official syllabus-requirements page provides three AI statements, produced by a fall 2023 provost task force, from which instructors choose one for their syllabus: broader use with citation, use only under some circumstances or with explicit permission, and no use. Unattributed AI-generated content is treated as academic dishonesty. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: CS 102, Syllabus, CSCI-UA 102, Klukowska
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus whose Generative AI Policy declines to ban AI tools and instead names three sanctioned roles (tutor, feedback generator, pair-programming partner), each with verification and documentation duties. It warns that exams are taken without AI and the integrity section requires acknowledging any non-human help.

unit: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Department of Computer Science
course: Introduction to Computer Science (NYU CS, instructor Amos Bloomberg)
title: Course Syllabus - Introduction to Computer Science
analyst_summary: Instructor-hosted syllabus for an NYU intro CS course stating that all integrity rules about getting help from humans apply equally to generative AI unless permission is given. AI may be used to research and understand material, but graded work must be produced and understood by the student; the policy also warns about inaccuracy, plagiarism and copyright issues in AI output.

unit: Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Department of Computer Science
course: Software Engineering (NYU CS, instructor Amos Bloomberg)
title: Course Syllabus - Software Engineering
analyst_summary: Software engineering syllabus that provides a course chatbot trained on the lecture notes, with a warning to verify its answers, and repeats the instructor's generative AI policy: AI rules mirror rules on human help, AI may support understanding, and graded work must be the student's own.

title: Generative AI Guide for Instructors
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Senate-approved instructor guide. The university does not restrict AI, so each instructor decides and must state the course rule and the expected citation format on the syllabus. It advises against banning specific tools and against AI detectors, forbids submitting student work to AI tools, notes AI's code-generation abilities, and suggests assessment redesign and equity limits on paid tools. Fetched via an Internet Archive snapshot because the live PDF sits behind a Cloudflare challenge.

title: Universal Guidelines for AI Use in Teaching and Learning: Course Syllabus Template Addendum
analyst_summary: Tier 4. A provost syllabus addendum that asks faculty to promote ethical AI use with proper attribution and to state their AI policy in the syllabus with reference to the Academic Dishonesty Policy. Faculty pick one of three options: not permitted, permitted for some activities with attribution, or permitted for all activities with attribution. It also covers licensing and terms of service and suggests alternative assessments.

title: CSC316 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus whose list of 'Examples of Cheating' includes using AI tools such as ChatGPT to generate full or partial solutions, even as a starting point to edit. AI services are prohibited for all assessed work in the course.

unit: NDSU Information Technology / Office of the VP for IT (AI work groups)
title: Artificial Intelligence at NDSU: Goals, Guidance, and Research
analyst_summary: University-wide summary of AI goals and guidance produced by NDSU work groups, explicitly framed as a framework rather than formal policy. It leaves course AI rules to instructors, requires that AI contributions be credited and documented, stresses accountability and privacy, and summarises separate instructor and student guidance documents. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

title: Sample AI Syllabus Policy Statement
analyst_summary: Tier 4. NEIU CTL's sample syllabus statement (2023), linked from the NEIU Libraries campus AI guide (text fetched via the public Google Docs plain-text export). It treats submitting AI-generated work as academic dishonesty and bars AI use unless the instructor permits it; when permitted, students must disclose use, keep AI as a supplement, cite prompts, tool, date and URL, and verify outputs.

course: CS 2100 Program Design and Implementation I
title: CS 2100: Program Design and Implementation I - Syllabus (The AI Policy)
analyst_summary: First-year program design syllabus that bars AI coding assistants and chat models for assignments on the grounds that AI skills should come after the basics (deferred to CS 3100). Search-engine AI overviews are tolerated for documentation lookups with a duty to verify, non-assignment AI use is allowed, and suspected overuse can trigger a meeting where students explain their code.

course: CS 3100 Program Design and Implementation II
title: Syllabus | NEU CS 3100 (Software Engineering in an Age of AI)
analyst_summary: Second program design course that restricts AI coding assistants on early assignments, then introduces them mid-semester with per-assignment levels from 'Not allowed' through 'Permitted' to 'Required' and explicit instruction in human-AI workflows. It also discloses how staff used AI to draft lecture notes, assignments, rubrics and the policy itself, with all AI content reviewed.

title: CS3650 Computer Systems - Syllabus
analyst_summary: Systems course syllabus that cites research showing early students using AI do not learn the material and therefore prohibits LLMs, chatbots and AI agents on homework and projects unless an assignment explicitly allows it.

title: Artificial intelligence resources for faculty
analyst_summary: Provost guidance asking faculty to state permitted and prohibited AI uses in syllabi, not to mandate student AI use, and to treat AI detectors cautiously. Offers three sample syllabus statements (full use with acknowledgment, limited use, no use) and data-protection rules for AI tools. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: NIU Artificial Intelligence (university guidance on teaching and learning)
title: Guidance on the Use of AI in Teaching and Learning
analyst_summary: University guidance setting principles (pedagogy first, transparency, equity, integrity) and affirming faculty responsibility for course AI decisions. Faculty must adopt one of three syllabus options (not permitted, limited, encouraged with transparency); it also covers disclosure, assessment design and a ban on uploading student work to public AI tools. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: NOVA Policies and Procedures (Winter Session and Spring 2026 syllabus insert)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. College-wide policy insert that NOVA attaches to course syllabi. Its academic integrity section warns that using AI to complete assigned work may violate the integrity policy, urges caution with assignment-help tools unless the instructor explicitly permits them, and notes faculty may use Turnitin.

unit: Department of Computer Science, McCormick School of Engineering
title: CS 213 Introduction to Computer Systems Fall 2025 (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for Northwestern's core computer systems course. A short section titled 'Cheating, AI, and Inadvertent Disclosures' warns that prompt-engineering or vibe-coding through labs and homework will prevent learning, notes that these graded tasks carry weight for that reason, and points to the university academic integrity policy for blatant cheating.

title: Faculty Resources for Artificial Intelligence (AI)
analyst_summary: NSU's teaching-center guidance for faculty on generative AI. It cautions against AI detectors and recommends redesigning assessment, asks faculty to set a clear syllabus policy and explain it repeatedly, to say whether and how students should disclose AI use, and covers faculty productivity uses, access/equity, environmental impact, AI literacy for careers, and privacy (no personal or proprietary data except in NSU-approved tools). Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (AI@OU Faculty page)
title: Faculty - AI@OU
analyst_summary: Oakland University's faculty guidance on generative AI, led by CETL. Unauthorized AI-assisted work is treated as potential misrepresentation; instructors must define and communicate course or assignment boundaries, report confirmed misuse, and avoid relying on detectors (they may request prompt logs). It lists guiding principles (disclose, cite, support learning, protect data, follow field norms), sample syllabus statements from prohibited to encouraged use, and a five-level AI assessment scale. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Hello, World! - CSCI 150: Introduction to Computer Science (Lab 1, Honor Code Reminders)
analyst_summary: The shared CSCI 150 lab website repeats honor-code reminders on each lab, including a blanket ban on generative AI that explicitly extends to debugging and reformatting one's own code.

title: Syllabus | CSCI 150 (Spring 2025) | Oberlin College
analyst_summary: A section syllabus that allows small cited snippets from sites like StackOverflow but lists using ChatGPT- or AI-generated code alongside paying others as prohibited cheating, with MOSS-based similarity checking.

unit: Center for Teaching, Learning, and Assessment (CTLA)
title: Generative AI Statements for Syllabi
analyst_summary: Teaching-center page recommending that every instructor set a course GenAI policy and offering more- and less-restrictive template statements, plus the College of Business policy as an example. Templates range from treating any GenAI use as dishonesty to requiring citation, prompts and validation notes when AI informs work. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Chat GPT & AI Support: Sample Syllabus Statements for AI in the Classroom
analyst_summary: Tier 4. ITLE page for faculty with OSU sample syllabus statements at three levels: generative AI not allowed, allowed in some circumstances, or fully allowed. It asks faculty to share their position in the syllabus or Canvas and in class. The OSU statements cover plagiarism penalties, permitted uses that support learning, a ban on fully AI-produced work, and attribution.

title: Syllabus - CS 312 - Internet Concepts
analyst_summary: Internet concepts syllabus that bans ChatGPT and other AI tools. The rationale is that school should build workplace skills. The syllabus notes that this rule applies only to CS 312.

title: CS 355: Syllabus (Spring 2026)
analyst_summary: Programming languages syllabus that does not prohibit ChatGPT and similar tools. Any use must be cited the same way as other online resources, inside a broader rule that all graded work must be the student's own.

title: Course Syllabus CS 422/522 Introduction to Machine Learning - Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Machine learning syllabus that bans copying homework code from ChatGPT or similar tools and treats it as an honor code violation. Students may use these tools to get ideas, but submitted work must be their own.

title: Should I Use ChatGPT? (decision tree, plain-text version)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Student decision tree linked from Ontario Tech's academic-integrity page on generative AI. It asks whether truth matters, whether the work must be the student's own, whether the student can check the output, and whether they will take full responsibility for errors. Each path ends in safe, unsafe or possible use, with reminders to check with the instructor, verify output and cite sources.

unit: Department of Medical Informatics & Clinical Epidemiology
course: BMI 510/610 Introduction to Biomedical & Health Informatics
title: OHSU Introduction to Biomedical & Health Informatics Course Policy for Use of ChatGPT and Generative AI
analyst_summary: Informatics course policy that lets students 'converse' with generative AI for ideas, but requires forum posts, quiz answers and the term paper to reflect their own thinking. It sets rules per activity, bans AI during the final exam, requires attribution, and bases the policy on the instructor's study showing LLMs can pass the course's assessments. Tier 2 (CS-related unit: biomedical informatics course; OHSU has no CS department).

unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), College of Engineering
title: Guidance on Drafting AI Use Policies
analyst_summary: School-wide floor for AI use across EECS courses, adapted from the OSU College of Science guidelines. It sets a restrictive default when a syllabus is silent, requires every syllabus to carry an AI statement keyed to an appendix of AI-use categories, specifies disclosure at submission, treats IDE-embedded assistants as GenAI, and covers faculty use for materials and grading, research use, and how detection and code-similarity evidence should be treated in misconduct cases.

unit: College of Engineering (Academic Integrity Resources for Faculty)
title: AI Chatbot Policy Example
analyst_summary: A model course policy offered to engineering faculty, written in the instructor's voice and aimed at software courses. It permits chatbots as a reference resource (error lookup, verifying algorithms, small code snippets, parts of reports) while prohibiting having AI write software or documents, and frames the rules around industry norms, licensing/IP risk and critical thinking.

unit: Center for Teaching and Learning (linked from EECS AI guidance)
title: Guidance for AI Use in Teaching and Learning
analyst_summary: University teaching-center guidance that the EECS AI guidance names as aligned and links to, including its syllabus template with tiered icons. Included under the scope addendum because EECS adopts it as the basis for course AI statements; it is not itself computing-specific. It covers instructor use of AI for materials and grading, data-privacy limits on uploading student work, a five-option tiered syllabus statement, and advice on writing course-specific statements.

unit: College of Information Sciences and Technology
title: GenAI - Teaching with Generative AI Tools
analyst_summary: College of IST instructor-facing guidance on generative AI covering AI literacy, ethics, course design with GenAI, a section on GenAI in programming classes, academic integrity, and accessibility. It points instructors to syllabus statement options, recommends assignment-level icons for acceptable use, and cautions against relying on AI detectors.

title: AI Use Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Provost page of sample syllabus statements organized into three levels (Prohibited, Assisted, Integrated), leaving inclusion of a statement to each instructor. It gives drafting recommendations (name tool categories, be explicit about conditions, mind equity) and examples ranging from treating AI submissions as plagiarism to requiring disclosure of prompts. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Département de génie informatique et génie logiciel
title: Plan de cours LOG2990 - Projet de logiciel d’application Web
analyst_summary: This French-language plan de cours for a team web-software project has a section on generative AI systems (SIAG). Students may use them for project work but not individual evaluations, provided most of the work is their own, use is declared, and they verify outputs they understand. The PDF sits in the teaching-support office's template folder, apparently as an example plan.

title: CS51 - Fall 2026 (course website, Academic Integrity section)
analyst_summary: The intro course places itself in Tier 1 of the department tier system but, in practice, forbids AI tools for assignment work while allowing collaboration on debugging and design with people. It also forbids submitting course materials to AI tools and states escalating sanctions.

title: Computer Science AI Policy Tier System
analyst_summary: A department-wide framework that every Pomona CS course must place itself in: four tiers ranging from no AI use (Tier 0) through syllabus-defined use (Tier 1), use with attribution (Tier 2), to open use without credit (Tier 3). It frames itself as a pilot to be revisited, focuses on usages rather than named tools, ties misalignment to the departmental honor policy, and acknowledges Harvey Mudd's AI-use course policy as its inspiration.

title: Academic Honesty Policy
analyst_summary: The CS department's general academic honesty policy, revised for Fall 2026 to name AI tools as unapproved sources by default and to defer AI-specific rules to the department's AI Policy Tier System. It also covers copying from AI, routine similarity/AI-content detection, citation of permitted AI in papers, a ban on feeding course materials to AI tools, and graduated sanctions.

unit: Artificial Intelligence at PCC (college AI site)
title: Student learning and AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. College-wide student page stating that each instructor sets AI expectations, that uncited AI-generated text breaches the Student Code of Conduct, and that PCC-provided tools are vetted for security. It points students to citation help and to grade-appeal and complaint processes when AI use affects grades or leads to accusations.

title: CS Graduate Student Handbook 2025-26
analyst_summary: The CS graduate handbook's academic misconduct section notes that rules on independent work and generative AI use vary widely across CS courses, and sends students to each syllabus. This is a thin department-level mention with no rules of its own.

unit: Center for Teaching Excellence (statements approved by the Office of Academic Affairs)
title: Syllabus Statements to Address the Usage of Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Teaching-center page giving three syllabus statements approved by Academic Affairs: AI allowed on any assignment with citation, AI allowed only on instructor-selected assignments, and ChatGPT prohibited. Permissive options make students responsible for fact-checking AI output, and the prohibitive option ties unauthorized use to the academic integrity guidelines.

title: COS 226 Policies (Spring 2026)
analyst_summary: Course policy that bans generative AI on exams, quizzes and in-lecture polls but does not ban LLMs on programming assignments, instead strongly discouraging substitutive use. It gives a fine/discouraged rule of thumb, grades understanding through code reviews, and requires penalty-free disclosure of any LLM use in an acknowledgments file.

title: CS252: Systems Programming (Fall 2026) – AI Policy
analyst_summary: Course information document embedded on the CS 252 homepage (cs.purdue.edu/homes/cs252) with a brief AI policy: AI may be used for learning but not for writing lab code. It justifies this by AI-free programming questions on exams plus in-person oral implementation exams and lab quizzes run by TAs.

title: CS59300-SER: Software Engineering for Robotics Spring 2026 Course Information
analyst_summary: Graduate special-topics syllabus with a short AI section. It allows generative AI on every assignment and requires a detailed account of how the tool was used.

title: Common Syllabus Information (2026-27)
analyst_summary: School-wide common syllabus text that applies to all Queen's Computing courses. It leaves AI permission to each course outline and tells students to check with their instructor. Its Turnitin section says submissions are also analysed for AI-generated text, and those results are not reported to instructors for now.

title: CSCI 1200 Data Structures - Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Data structures integrity page forbidding chatbots, IDE-integrated AI and AI development assistants on both labs and homework. It argues that reliance is a crutch for introductory programming, notes that exams are paper-based and that employers bar AI in interviews, and requires listing all collaborators and resources in a README.

title: COMP 321 Course Information (Honor Code Policy)
analyst_summary: Systems programming course page whose honor code bans all AI-based tools, naming ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, and TabNine, for any purpose, alongside a rule that students write all their own code. Exams are in person, closed book, with no computer access. The page gives no term label; its exam dates match Spring 2026.

unit: Department of Computer Science, Golisano College of Computing and Information Sciences
title: CSCI-633 Biologically-Inspired Intelligent Systems: Syllabus
analyst_summary: Graduate CS syllabus with a short 'Policy on Large Language Models' that folds LLM use into the strict academic integrity policy: LLM-written code or text counts as not one's own work. The rationale stresses doing the mathematics and thinking oneself to build machine learning literacy.

unit: Department of Software Engineering, Golisano College of Computing and Information Sciences
title: SWEN-261: Intro to Software Engineering — Syllabus
analyst_summary: The 'ChatGPT/ AI Policy' says generative AI is not part of the course toolkit and that submitted work (code or written) must not be created or modified by AI. Unless an assignment allows otherwise, AI is limited to search and reference, and students must submit their prompts with a statement that the work is original. Suspected work must be reproduced or explained without help, with penalties up to a failing grade, and the instructors invite students to share how they use these tools.

unit: Center for Teaching and Learning (with Computer Science, School of Information and Cybersecurity examples)
title: Syllabus Guidance for Generative AI
analyst_summary: University teaching-center guidance urging faculty to state GenAI expectations, followed by example syllabus statements from RIT faculty. Two Computer Science examples set out allowed and disallowed uses (code completion, chat about concepts vs. pasting assignments), disclosure via chat logs, privacy rationale and verification interviews; computing examples from the School of Information and Cybersecurity are also included.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering (CSSE)
title: CSSE232 : Computer Architecture I - Syllabus
analyst_summary: A computer architecture syllabus that restates the department's (CSSE) AI policy: AI, including IDE assistants and chatbots, is barred on all assignments unless the instructor explicitly directs its use. The underlying CSSE integrity policy documents are linked but sit on a login-only SharePoint, so this course page is the public trace of the departmental rule.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Software Engineering (CSSE)
title: CSSE 332 Syllabus
analyst_summary: An operating systems syllabus that forbids generative AI for all coursework, explicitly counting IDE code-completion plugins such as Copilot as misconduct, and runs exams in a terminal editor on a remote server without an IDE. It explains the ban through skill-building, confidentiality risks of feeding data to AI platforms, and the need for humans to judge AI output.

course: CS 04.113 Intro to Object Oriented Programming
title: SYLLABUS IOOP (C. Chien)
analyst_summary: Intro object-oriented programming syllabus that prohibits generative AI, explaining that it would defeat the purpose of assignments meant to build and measure mastery. Using any GenAI without instructor permission is a violation with sanctions up to course failure, and every lab must carry an academic integrity statement. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: Undergraduate Academic Regulations
analyst_summary: Tier 4: The undergraduate academic regulations write generative AI into the definitions of cheating and plagiarism. Students may use AI for search-engine- or dictionary-like tasks unless an instructor says otherwise; any further use needs instructor authorization and full disclosure. A mandatory academic integrity course covers GenAI rules.

unit: Center for Teaching Excellence and Innovation
title: Your Classroom Faculty Guide to AI
analyst_summary: Rush's teaching-center guide on AI in the classroom. It advises instructors to set clear expectations, require an AI Use Disclosure and citations for AI-generated content (including code), have students verify facts against non-AI sources, design assessments around process artifacts, and not rely on AI detectors. The binding university policy (UAC0039) is login-only. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; health-sciences institution with no computing school).

unit: Department of Computer Science (School of Arts and Sciences)
title: Introduction to Computer Science (CS 111 course site)
analyst_summary: Intro CS course site with a collaboration table in which 'AI Chatbots' may not be used to discuss concepts, may not see or supply code, and must be acknowledged, plus an explicit ban on generative AI for creating or debugging programming assignments. Autolab runs JPlag and violations are reported to the Office of Student Conduct; the Data Structures (CS 112) site carries the same rules.

title: Guidance on the use of AI at Rutgers
analyst_summary: Rutgers' universitywide AI guidance, which applies to Rutgers-Camden. It says AI expectations vary by discipline, course and instructor, that AI is not permissible for coursework unless instructors clearly allow it, ties this to Academic Integrity Policy 10.2.13, and adds rules on approved tools, confidential data and verifying AI output. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of Teaching Evaluation and Assessment Research (OTEAR), Rutgers University (university-wide)
title: AI in Education - OTEAR Rutgers
analyst_summary: Rutgers-wide teaching guidance (covering the Newark campus) that tells faculty to try AI tools on their own assignments, learn the conduct process, redesign assignments and rubrics, and write a clear course policy grounded in the code of conduct. It offers three sample syllabus sentences ranging from no AI use to full use with citation and the ability to explain submitted work. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Office of the Provost, Center for Teaching Excellence
title: Generative AI and Pedagogy at SMU
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost and CTE page whose 'SMU Generative AI Policies' section leaves classroom use to each faculty member but requires faculty to tell students about AI use in the syllabus, using an SMU statement builder. Faculty who use AI must give clear guidelines and disclose their own AI use in assignment building or grading. The page also covers data privacy rules for prompts and teaching tips that include plagiarism detection.

university: SUNY College of Environmental Science and Forestry
title: Generative AI at ESF
analyst_summary: IT services page introducing generative AI tools available to students, faculty and staff and recommending that college data be entered only into approved tools. It says users are responsible for reviewing AI output but contains no coursework or academic integrity rules. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Academic Affairs Principles for AI
analyst_summary: Academic Affairs principles stating that AI should support rather than replace learning, that faculty judgment sets course AI expectations, and that AI literacy (including bias and environmental cost) is part of student preparation. It also holds faculty and students accountable for the integrity of AI-assisted work. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Saint Louis University – Course Syllabus Components (Print-Friendly)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost list of required syllabus components under SLU's Course Syllabus Policy. Every syllabus must state in writing whether and how generative AI may be used. The decision rests with each instructor unless academic leadership directs otherwise; there is no single university statement, and the Reinert Center offers templates.

unit: Department of Mathematics and Computing Science
course: CSCI 1226 Introduction to Computers and Programming
title: CSCI 1226 -- Introduction to Computers and Programming (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Intro programming syllabus whose academic integrity section bans submitting LLM-generated code as one's own work but allows AI for learning purposes if its use is declared. Violations fall under the university's academic regulation and earn a zero on the whole submission.

unit: Department of Mathematics and Computing Science
course: CSCI 2341 Data Structures and Algorithms I
title: CSCI 2341 Fall 2026 | Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Data structures syllabus with a dedicated AI policy that encourages AI help for assignments and labs while requiring students to review and understand generated code. Mastery is checked by an in-person, paper final exam without AI, and AI-written code may be submitted only on activities where permission is given.

title: SHSU Generative AI Guidance
analyst_summary: Academic Affairs' living guidance for SHSU students, faculty and staff. It notes there is no single university AI policy, leaves course rules to each instructor, asks students to acknowledge AI where permitted, treats undisclosed out-of-bounds use as a possible honesty violation, warns faculty against acting on AI detector results, links sample syllabus statements ranging from bans to required use, and points to licensed tools (Copilot, Gemini, NotebookLM) and privacy cautions. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: University Senate (published in the Curriculum Guide by Curriculum, Assessment, and Accreditation)
title: Artificial Intelligence, Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI (GenAI) in Assessments and Deliverables at SDSU (SDSU Curriculum Guide)
date_or_term: Curriculum Guide last updated July 2026; guidelines adopted by University Senate May 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Senate-adopted guidelines that classify each assessment or deliverable into four AI-use levels, from disallowed to unrestricted, built on the principles of proficiency, verification and documentation. Students must document AI use at the restricted and documented levels with citations or a summary statement that lists the tool, purpose and prompts. The syllabus section of the same guide requires every syllabus from Fall 2025 to state the permitted level of AI use, and it notes the Senate's expansion of plagiarism to cover AI-produced work.

unit: Center for Equity and Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CEETL)
title: Teaching with Generative AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. SF State's teaching-centre page on GenAI. It cites the university Course Syllabus Policy S25-257, which requires every syllabus to say how and why GenAI may or may not be used, and recommends transparency whatever the instructor's stance. It frames course design through 'Three Laws': teach about AI, teach with AI where appropriate, and protect learning by making assignments AI-resistant.

title: Data Structures and Algorithms CS 146 Spring 2026 (Sections 2-3, Taylor)
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus in the instructor's own informal voice: do not have LLMs write your code. The instructor says he will recognize odd LLM solutions, may question students about their code, and argues that AI hurts the course's goal even though it will be a useful tool later at work.

title: Introduction to Programming CS 46A Spring 2026 (Section 01, Tshukudu)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus (one of many section syllabi the CS department publishes). AI may support studying, but AI is not permitted on assignments unless explicitly allowed; submitting AI-generated code or text is plagiarism, and students may be asked to explain their code.

unit: School of Engineering (AI Squared initiative; includes Computer Science and Engineering)
title: AI Squared in Student Learning - School of Engineering - Santa Clara University
analyst_summary: School of Engineering guidance for instructors with four sample scenarios (prohibited, allowed for specific tasks, allowed with permission, allowed with attribution) and statements from each department. It is school-level rather than a CS department page, but it has a Computer Science and Engineering section (COEN 11 bans code generators, COEN 346 expects GenAI with attribution), an ECE section on AI-generated Verilog, and notes on AI detectors and code.

unit: Academic Senate (Student Affairs Committee) / Santa Monica College
title: AR 5500.1 Standards Code of Academic Conduct (old 4111#)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Santa Monica College's administrative regulation on academic conduct, published as a 2024-25 Academic Senate committee revision draft with tracked edits. It adds the violation of an instructor's AI policy (stated in the syllabus or course materials) to the definition of academic dishonesty, requires faculty to communicate expectations in writing, and sets instructor and conduct-office sanctions. It is the college's only formal AI rule found; no CS syllabus AI text was found.

title: Syllabus Template (Generative AI policy section)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Seattle University's official syllabus template, which since August 2025 has a GenAI policy section. Instructors are asked to state a policy (prohibited, sometimes permitted, always permitted, required) with a rationale, and are given three sample statements (not permitted, limited, permitted). These include citation and AI disclosure requirements, fact-checking duties, and treating use beyond the policy as an academic integrity violation.

unit: Department of Information Technology (AI resources for teaching)
title: Developing an AI Use Statement (Syllabus Statements)
analyst_summary: University IT teaching page noting that academic-integrity policy has no separate AI clause and asking instructors to put an AI statement in syllabi. It offers five example statements, from no AI use to general use with attribution, including a proposal-and-approval model and repeated notes on disability accommodations. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

course: CMPT 120 Introduction to Computing Science and Programming I
title: Course-Info (CMPT 120, Brian Fraser)
analyst_summary: Intro programming course page that allows any AI tool for writing code on assignments and labs, with no grade deduction, provided use is noted in a code comment. Quizzes and exams are taken without computers or AI, so most of the grade depends on being able to code unaided. Term not stated on the page; curl to the host timed out, so wording was confirmed via WebFetch.

title: CMPT 373: Software Development Methods
analyst_summary: Team-project software engineering course whose 'Academic Honesty & AI' section treats using AI to generate code as both harmful to learning outcomes and an integrity violation. Students are told to avoid or disable Copilot and similar tools for the duration of the course.

title: CSC 370 AI Guidelines
analyst_summary: Course AI guidelines linked from the CSC 370 syllabus. AI use is cautiously encouraged, with the choice tied to learning goals: write the code yourself to understand a technique, and use AI to explore variations. Any permitted use needs an AI statement plus a full transcript, and AI-free work must say so. The page also gives prompting tips for code generation.

title: Policy 2:3 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: SDSU's course-syllabus policy lists required and optional syllabus components; it requires faculty to state their expectations for generative AI use in coursework and commits the university to provide example statements at different levels of permitted use. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Generative AI | Southern Connecticut State University
analyst_summary: Office of Online Learning guidance for SCSU instructors describing generative AI capabilities, limits and privacy risks. It declines to endorse AI detectors, asks instructors to state in the syllabus whether and how AI may be used, and suggests assessment changes such as more low-stakes formative work and harder-to-automate assignments. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Faculty Senate (guidelines presented on Morris Library research guide)
title: AI: Guidelines for SIUC Faculty
date_or_term: Faculty Senate guidelines adopted July 2024; guide last updated Aug 25, 2025
analyst_summary: Library research guide presenting the SIUC Faculty Senate's July 2024 AI guidelines, organised as three action items: be transparent about AI tool costs, include a syllabus AI statement, and learn about harms of AI requirements or bans. Only the Senate-attributed text is excerpted; the guide also contains the librarian's own opinions. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Southern University and A&M College (University Policy Office; policy SUS-6-001)
title: Recent Policy Approval Briefs: Comprehensive AI Use Policy (SUS-6-001)
analyst_summary: Official policy-approval brief summarizing the university-wide Comprehensive AI Use Policy, which defines acceptable AI use, creates an AI Advisory Council and ties AI use to academic integrity, privacy and security. Only the brief, not the full policy text, is publicly available. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Computer Science 161 Section 10 — Introduction to Programming (Outline)
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Intro programming course outline. Its only explicit AI rule is a ban on AI in the weekly labs, where students caught using AI are removed and get a zero for that lab. The outline also relies on similarity-detection software for assignments and closed-book tests.

title: CS106B and the Honor Code
date_or_term: Summer Quarter 2026 (archived page; current-quarter URL returned 404)
analyst_summary: Honor-code page for Stanford's second intro programming course. Generative AI is banned on all graded work regardless of disclosure, with a skills-development rationale, the university's analogy of AI to human assistance, and a note that departmental plagiarism tools compare submissions against AI-produced code.

title: CS221: Artificial Intelligence: Principles and Techniques
analyst_summary: Course policy treating generative AI like a human collaborator: allowed for help such as syntax or debugging but not for answers, self-checking, or substantially completing work. Every use requires a shareable transcript, tools that cannot provide one (e.g., agentic coding tools) are barred, and staff may inspect commit history; students who self-report get lighter consequences.

title: Guidance for Appropriate Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools at Stevens
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Institute-wide guidance tying AI use to Stevens' security and privacy policies and data classification levels, permitting Stevens data only in licensed tools and prohibiting restricted data. It flags grading or assessment of student work as a use case requiring additional review; it says nothing about student coursework use.

title: CSE 114 - Introduction to Object-Oriented Programming (Course Info: Policy on AI Tools)
analyst_summary: Intro course info page with a 'Policy on AI Tools' that acknowledges AI can aid learning but strictly prohibits it on exams, quizzes and programming assignments, treating AI-generated code as unauthorized assistance subject to disciplinary action. The same statement appears on the CSE 214 Data Structures course page.

title: CS35: Policies
analyst_summary: The course frames integrity around whether an action shortcuts or promotes learning, and classifies generative AI as unauthorized collaboration with an outside source. It reproduces the faculty handbook's severe plagiarism penalties and a department-wide exam policy barring electronic devices.

title: CS75: Policies
analyst_summary: An upper-level course using the same learning-shortcut framing as other Swarthmore CS courses; it explicitly lists generative-AI-produced solutions among prohibited outside solutions.

title: IST256 Syllabus
analyst_summary: This intro Python course embraces AI with disclosure. It provides a course-tuned chatbot whose use needs no reporting, while use of any other AI tool must be disclosed with each submission. The course honor code counts AI as 'someone else', so passing off AI output as one's own work is a violation, and AI-generated code has to be cited like any other source.

title: AI Ethical Considerations and Guidance
analyst_summary: Tarleton's AI Council guidance on responsible generative AI use, grounded in Texas A&M System regulations. Faculty should credit AI used in course design and assessment, model ethical use, and state in the syllabus what is allowed, what needs disclosure and what is banned; students should use AI within integrity policies, cite AI contributions, and understand accuracy and bias limits; privacy-protective platforms are recommended. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Digital Futures Institute (TC AI and Pedagogy Working Group)
title: TC Guidance: Developing a Generative AI Policy for Your Course
analyst_summary: Teachers College guidance asking instructors to state their generative AI policy explicitly in the syllabus, in class and in assignments, weighing learning goals, equity, privacy and integrity. It offers five sample syllabus statements from full prohibition through assignment-specific, task-specific and approval-based permission to general permission with attribution, each requiring disclosure of tools and models and noting disability accommodations for AI. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer and Information Sciences
title: CIS 1068 Syllabus (Program Design and Abstraction)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for Temple's second programming course. Its short 'use of AI' section acknowledges generative AI is worth exploring in free time but argues students must build skill through their own practice, points them to instructors and peer tutors when stuck, and forbids using generative AI as a shortcut on course assignments.

unit: TSU Libraries and Media Center (LibGuide relaying TSU syllabus AI options)
title: How should I use AI? - Artificial Intelligence (AI) - LibGuides at Tennessee State University
analyst_summary: Library guide page that reproduces the three university syllabus options for generative AI (strictly prohibited, permitted with permission, broader use with citation), each tying misuse to the University Code of Honor as plagiarism. It also tells students to cite AI and stay within instructor parameters. Included as the only fetchable statement of TSU's syllabus options; the Board AI policy PDF is no longer online. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Center for Innovation in Teaching and Learning (CITL)
title: Generative AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Teaching-center page offering three tiers of syllabus statements (open use with attribution, moderate use when assigned with attribution, closed/no use), each with a required acknowledgement template. It also warns faculty and students not to enter sensitive data into AI tools. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCE 312, Fall 2023 Course Information
analyst_summary: Course information page whose collaboration rules name ChatGPT and other large language models as outside sources. Their use must be attributed, and failing to do so counts as plagiarism.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCE 420: Intro to AI Syllabus
analyst_summary: Undergraduate AI course syllabus with separate AI rules for writing and for code. AI is allowed for writing if cited. AI-generated code may be submitted if documented with the prompts and outputs, and students stay responsible for correctness through documented testing.

title: Teach: Harnessing AI in Teaching
analyst_summary: TAMU-CC's teaching-with-AI hub page gives faculty assignment and curriculum ideas, notes Turnitin AI detection with caveats, and tells instructors to use the syllabus to state AI expectations, name allowed platforms, and warn that unauthorized AI use can lead to a student conduct referral. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of the AVP for Academic Affairs and Center for Academic Technology (Center for Faculty Excellence)
title: AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Memo to TAMUK faculty from academic affairs offering three optional syllabus statements on AI writing tools: prohibit all use, limited use as directed by the instructor, and broad use with citation. Each ties unauthorized or unattributed use to the university's academic misconduct policy. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Department of Computer Science (College of Science & Engineering)
title: COURSE SYLLABUS INTRODUCTION TO PROGRAMMING COSC10403-074
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that requires any AI-generated material used in classwork (ChatGPT, Bard, Bing) to be clearly acknowledged, under a zero-tolerance cheating policy. A technology-policy section states that unauthorized AI use may be misconduct or a breach of professional ethics, with sanctions up to expulsion. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: Department of Computer Science (College of Science & Engineering)
title: COSC 30203 055 - Computer Organization (Dr. Michael Scherger)
analyst_summary: Systems course syllabus that bars AI and other unapproved assignment-help tools unless the instructor explicitly authorizes them. It lists concrete prohibited activities, from submitting the assignment statement to an AI to using AI to brainstorm or to refine one's own work. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: CS 3358 - 008/011 Data Structures & ALGM syllabus
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus (posted on the lecturer's personal site) whose academic-offenses section treats work produced with help from generative AI such as ChatGPT, Copilot or Grok as cheating unless the instructor allows otherwise in writing, with a zero and a report to the Honor Code Council. It also warns programs may be run through code-plagiarism detection such as Moss and keeps exams face-to-face. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: CS3358 Syllabus page
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus with an AI-usage statement that defines AI broadly (any tool that edits writing or creates text, images or code) and allows it for brainstorming, exploring responses and creative work as each assignment permits. It stresses that coding assignments must follow the given starter code and specifications or earn little credit, and that exams reference assignments. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: Texas Tech University Department of Computer Science - CS 4366 Syllabus Fall 2025
analyst_summary: Capstone syllabus whose AI Use Policy adopts the university TLPDC 'AI allowed for specific assignments' template: traditional and generative AI tools are barred except on assignments the instructor designates. Submitting AI-generated content as one's own is an integrity violation that may be referred to student conduct.

university: Texas Tech University Health Sciences Center
unit: TTUHSC Operating Policy (Chief Information Officer / AI Governance and Risk Committee)
title: HSC OP: 52.21, Acceptable Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools
analyst_summary: Institution-wide operating policy on AI tools across education, research, clinical care and administration, built on transparency, accountability, fairness, privacy and human-supervision principles. For academics it bars completing academic work in ways the instructor has not allowed, AI-generated non-public instructional materials and grading, and entering FERPA-protected records into unapproved tools; it sets up an AI governance committee and biennial review. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: University AI Collaborative page with ready-made syllabus language: a FERPA data-protection pledge limiting what faculty may put into AI tools, and three student-use options (permissive with disclosure, mixed use only where assignments allow, and required AI use with an opt-out variant). It recommends disclosure over bans because AI use is hard to detect. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Guide to Teaching and Learning (Provost's Office / The Faculty Center)
title: AI Sample Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: The New School's faculty teaching guide offers sample AI syllabus statements, from a generic allow-with-documentation statement by The Faculty Center to a generic prohibition, plus discipline examples for writing, image tools and a Design and Technology course that requires disclosure of AI use including in programming code. It urges transparent conversations with students about how AI supports or undermines learning. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSE 2221 and CSE 2231 Course Policies
analyst_summary: Shared course-policy page for Ohio State's two-course Software I/II sequence. A 'Note on the use of Generative AI' bans ChatGPT, Copilot and similar tools for writing code and gives three reasons: no AI on exams, novices cannot spot plausible-looking AI errors, and AI undercuts the learning that comes from problem solving.

unit: University of Montana Teaching and Learning (Associate Director of Academic Assessment and Faculty Support)
title: Teaching in the Age of Generative AI
analyst_summary: University-wide faculty guidance from UM's teaching office. It asks every instructor to include a GenAI syllabus statement (sample welcome, limited and discouraged statements), offers talking points, tells faculty not to use AI detectors because UM lacks an enterprise contract and detectors are unreliable, and sets out an educational, intent-based procedure for suspected misuse. It notes that in a coding class collaboration with tools may be part of the process. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

university: The University of Tennessee Health Science Center
title: Syllabus Course Policies and Procedures (Course Syllabus Guide)
analyst_summary: UTHSC teaching-center syllabus guide whose Generative AI item asks instructors to state a course AI policy and offers three sample statements: permitted with acknowledgement, permitted only on designated assignments, and prohibited. Permitted use must be cited, students own the accuracy of AI output, and violations count as academic dishonesty under the Honor Code. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; health-sciences institution with no computing school).

university: The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston
title: Educational Technology - Current Students (Generative AI Tools)
analyst_summary: Current-students technology page of the biomedical informatics school with a Generative AI Tools section. It warns that external GPTs are unsuitable for intellectual property or research data, points students to a university comparison matrix before using GPTs for coursework, notes which licenses are FERPA/HIPAA compliant, and offers a school-hosted Llama chatbot for IP-sensitive work. Tier 2 (informatics school).

university: The University of Texas Medical Branch at Galveston
unit: UTMB (Legal Affairs, Institutional Compliance, Information Security Services, Information Services)
title: UTMB Artificial Intelligence (AI) Joint Policy
analyst_summary: Institution-wide AI policy, adapted from UT Austin language, covering academic use, data security and acceptable use. Faculty are encouraged to set course AI policies; without a syllabus statement, AI help is treated like help from another person, and students must protect confidential data, cite AI contributions and own their work's accuracy. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

university: The University of Texas at Arlington
unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
course: CSE 1310: Introduction to Computers and Programming
title: CSE 1310: Introduction to Computers and Programming Fall 2024 (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus whose academic integrity section bans generative AI tools for all assignments and assessments. The ban is justified by the course's focus on independent thinking and on measuring each student's own mastery against learning outcomes, and work judged AI-generated is referred for academic review. Tier 1 (CS course policy).

university: The University of Texas at Austin
title: Syllabus - Computer Science 314 - Data Structures (Computer Programming 2)
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that completely bans generative and agentic AI on graded work, citing a sharp rise in cheating, and states that the CS department forbids AI on point-bearing work in foundational courses. It encourages chatbots for studying concepts and for understanding failed tests after the deadline, and warns of plagiarism detection and dean referrals.

university: The University of Texas at Austin
title: Syllabus for CS371N: Natural Language Processing (Policy on ChatGPT, Copilot, and other AI assistants)
analyst_summary: Upper-division NLP syllabus that actively encourages ChatGPT and Copilot because understanding these systems is a course goal. Coding assistance is allowed within the same limits as other external resources, conceptual-question use is discouraged, and AI is banned during exams.

university: The University of Texas at Dallas
title: CS/CE 2336 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: CS II syllabus that lets students use AI code-generation tools for learning, while requiring that all submitted project and assignment code be written by the student. The statement is repeated for the project and the programming assignments.

university: The University of Texas at Tyler
title: COSC 1337 – The Object-Oriented Paradigm Syllabus (Spring 2026, Morris)
analyst_summary: Second-semester programming syllabus that bans AI-generated homework unless assigned, but lets students consult AI or websites for code examples when stuck. Borrowed code must be commented with the problem, source and prompt, annotated line by line, rewritten in the student's own style, and explainable in person; otherwise it counts as plagiarism. The same policy appears in the instructor's COSC 2336 syllabus. Tier 1 (CS course policy).

university: The University of Texas at Tyler
course: COSC 3315 Social and Professional Issues in Computing
title: COSC 3315-060 Social and Professional Issues in Computing Spring 2026 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Computing ethics syllabus that opens with UT Tyler's required AI policy language (acknowledge all AI use, protect data, verify outputs, misuse is an integrity breach) and then selects the no-AI option for this course. (The archive file name says COSC 1315 but the document is COSC 3315.) Tier 1 (CS course policy).

unit: Dean of Students, Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities
title: AI Academic Misconduct
analyst_summary: Faculty-facing guidance from the student conduct office listing unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct and asking instructors to state in syllabi whether AI is permitted, what help is allowed and how to cite it. It also covers assessment design to reduce misconduct and the reporting process. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Thomas Jefferson University (University policy; student policy handbook)
title: Artificial Intelligence (Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) Policy)
analyst_summary: University-wide policy on generative AI in academic coursework. Faculty decide (with department/college approval) whether a course or assignment is Permitted or Restricted Use, documented in the syllabus; students using permitted AI own the validity of their work and must acknowledge AI contributions; embedded assistive AI (spell-check, search) is allowed unless prohibited; uses beyond approval or without citation violate academic integrity. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Senate / VP Academic (Centre for Academic Integrity)
title: Academic Integrity Policy (ED 05-0)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. TRU's university academic integrity policy; TRU chose to handle AI through its integrity rules rather than a separate AI policy. It classes use of unapproved generative-AI tools as fabrication, with examples such as AI-produced text, images or code and submitting unapproved AI output as one's own work; the rest of the policy sets out the investigation process and sanctions.

title: Toronto Metropolitan University ⊚ CPS188 Official Website
analyst_summary: The intro programming course site allows GenAI for grammar correction only. Use beyond that breaches TMU Policy 60.

title: CPS 420: Discrete Structures – W2025
analyst_summary: The outline limits GenAI to grammar correction and studying for tests. Any other use breaches TMU Policy 60, and GenAI code generation is completely prohibited. CPS 710 uses the same wording.

unit: Office of the Vice-President Academic (Teaching & Learning Advisory Committee)
title: Generative Artificial Intelligence: Trent University Guidelines, 2024
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Trent's university-wide guidelines on generative AI, organized by phase of a semester. Instructors choose whether and how to use AI, must disclose their own AI use for materials or grading, and pick one of three standard Syllabus Builder statements (not permitted, permitted as outlined, required). Students should assume AI is prohibited unless stated; unauthorized use is an integrity violation, AI detectors are not recommended, and process documentation and less vulnerable assessments are encouraged.

unit: Office of the Associate Provost, Teaching + Learning (AI Task Force)
title: Guidelines for Use of Generative AI in Teaching and Learning (Series A 2-31)
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Guidelines supporting TWU's generative AI teaching policy. They set three permitted course approaches (limited, partial, full use), forbid course-wide bans, reject AI detectors, require a syllabus AI policy, and provide sample syllabus statements for each tier plus assignment-design advice. Ethical concerns (labour exploitation, environment, Christian values) are framed explicitly.

unit: Department of Computer Science (School of Engineering)
title: CS15 Reference (CS 15 Chatbot)
analyst_summary: Course reference page introducing a course-built, LLM-backed chatbot grounded in course materials that guides students without solving problems. It places responsibility for verifying output on students, explains that interactions are logged anonymously to improve the tool, and invites feedback on the experiment.

unit: Office of Academic Affairs & Provost (AI at Tulane site)
title: Artificial Intelligence at Tulane University: Guidelines for the Ethical and Responsible Use of AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Tulane's university AI page with guidelines for ethical and responsible AI use. It says student AI use is governed by existing academic integrity policies, restricts entering non-public data into public AI tools, requires security review of procured AI tools, and asks faculty to explore AI, set clear course-specific rules, and have students describe their AI use when it is allowed.

title: Suggested Syllabus Policies & Notices
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UNC Charlotte's official suggested syllabus language, including two generative AI options (AI permitted in all work with attribution, or only on designated assignments). Both require disclosure and an acknowledgment statement, warn about data privacy, and the page explains that AI detection tools are designated do-not-use and require student consent if used anyway.

unit: Center for Online Learning and Teaching Technology (COLTT)
title: Generative AI Technology
analyst_summary: Tier 4. COLTT resource page for UTRGV instructors on generative AI. It lists completing programming assignments among misuse concerns and advises clear syllabus policies on permitted use, citation and consequences. It encourages transparency and talking with students, offers assessment-design and exam tips, says detectors must never be the only basis for misconduct decisions, and suggests assignments that deliberately include AI.

unit: Center for the Advancement of Teaching, Learning, and Online Education (CATLOE)
title: Design and write AI policies
analyst_summary: Tier 4. CATLOE guide that walks instructors through three phases of writing a course AI policy: identifying the skills a course targets and whether AI helps develop them, communicating when and why students should or should not use AI, and using the policy to open conversations with students. It frames policies as learning guidance rather than rules and gives sample course-policy language.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSE 331 Homework Policies
analyst_summary: The homework policy page for an upper-level algorithms course bans generative AI on every homework question, including programming, and makes any GenAI-related violation an automatic course F regardless of prior record. Students must declare an allowed source (or none) per question at submission, and some homework questions are deliberately designed to detect use of disallowed sources.

title: Human-Computer Interaction (syllabus)
analyst_summary: CS course syllabus whose academic-honesty section requires all assignments and tests to be the student's own work, not produced by others or AI, with violations reported to the department. It adds the university statement that students should look to instructors on fair AI use and that misuse violates the Code of Student Conduct. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: Guidelines for Faculty in Dealing with the Use of Generative AI Tools
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Office for Academic Affairs guidelines (on its Policies & Guidelines page) explaining generative AI tools, including code tools like Codex, and their limits (errors, bias). It advises faculty to experiment with tools, discuss AI and integrity with students, include a syllabus statement, redesign assignments and require citation; it gives three suggested syllabus statements (allowed with referencing, allowed for specific assignments, not allowed).

unit: Office of the Provost (Provost-appointed AI Working Group)
title: A Report on AI and the UAB Community
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Provost working-group report setting UAB's approach to AI. UAB does not tell instructors to require or ban GenAI; course decisions go in the syllabus, and instructors may demand full documentation of AI use. Its sample syllabus statements include separate 'Computer Code' options: one bans AI for developing code, the other allows AI-generated code if prompts and responses are recorded in comments and the student tests the code. Because of that code-specific section it is coded university-computing.

title: AI Guidance for Faculty
analyst_summary: Teaching-center guidance encouraging instructors to set their own AI policies, understand the tools, design instruction that accounts for AI, and add a separate AI statement to syllabi. It gives three sample statements: prohibited, allowed only for listed assignments with citation, and treated as documented collaborative work. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
analyst_summary: UAF's teaching-center page on generative AI. It asks instructors to explain plagiarism, state AI expectations in the syllabus, teach students how to cite AI, and set a protocol for deliberate misuse; it flags copyright, bias and FERPA/HIPAA concerns, suggests student and faculty uses, and frames AI as possible assistive technology. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: CMPUT 301 - Course Outline Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Software-engineering course outline that uses the U of A 'AI Use Generally Permitted' category: GenAI is allowed within each assessment's rules, but students must acknowledge it, cite it in code comments, and estimate the extent of use in the README. It also discloses that instructors use Gemini for AI-assisted grading, with privacy commitments, human responsibility for grades, labelled feedback and an opt-out.

course: CMPUT 401 Software Process and Product Management
title: Course Outline - CMPUT 401 Course Docs
analyst_summary: Capstone software-engineering course outline with a 'Statement of Expectations for AI Use'. It bans passing off ChatGPT output as one's own and requires citations (with a code-comment example).
