It warns that LLMs are often wrong, rates Stack Overflow as a better resource, and raises privacy concerns, using a worked CMPUT 229 example of a wrong ChatGPT answer.

title: CSC 120: Introduction to Computer Programming II (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Second-semester programming syllabus that requires individual work on all programs and forbids submitting work from ChatGPT or any AI, grouped with Stack Overflow and GitHub, with possible loss of credit. The CSC 210 Fall 2026 syllabus uses the same wording.

title: Academic Integrity at the College of Information Science
analyst_summary: A college-wide integrity policy covering text, code and media. It lists generating and submitting text or code with AI (e.g. ChatGPT) as prohibited in every course unless the instructor gives written permission. Instructors who require or allow such tools must say so in clear written instructions.

unit: Teaching Innovation and Pedagogical Support (TIPS); statements approved by the Faculty Senate committee and Provost's Office
title: Creating a Syllabus for Your Course (Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI))
analyst_summary: Tier 4. TIPS syllabus guide whose generative-AI section gives three standard statements (Prohibited, Restricted, Unrestricted Use) approved by the Faculty Senate academic integrity committee, integrity boards and the Provost's Office. Faculty choose; unauthorized or uncited AI use is academic dishonesty reported to the Office of Academic Initiatives and Integrity, and permitted users must verify and attribute AI content.

university: University of Arkansas at Little Rock
unit: Office of the Executive Vice Chancellor and Provost
title: Resources for Faculty on Student Use of AI
analyst_summary: Provost-office guidance for UA Little Rock faculty on setting course AI expectations, spotting likely AI use, and reporting misuse. It asks instructors to state AI rules in the syllabus with examples, treats detectors such as Turnitin as one input alongside instructor judgement, and describes talking with the student before reporting. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

university: University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences
unit: Division of Academic Affairs (Council of Deans, Provost)
title: UAMS Academic Affairs Policy 2.1.6: UAMS Artificial Intelligence Generative Tool Use Policy
analyst_summary: UAMS's formal academic-affairs policy on generative AI. It treats unattributed AI-generated work as plagiarism, requires disclosure of AI use (with exemptions for approved tools and mechanical uses), requires instructor authorization for student use with three course levels (prohibited, restricted, unrestricted), bars instructors from putting student work into AI or AI detectors without approval, calls detectors unreliable, requires governance-committee approval for AI-assisted grading, and mandates annual AI training. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Okanagan campus, Department of Computer Science, Mathematics, Physics and Statistics (Irving K. Barber Faculty of Science)
title: COSC 111-001: Computer Programming I, 2026W Term 1
analyst_summary: UBC Okanagan intro programming syllabus that allows ChatGPT and Copilot as learning supports, such as explaining material or comparing your own code with AI versions. Only specific assignments may use AI, other assessed work must be the student's own code, exams are AI-free, and unauthorized AI use counts as plagiarism.

title: CPSC 110 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Intro programming (CPSC 110) syllabus whose academic-integrity rules treat any copied code, explicitly including generative-AI output, as misconduct; designs must start from scratch or course starter files, and violations get a zero plus a report to the Dean of Science. The live site refused connections from this network, so the verbatim text was taken by curl from the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2025-08-05 (http://web.archive.org/web/20250805124957/https://cs110.students.cs.ubc.ca/admin/syllabus.html).

title: CPSC 210: GenAI and You
analyst_summary: A long rationale chapter in the CPSC 210 (Software Construction) textbook explaining why GenAI is allowed on the open-ended project and labs but not on in-class exercises or exams. It grounds the policy in learning-as-process and cites studies on learning loss, notes the instructors' own GenAI use, raises equity, and declines to teach fast-changing prompting tricks in favour of code fluency and decomposition skills.

title: CPSC 219 - Introduction to Computer Science for Multidisciplinary Studies II, Course Outline - Fall 2026
analyst_summary: A structured GenAI section (purpose, acceptable and unacceptable use, guidelines, consequences) with example prompts. AI is encouraged for learning, research and debugging help but may not produce submitted work or be used on exams. Students must disclose use and cite prompts, may be asked to explain code in an interview, and face graduated sanctions.

title: CPSC 231 - Introduction to Computer Science for Computer Science Majors I, Course Outline - Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Intro course outline that treats AI like any other outside help. Students must state the source and extent of any aid; 1-3 cited lines of code from outside sources, AI included, are allowed, but an assignment that is more than about 10% borrowed gets no credit even when cited. Exams allow no aids.

title: CPSC 331 - Data Structures, Algorithms, and Their Analysis, Course Outline - Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Data-structures course outline that strongly recommends solving practice and in-class problems without GenAI to prepare for coding exams with no internet or AI. It encourages supporting uses such as rubber-duck debugging, extra practice problems and concept explanations.

title: CSE 123, Spring 2026: Computer Networks
analyst_summary: Networking course policy (adapted from a data-science course's statement) that allows GenAI for understanding material and assisting on assignments, including C syntax and debugging, while reminding students that exams test their own understanding and that GenAI output is unreliable.

title: CSE 29 Winter 2025 - Syllabus
analyst_summary: Systems programming syllabus that prohibits generative AI on assignments, with a learning-integrity rationale. Grades take the minimum of assignment and assessment scores so that work done with outside help cannot carry the grade, and unusual code triggers in-person code reviews.

title: Syllabus | DSC 10
analyst_summary: DSC 10 permits GenAI for learning and for help on assignments, lists useful uses such as previewing material and debugging, and warns, with a worked ChatGPT example, that outputs can be subtly wrong. It sets guidelines (careful prompting, testing outputs, not submitting code you don't understand or that goes beyond course content) and requires citing AI-generated content in a space provided on each assignment.

course: DSC 80 (The Practice and Application of Data Science)
title: Syllabus | DSC 80
analyst_summary: DSC 80 shares DSC 10's GenAI framework (allowed for understanding and assignment help, with guidelines) but stresses that AI-written code often looks right without being right, and reports that students who leaned on ChatGPT the previous quarter produced code neither they nor staff could follow. Each assignment includes a space to explain and reflect on GenAI use.

title: Syllabus | CS 61A
analyst_summary: Syllabus for Berkeley's CS1, redesigned for the AI era. Students may not use AI to fill in or correct their code and take weekly quizzes without AI, yet homework is done with a course AI tutor that checks understanding (with a human alternative), a logging extension records how submissions were produced, and the final project uses AI coding agents.

title: Policies | CS 61B Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Data-structures course policy that bans any AI tool from touching student code or repositories (IDE assistants and agentic CLIs included) and bars LLM-generated code, while allowing high-level conceptual questions through browser chatbots. It lists reasonable versus forbidden prompts, uses random code interviews to check understanding, and explains the choice to hand-write code despite LLMs dominating professional coding.

unit: College of Computing, Data Science, and Society (CDSS)
course: Data C100 (Principles and Techniques of Data Science)
title: Syllabus | Data 100
analyst_summary: Data 100 prohibits using LLMs to generate written or code solutions unless an assignment designates a section where LLM use is allowed, and it bans pasting problem text into an LLM. It gives example 'productive' prompts (error messages, library syntax) and spells out escalating sanctions for inappropriate LLM use.

unit: College of Computing, Data Science, and Society (CDSS)
title: Syllabus | Data 8
analyst_summary: The Data 8 syllabus folds AI into its academic misconduct section: answers generated by AI are treated like answers copied from online sources and may not be used. It frames reliance on AI as both a misconduct risk and poor exam preparation.

title: Info 256. Applied Natural Language Processing
analyst_summary: The 'AI Assistants' section of this graduate iSchool NLP course ties AI use to the course's learning outcomes: coding assistants are fine for low-level Python tasks, but students must understand and be able to modify any code, and must author their own prose. Students are held responsible for anything an assistant produces, and final-project AI use must follow the ACL policy on AI writing assistance.

title: ECS 154B/201A: Computer Architecture - Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course syllabus for UC Davis's computer architecture course (Prof. Jason Lowe-Power), with a section on generative AI tools. It encourages students to use GitHub Copilot and ChatGPT when appropriate, lists acceptable uses (code help, drafting from one's own inputs, grammar) and one unacceptable use (unedited AI-written text), and holds students responsible for reviewing all submitted code and text.

unit: Donald Bren School of Information and Computer Sciences
title: ICS 33 Fall 2026, Course Reference
analyst_summary: Intermediate programming course that prohibits generative AI on skill-building grounds. Unusually, it pairs the ban with an instructor 'humanity pledge' not to use AI to communicate with students, and asks students to write their own messages to staff.

title: Using Generative AI Reflectively and Responsibly in Teaching and Learning
analyst_summary: Tier 4. A teaching-center guide that explains what generative AI is, its benefits and drawbacks (bias, inaccuracy, environmental cost), and how instructors should set course policy. It asks instructors to put their AI policy in the syllabus, possibly co-created with students, and offers three sample statements: not permitted, limited use with citation, and unrestricted. It also covers suspected misconduct, discussion of ethics, and equity and accessibility, including UCLA-licensed tools.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSE176 Introduction to Machine Learning (Fall semester 2025)
analyst_summary: Course page whose integrity policy requires students to disclose all sources, including any AI system with its URL and the prompts used. It discourages AI use and reserves the right to give zero for excessive use such as prompting with the assignment statement. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CS 141 Winter 2025 @ UCR (Intermediate Data Structures and Algorithms)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Course site for UCR's algorithms course. The collaboration policy allows outside sources when cited but requires students who use ChatGPT or other LLMs to submit the full conversation, requires close-book write-ups, and sets a minimum zero (typically -100%) penalty for cheating, including uncited use of ML tools.

title: Agentic AI - Using AI Agents (Claude, Codex, Copilot, etc.) to complete issues and PRs
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A page on the CMPSC 156 course website that lays out four ways to work with AI on development tasks: no AI, hand coding with AI help on demand, AI autocomplete in the editor, and agentic AI that completes whole issues and pull requests. The course encourages students to try all four at different stages. It says the no-AI mode is appropriate when learning a new technology.

title: Coding With AI - Hints on using AI agents to assist with coding tasks
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A CMPSC 156 course-website page with practical advice on using AI agents (GitHub Copilot, Gemini, ChatGPT and others) for coding tasks, using the writing of a test as its worked example. It tells students to give the agent full context, to expect several rounds, and to read and understand the generated code. It asks students to treat the agent as a way to learn testing rather than a way to avoid learning it.

title: Drafting a generative AI-use policy for your course
analyst_summary: Tier 1. TLC guide (linked from its 'Generative AI-Use Policy for Your Course' page) for writing a course AI policy: required components (allowed tasks, including writing, editing and debugging code; allowed tools; attribution and consequences), cautions and campus conditions on AI detectors, and four sample policies ranging from highly restrictive to substantial use. Two samples come from UCSC computing courses (a Python programming course and a lab course), which is why it is coded university-computing.

title: COP 3502C Section 1 Computer Science I - Fall 2025 Syllabus
analyst_summary: A CS1 (C and data structures) syllabus at a large Hispanic-Serving public university that allows AI tools only for general concept learning and bans them for any part of assignments, projects or exams. It grounds the rule in the instructor's own observation that AI harms learning, and treats AI-produced solutions as cheating with escalating negative-score penalties.

title: Policies - CMSC23530: Advanced Database Systems (Policy on Generative AI)
analyst_summary: Course policy page (stating it adapts the generative AI policy of the department's CS142 intro course) that forbids using GenAI such as ChatGPT or Copilot to write or generate any code, while allowing reference-style conceptual questions. Students must cite GenAI use with the exact prompt and a chat link, treat outputs critically because they may be wrong or conflict with course guidance, and think of GenAI as a helpful but fallible classmate.

title: CMSC 25700/35100: Natural Language Processing (AI tools policy)
analyst_summary: Short AI tools policy on an upper-level NLP course site that allows tools such as Claude Code and ChatGPT provided their use is disclosed for each submission. It nudges students to implement individual assignments themselves for learning, while encouraging creative use of AI as a learning collaborator.

course: CMSC 25910 (Engineering for Ethics, Privacy, and Fairness in Computer Systems)
title: CMSC 25910: Engineering for Ethics, Privacy, and Fairness in Computer Systems
analyst_summary: The AI/LLM policy bans generative models for all prose, even with citation. In coding tasks it treats them like StackOverflow: allowed with the prompt and influential output disclosed, capped at a few lines at a time, and never for the main intellectual work. A dated mid-term revision adds per-snippet prompt comments and bans feeding assignment text to an LLM.

unit: Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (CEAS)
title: EECE 6083/5183: Compiler Theory/Compiler Laboratory syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for an EECS compilers course. Its AI Policy section states that generative AI does not fit the course goals, that students must not seek help from tools like ChatGPT, and that any use to complete an assignment is academic dishonesty.

title: Syllabus - Fall 2026 | CSCI 3308
analyst_summary: Software development course syllabus that discourages generative AI but allows AI-generated code if the prompt and key parts of the response are documented in comments. Students must test and validate generated code. Undocumented use is treated as plagiarism, with a zero and escalation to the Honor Code process for repeat cases.

title: AI in Academics
analyst_summary: Faculty Resource Center page with sample syllabus entries (acceptable vs unacceptable uses, embrace, limited use), advice against prohibiting AI and against relying on detectors, and a five-level AI-Integrated Assessment Scale. It also recommends alternative pathways for students who do not want to use AI. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

university: University of Colorado Denver/Anschutz Medical Campus
unit: Division for Teaching Innovation and Program Strategy (TIPS)
title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
analyst_summary: TIPS resource hub for CU Denver instructors, framed as support for course-level decisions about AI. It lists approved AI tools, warns that outputs must be verified, points to the academic integrity policy and CLAS sample syllabus statements, and says campus AI policies are still being developed. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: School of Computing (Computer Science and Engineering)
title: CSE 1010 Introduction to Computing (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Intro computing syllabus (from UConn's public syllabus repository) that discourages AI as a first resource but allows it afterwards to diagnose a flawed approach, with disclosure required. It gives a five-step procedure for learning from AI without copying, and treats copied AI solutions as misconduct.

course: CSE 2050 Data Structures and Object-Oriented Design
title: CSE 2050 Data Structures and Object-Oriented Design, Fall 2024
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that bars submitting AI-written code while allowing AI to help understand concepts. AI assistance is banned during computer-based conceptual exams, and using ChatGPT to write assignment code is listed as academic misconduct carrying an F in the course.

unit: Academic Honor Code (Academic Catalog, Office of the Provost)
title: The Academic Honor Code
analyst_summary: The university honor code defines cheating to include AI use that violates instructor guidelines and adds a dedicated standard on AI products. It leaves permission to each instructor, tells students to check with the instructor before using AI, and notes guidelines may change over time. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: University of Delaware Information Technologies (UDIT), implementing the Directive for Appropriate Use of Generative AI Tools and Services
title: Guidelines and FAQs for Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence Tools at the University of Delaware
analyst_summary: Tier 4. University-wide FAQ accompanying UD's directive on generative AI. It limits which tools and data classifications may be used, says the instructor decides whether students may use AI for assignments (pointing to CTAL guidance), asks users to verify output, check for bias and be transparent about AI use, and covers course-content IP, FERPA, and instructor syllabus statements when AI tools are used in a course.

title: Concerns About Student Use (Artificial Intelligence)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. OTL faculty guidance on student AI use (DU has no campus-wide course-level AI policy). It advises discussing the Honor Code early, stating in the syllabus whether and how AI may be used, designing assessments around process and synthesis, not relying on AI detectors, and handling suspected misuse through conversation and DU's academic misconduct processes.

unit: Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering (CISE)
title: Programming Fundamentals I, COP3502C (Ashish Aggarwal, Fall 2025)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus whose academic honesty rules bar AI-generated or AI-suggested code along with copying and online solutions, require citing peers or internet resources consulted, and set escalating grade penalties plus Honor Court referral. The Spring 2026 version posted on the CISE syllabus page carries the same AI clause.

unit: Department of Computer & Information Science & Engineering (CISE)
title: Data Structures & Algorithms, COP 3530, Spring 2026 (GenAI and coding policy for assessments)
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that forbids generating whole functions or programs with genAI and using AI to write or translate reports, but allows AI for learning concepts or subtasks with citation of tool, model, and prompt. Violations bring an E and Honor Court referral, softened by a 48-hour regret clause.

title: Generative AI Policies for Teaching & Learning
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UGA CTL guidance on writing course generative-AI policies. It recommends treating AI policy as a pedagogical design decision, presents the five-level AI Assessment Scale, suggests student declaration and reflection statements with examples, and offers permissive, moderate and restrictive syllabus templates plus a traffic-light chart of uses. Violations are tied to UGA's 'A Culture of Honesty' and the Office of Academic Honesty.

unit: Office of the Associate Vice-President (Academic) / Office of Teaching and Learning
title: Provisional Recommendations for the Use of Generative AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Fall 2026 memo to Guelph educators from the Acting AVP (Academic) and the AVP Graduate Studies. Instructors decide whether AI is banned, allowed or required, and spell this out for each assessment. Existing misconduct rules cover unauthorized AI, detectors are not approved, identifiable student work must stay out of public AI tools, AI may not grade on its own, and TA use and instructors' own use are addressed.

unit: Department of Information and Computer Sciences
title: ICS 311 Fall 2026: Course Policies
analyst_summary: The course policies treat using LLMs such as ChatGPT or Claude to find problem-set solutions as plagiarism, alongside search engines and Q&A sites. The stated reason is that struggling with problems builds the skills needed for exams. Any academic dishonesty earns an F in the course.

title: COSC 4368 - Department of Computer Science (syllabus)
analyst_summary: AI course syllabus that permits ChatGPT and similar tools. Student reports must cite every AI tool used and say what it was used for. Failing to acknowledge AI use is a serious academic honesty violation.

unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
title: AI Guidelines (AI at the University of Idaho)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Teaching-center guidance (archived 2025 copy; live page now behind sign-in) that leaves the AI decision to each instructor and asks them to explain it and their rationale in the syllabus and assignment instructions. It lists possible student uses (including outlines for writing or coding), possible instructor uses for course materials, advice on citing AI, and links three syllabus templates: no AI, some AI, and unconditional AI.

title: Fall '25 Data+AI (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: A course site for an introductory data and AI course in UIC's CS department (a Hispanic-Serving Institution) that builds generative AI into nearly all activities, grades students partly on reflecting on their AI process, and expects a blanket attribution statement. Its do/don't lists permit using GenAI to generate code and content but forbid having ChatGPT do one's work or submitting unattributed GenAI output, with a grade penalty per offense.

unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
title: AI in CS 124
analyst_summary: Course-level position statement explaining why the intro course has embraced AI coding agents, requiring them (Claude Code) on an individual independent project while keeping AI banned on proctored quizzes that carry most of the grade. It gives rationale (career relevance, non-majors), describes scaffolding for AI-supported work, cost and equity notes, and an FAQ that clarifies scope and responsibility for validating AI-generated code.

unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
title: CS 124: Fall 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Syllabus that splits the course into two regimes: homework and quizzes where all code must be the student's own (AI may explain concepts but not produce code), and an independent project where an AI coding agent is expected to write most code and grading is based on logged hours of engaged work. It redefines integrity violations for the project around session logs, describes automated checks, and adds a responsible-AI section on differing policies elsewhere and AI's costs.

unit: Siebel School of Computing and Data Science
title: Syllabus (AI Policy)
analyst_summary: The CS 128 (C++) syllabus defines AI tools broadly, makes AI optional, and allows it only to support process (understanding, planning, debugging, reviewing) while the submitted code must be written and explainable by the student. It contrasts appropriate and inappropriate prompts, names vibe coding as a violation, cites prior-semester outcome data, requires a reflection form plus full transcript whenever AI is used, and bans all AI in proctored quizzes.

title: Syllabus | IS445 - Data Viz - BCU
analyst_summary: IS 445 limits LLM use to brainstorming, inspiration, expanding ideas, and improving writing. Pasting assignment questions into an LLM or having it answer questions directly is prohibited. Any LLM use must be documented with the model name, date, prompt, and a validation plan (sources for written claims, the student's own tests for code), and AI-generated sections must be marked. The policy notes that it was itself drafted with ChatGPT and then edited by two instructors.

title: AI Guidance: Sample Statements for Engineering
analyst_summary: College of Engineering (which houses the Siebel School) page offering four tiers of template syllabus statements (Restricted, Limited Use, Use When Instructed, All Use) with documentation and attribution requirements. It also reproduces the AI policy of CS 411: Database Systems as a computing-specific example that prohibits AI on some work and forbids it for database code.

unit: College of Liberal Arts and Sciences (CLAS), Dean's Office
title: Fall 2024 syllabus template
analyst_summary: Tier 3. Memo from the CLAS associate deans to department heads and faculty of the college that houses Iowa's Department of Computer Science, announcing the revised Fall 2024 collegiate syllabus template. Its AI section asks instructors to state permissible AI uses and integrity expectations, keep discussing AI policies through the semester, and teach students how to cite AI use; department heads must review all syllabi for compliance. The AI guidance points to the Provost's 'AI in the Classroom' page.

unit: KU Artificial Intelligence (ai.ku.edu, university AI task force)
title: Guidance for Instructors
analyst_summary: Tier 4. University-wide GenAI guidance for KU instructors. It leaves teaching about or with GenAI to instructors by course and discipline, asks them to state expectations in the syllabus and remind students about academic integrity, and advises against AI plagiarism detectors because of false positives and bias. It points to the Center for Teaching Excellence for syllabus language and modules.

unit: UK ADVANCE (Office of the Provost generative AI committee)
title: UK ADVANCE 2025 Guidelines and Recommendations for Generative AI in Instructional Contexts
analyst_summary: Tier 4. University-wide guidance from UK's generative AI committee for instructors. It covers AI capabilities and risks (privacy, accuracy, learning, ethics), what an effective course AI policy should contain along a four-point spectrum from no use to free use, how to respond to suspected misuse, and assignment design. It recommends against using AI detectors to determine academic offenses.

title: Understand AI Policies that Affect You and Your Teaching
date_or_term: Student Code of Conduct Policy, Summer 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Teaching Centre page that reproduces section 5.2.1.10 of the 2025 Student Code of Conduct on AI tools. Under it, instructors may permit, limit or ban AI, students must consult them, and breaking those instructions is an academic offence. The page advises instructors to state AI expectations and their rationale in several places.

unit: Academic Affairs Division / Office of the Provost
title: UL Lafayette Guidance on Generative Artificial Intelligence in the Classroom
analyst_summary: Provost-level guidance that leaves AI rules to colleges, departments and faculty, and lists what course policies should cover: the range of permitted uses, responsible use, transparency/citation, and penalties. It ends with sample prohibiting, mixed and encouraging syllabus statements. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Committee on Use of Generative AI in UofL Academics (formed by the Provost)
title: Report of the Committee on Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in University of Louisville Academics
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Committee report commissioned by the Provost at the Faculty Senate's request. It recommends that every syllabus state a GenAI policy chosen from three options (none, permission plus citation, unrestricted), proposes Student Code revisions, urges caution about AI detectors, and covers teaching, training, research uses (including programming) and data-protection risks.

unit: University Teaching Council / Office of Community Standards, Rights, and Responsibilities
title: Generative AI Teaching and Learning Guidelines
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UMaine-wide guidelines on generative AI in teaching and learning, covering responsibilities, equity, privacy/FERPA, syllabus statements with a spectrum of use categories from requiring to forbidding AI, disclosure and citation, academic integrity, instructor use of AI for teaching and assessment, professional development and annual review.

unit: Centre for the Advancement of Teaching and Learning (CATL)
title: Syllabus statements: academic integrity and generative artificial intelligence (genAI)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Teaching-centre page of adaptable syllabus statements in three groups: genAI allowed (with documentation, appendices of prompts and citation), allowed with boundaries, and prohibited (several wordings explicitly naming AI coding assistants and computer code). It also advises instructors on opt-outs for cost and privacy, explaining their rationale, and reminding students that rules differ across courses.

unit: UMB Information Technology / Office of Institutional Policy Management
title: University of Maryland, Baltimore Artificial Intelligence (AI) Guidelines
analyst_summary: Campus-wide AI guidelines for faculty, students, researchers and staff. For teaching, it leaves AI use to course-instructor discretion with a required syllabus statement, treats undisclosed or prohibited use as misconduct akin to cheating or plagiarism, discourages reliance on AI detectors (FERPA/privacy risk), and addresses instructor use of AI for grading, HIPAA/FERPA data limits, and research use. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Electrical Engineering (CSEE)
title: CMSC 491/691 Active Cyber Defense
analyst_summary: A cybersecurity course page whose generative AI section permits AI use but requires full disclosure of prompts, raw outputs and student edits for prose and code, with credit scaled to how much the use circumvented learning outcomes. Grammar checkers and small-scale predictive text are exempted from disclosure. The same wording appears in other UMBC CSEE syllabi (e.g., CMSC 671), suggesting a shared departmental template.

title: CMSC131 (Fall 2026) - Object-Oriented Programming I: Syllabus
analyst_summary: First programming course syllabus that lists AI use to develop code as a violation of the Code of Academic Integrity alongside copying and outside help, with referral to the Office of Student Conduct.

title: CMSC 132 Object-Oriented Programming II, sections 010X and 020X, Fall 2026 (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Second programming course syllabus that prohibits using AI to produce any graded coursework but allows AI for looking up course-material information, while steering students to office hours because AI answers can be wrong. It also forbids uploading the instructor's course materials to AI sites on copyright grounds.

title: CMSC216: Introduction to Computer Systems (Syllabus, Sections 1xx / 2xx)
analyst_summary: Systems course syllabus with a two-zone design: take-home work is free collaboration where LLMs and chatbots are allowed, but students lose credit if they cannot explain their work, and projects carry a reflective work disclosure. Exams are open-resource but ban all AI tools, including AI features in eyewear or hearing aids, and the provided exam environment disables AI.

unit: Manning College of Information & Computer Sciences (CICS)
title: Course Policies - Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI Policy)
analyst_summary: AI course policy that treats prompt engineering as a career skill but channels student use through a course-built tool ('383GPT') that logs prompts for staff review. Code produced through the course tool may be submitted without attribution, while external generative AI tools are prohibited unless an assignment says otherwise.

unit: Office of the Provost (Academic Integrity), per Faculty Council recommendation
title: Faculty Guidance - Academic Integrity (Academic integrity and AI)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost's academic integrity guidance for faculty. Its AI section relays the Faculty Council recommendation that every syllabus include one of two statements: one barring AI tools such as ChatGPT for any portion of an assignment, and one allowing AI on specified assignments with detailed citation and the full AI transcript as an appendix, treating misuse or uncited AI help as academic dishonesty.

unit: Faculty Senate (UMass Dartmouth Guidelines on the Use of Generative AI)
title: UMass Dartmouth Guidelines on the Use of Generative AI
analyst_summary: Faculty Senate-approved guidelines (official PDF, publicly available only via a news outlet's copy). They frame generative AI as mimicking rather than replacing human work, encourage syllabus AI statements, prohibit student AI use absent explicit permission, require students to disclose and describe AI's role, ask faculty requiring AI to protect student identities and work, and treat unattributed AI-generated text, images or code as academic dishonesty. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Office of the Provost / Faculty Senate (Undergraduate Catalog academic policy)
title: Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UMass Lowell's undergraduate Academic Integrity Policy, amended in 2024 to address AI. It defines as academic dishonesty the use of AI as an unauthorized material and specifically the use of generative AI tools, including code generators, without explicit instructor permission, including pasting questions into AI, submitting AI output as original work, and failing to disclose AI use. It then lists instructor and university sanctions.

title: COMP 1900 CS 1 – Introduction to Programming – Fall 2026 (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus whose plagiarism policy requires all graded work to be individually written code. Copying code from generative AI tools is listed alongside homework-help sites as unacceptable behaviour, with a zero-tolerance sanction scheme. Tier 1 (CS course policy).

title: COMP 4745/6745 Machine Learning Fall 2024 (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Machine learning syllabus that bars using generative AI to write project reports or code, but allows it for polishing writing and debugging. Students remain responsible for correctness and may be asked to explain or re-create code if authorship is in doubt. Tier 1 (CS course policy).

title: Course Syllabus: Spring Term 2026 Data Mining (COMP 7118)
analyst_summary: Graduate data mining syllabus that allows unrestricted use of foundation models (chat, code, and image generators) and encourages it. Students are responsible for any inaccurate, biased or offensive content they submit and must acknowledge model contributions, with penalties for unacknowledged use. Tier 1 (CS course policy).

title: CSC120 General Information (Fall 2024)
analyst_summary: Intro programming course page that welcomes AI tools for help with programming and for discussing general solution techniques, but forbids copying solutions. It warns that AI-generated code often uses constructs the course has not taught yet and does not meet its style rules.

title: Syllabus – EECS 183 Python
analyst_summary: The Python section of the intro programming course grounds a restrictive AI policy in the need for students to struggle with logic themselves. AI (explicitly including university-licensed tools and autocompletion) is barred from all graded tasks, with limited study uses allowed outside graded work and some later activities designed for AI; violating the AI policy is listed as an Honor Code violation.

title: EECS 280 Syllabus
analyst_summary: The EECS 280 syllabus ties generative AI and AI-assisted editors to the course's collaboration rules: AI may be used only where help from another person would be allowed. A two-column table lists allowed uses (learning concepts, understanding compiler errors, brainstorming edge cases, practice questions) and prohibited ones (generating submitted code or tests, exhaustive proofreading, exams), plus a ban on deceptive or malicious AI use; suspected violations go to the Engineering Honor Council.

course: SI 301 Models of Social Information Processing
title: Syllabus for SI 301 001 FA 2024
analyst_summary: Public PDF of a UMSI course syllabus with a 'Use of AI-Generated Text' section. It encourages AI for exploring concepts and polishing explanations while discouraging its use on weekly problems, warns about hallucination, privacy and carbon cost, and requires a disclosure paragraph with prompts and outputs.

title: Generative AI and Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Campus page leaving AI adoption entirely to each instructor and telling students to check professor, syllabus and assignment. It frames AI as a collaborative tool rather than sole author, explains Academic Code of Conduct consequences, and states the campus will not adopt AI detection and detector results cannot be used in discipline. Verbatim text taken from a 2026 Wayback snapshot because the live page blocks automated fetches. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSci 5271: 5271 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: The syllabus treats AI tools like asking a person outside the class. Students may use them to understand concepts and for ungraded work, but not to replace their own understanding or effort on graded assignments unless an assignment says otherwise. This includes taking the idea of a solution from a tool.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCI5421: Syllabus
analyst_summary: An algorithms syllabus that requires homework and exams to be done without AI. It defines using AI to generate solutions as plagiarism in the course.

unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (CETL)
title: CETL Syllabus Template: Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Section of the CETL syllabus template, linked from the UM Libraries AI guide. Policy text lets each instructor decide which AI uses are allowed or count as misconduct, and asks for clear syllabus statements. CETL warns that detectors are unreliable and may breach privacy, notes that bans are hard to enforce, and gives permitted and not-permitted model statements covering disclosure and responsibility.

title: AI Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost reference document for building a course GenAI policy at Mizzou. It sorts example syllabus statements into three levels (prohibited, limited use, integration allowed), adds transparency and citation guidelines, and points to discipline examples. Several statements make prohibition the default unless use is explicitly allowed and ask students to keep drafts or AI logs.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) Tools and Sample Syllabus Policy Statements
analyst_summary: Provost page recommending an AI policy in every syllabus, framed in three levels (restrictive, supervised, permissive), with cautions on instructor transparency, FERPA, and AI detectors. Its permissive examples include a statement from the School of Science and Engineering Computer Science program that allows documented AI use and treats undocumented use as dishonesty. Tier 1 (CS-program statement from the School of Science and Engineering, published on a university-computing provost page).

title: Deep Learning (CMPSCI 4390/5390)
analyst_summary: Course website with an activity-by-activity GenAI table: no AI on quizzes, exams, presentations or reading summaries; AI allowed on assignments only for explaining errors and reviewing one's own code; broad use including agentic coding tools on the semester project with disclosure. Students must be able to explain any AI-assisted work, checked via an oral final exam and process-revealing tools. Tier 1 (CS course).

unit: AI Learning Lab (Division of Innovative and Learning-Centric Initiatives)
title: AI for Students: Policies, Responsible Use, and Practical Applications
analyst_summary: A UNO AI Learning Lab template page for course Canvas sites: faculty insert their own AI course policy, and the page tells students that instructors decide whether AI is allowed, that pasting AI answers to assignment questions violates UNO's academic integrity policy, that AI-assisted work must be cited, that students remain responsible for submissions, and that private data must not be entered. It ends with examples of AI uses for learning. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Developing course policies around A.I.
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UNL teaching-center guidance noting that the Faculty Senate now requires an AI policy in every syllabus, with the choice of policy left to the instructor. It ties AI to the Student Code of Conduct's cheating definition, advises communicating the policy often, varying it by assignment type, explaining the rationale, naming embedded AI tools, and requiring citation when AI is allowed, and offers example policies in three categories (permitted, allowed under conditions, prohibited).

title: CS 301: Social Implications of Computer Technology, Course Syllabus (Spring 2026)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Spring 2026 syllabus for UNLV's required computing ethics course. Students are responsible for their submitted work whatever tools they used, must openly acknowledge any generative AI content or translation (tool name and marked passages), and must keep the full AI output until the end of term. Exams are closed-book with devices off.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CS 474/674 Image Processing and Interpretation, Fall 2026 (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Syllabus with a 'Use of Generative AI' section treating unauthorized use as cheating under UNR policy, with exceptions described in individual assignment instructions. It lists specific banned practices, such as pasting assignment or test questions into an LLM and using AI to summarize readings. The wording appears to follow UNR template language.

course: Courses taught by D. Bremner (e.g., CS 2613, CS 4613, CS 6905)
title: Policy on the use of generative AI
analyst_summary: One instructor's generative AI policy covering all his CS courses. It reads the UNB plagiarism policy's 'someone else' as the creators of the training data, so students must cite original sources and not only the AI service. AI is not a source of facts. Writing feedback is allowed, but copying large blocks counts as plagiarism or non-completion.

unit: University of New England academic administration (AI Policy Guidance for Faculty, supporting the Institutional AI Policy)
title: AI Policy Guidance for Faculty
analyst_summary: UNE guidance implementing its institutional AI policies for teaching. Every syllabus must state a specific AI policy (required since September 2024) and faculty must disclose their own AI use in course design; it covers AI literacy, citation and transcript-based disclosure, protected data, and advises against relying on AI detectors. Sample syllabus statements are in an appendix. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

title: Syllabus Guidance Fall 2026 for UNH Durham and Manchester (1.5 Artificial Intelligence)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost's syllabus guidance for UNH Durham and Manchester. Its AI section asks instructors to state explicitly whether and how AI may be used (including their own use), says the university prefers guided use over blanket bans, suggests an AI Assessment Scale, and offers two sample statements: one prohibiting AI (including lecture transcription and uploading course materials) and one permitting AI with citation and student responsibility for accuracy.

title: CS 491/591-006 (CS 422/522) Digital Image Processing
analyst_summary: AI is allowed for learning, but students must fully understand their code. Random oral checks after each submission enforce this, and submitting AI-generated code counts as academic dishonesty.

title: CSC 365 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Web development course syllabus whose AI Use Policy allows AI for brainstorming, coding assistance and understanding but not for completing whole assignments. Students must disclose prompts and contributions, comment AI-generated lines in code, and receive a zero for undisclosed AI work or work over 20% AI-generated. Tier 1 (CS course).

university: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill
title: Syllabus - COMP110 - 26S (Artificial Intelligence (AI) Use Policy)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that reproduces UNC's campus-wide student AI guidelines (help you think, evaluate outputs, document and cite use) while separately listing copying code from generative AI models among non-permitted resources on graded work. The prior Fall 2025 version had no such AI-guidelines section.

university: University of North Carolina at Greensboro
unit: Department of Information Systems and Supply Chain Management, Bryan School of Business and Economics
title: SYLLABUS SPRING 2025 ISM 671-01: Organizing Data for Analytics
analyst_summary: Syllabus for a graduate database design and SQL course in UNCG's information systems program. Its Generative AI Use Policy (adapted from Harvard) requires all submitted work to be the student's own, forbids generative AI at every stage including preliminary work, treats violations as academic integrity violations, and reminds students that policies differ across courses. Tier 2 (CS-related unit: information systems course; no CS department or CS course AI policy found).

title: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
analyst_summary: UND Provost's general guidelines and FAQ on generative AI for faculty, staff and students. It stresses user responsibility for accuracy and transparent documentation, bars private or restricted data, asks faculty to state AI expectations in syllabi and warns about flawed detectors, and tells students that policies vary by course and that uncited or non-compliant AI use may be academic dishonesty. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: UNF Artificial Intelligence site (Faculty Resources; CIRT / Office of Faculty Excellence)
title: UNF: Faculty Resources (Artificial Intelligence at UNF)
analyst_summary: University AI faculty-resources page telling instructors to update course policies and set clear, upfront boundaries on allowed and prohibited AI uses. It points to Office of Faculty Excellence syllabus language (intranet only) and encourages faculty to teach AI's benefits and limits and to state consequences when AI is not allowed. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCE 1030: Computer Science I Syllabus, Summer 2025 10W
analyst_summary: Tier 1. The academic-integrity section of an intro programming syllabus. Individual programming projects must be solo work, and students may not use answers from generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot; similarity software checks submissions. Unauthorized AI use counts as cheating under UNT policy, and a first violation means an F in the course.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCE 3201 – Applied Artificial Intelligence (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A brief AI rule in the programming-assignments section of an applied AI course. Students may use ChatGPT or Copilot to check syntax and debug, but not to write solutions for them.

unit: Office of the Provost (AI Task Force)
title: Guidance on the acceptability of using generative AI in coursework
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Non-binding guidance from the Provost's AI Task Force clarifying course-outline expectations for generative AI. Instructors choose whether and how AI is used and must communicate it; silence implies use is unrestricted, while students are told to assume possible restriction. It addresses privacy impact assessment before requiring tools, alternative assignments for students unable to use AI, citation, and sample syllabus statements.

unit: Center for the Enhancement of Teaching and Learning (CETL)
title: Syllabus Statements
analyst_summary: CETL syllabus-statement bank whose academic integrity statement lists unauthorized AI use as misconduct, and whose AI section groups sample statements (mostly borrowed from other universities) into three levels: no use, use under some circumstances or with permission, and broader use within guidelines. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSE Guide to the Honor Code
analyst_summary: Department-wide honor-code guide for all CSE courses. It treats generative AI such as ChatGPT, LLaMA or Copilot like any other source, citing the university policy that AI output is someone else's work. It sets a resource-vs-solution and consult-vs-copy framework that syllabi use to mark each activity as allowed, allowed with citation, or not allowed, with worked ChatGPT/quicksort examples and a sample citation.

unit: School of Computer Science, Gallogly College of Engineering
course: CS 1323 Introduction to Computer Programming for Programmers
title: CS 1323 Syllabus Spring 2026 University of Oklahoma
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus (posted on the department's public syllabus page). It allows AI only on assignments that explicitly permit it, saying no evidence shows AI-completed assignments build understanding. Copying AI output is plagiarism, and students suspected of AI use must explain their solution in person. CS 1324 (Trytten) uses nearly identical text.

unit: School of Computer Science, Gallogly College of Engineering
title: CS 2334: Programming Structure/Abstractions Spring 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Second-year programming syllabus that bans generative AI (ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, Gemini, Grammarly AI) for every part of the coursework, including brainstorming and editing, because the process is part of the learning. Assessments are designed for controlled settings, and violations can mean a zero or a failing grade.

unit: School of Computer Science, Gallogly College of Engineering
title: CS 2414 – Data Structures – Spring 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that allows ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot for understanding concepts, debugging and generating ideas. Students must mark AI-assisted parts in code comments, hand in their prompts as a separate document, and stay responsible for correctness; copying AI solutions without understanding may be misconduct.

unit: School of Computer and Data Sciences (Computer Science)
title: Syllabus for Fall 2023 CS 212
analyst_summary: A short generative-AI paragraph in an intro-sequence syllabus. Students may choose to use generative AI on projects, it is banned on closed-book exams, and students bear responsibility for being able to produce comparable work without it.

unit: School of Computer and Data Sciences
title: CS 322, Fall 2025
analyst_summary: Software engineering course redesigned around three stages of AI use: no AI for the early projects, AI as a pair programmer (with prompts submitted) for projects 5 and 6, and unrestricted AI for the final project. It notes hallucination risks and that suspected unauthorized use may be reported for misconduct.

unit: Academic integrity (Study / Office of the Vice-Provost, Academic Affairs)
title: Academic integrity
analyst_summary: Tier 4. The university's official student-facing academic integrity page, which includes an FAQ on artificial intelligence. It says AI permission varies by course and assignment, that students must check the syllabus or ask the professor, and that any AI use must be disclosed and cited. It also lists AI limitations (bias, hallucinated citations) and privacy cautions.

unit: Department of Computer and Information Science (School of Engineering and Applied Science)
title: CIS 1100 Policies Governing Academic Integrity
analyst_summary: Intro programming policy that bans AI on exams and homework presentations while allowing (though not advising) AI help on homework projects without copying AI-generated solutions. It lists acceptable uses (clarifying notes, error messages, research) and unacceptable ones (generating code or README text, pasting assignment instructions), requires citing AI-taught techniques, and warns of academic consequences.

unit: Department of Computer and Information Science (School of Engineering and Applied Science)
course: CIS 1200 Programming Languages and Techniques I
title: CIS 1200 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Second-course syllabus whose academic integrity list forbids using AI tools to generate code and forbids asking tools such as ChatGPT to debug student code, alongside conventional rules against copying and sharing files.

unit: School of Computing and Information, Department of Computer Science
title: CS 0445 - Algorithms and Data Structures 1, Fall 2023
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus whose 'No Use of Generative AI Permitted' section (worded like Pitt's teaching-center template) bans ChatGPT and all other generative AI at any time and requires all work to be the student's own. This is an older (Fall 2023) term, but it is the only public Pitt CS course AI statement found.

unit: School of Computing and Information (Department of Computer Science)
title: CS1632_Fall2026 syllabus.md
analyst_summary: This software engineering course sets AI rules by type of assessment. Formative exercises allow help from instructors, classmates, and generative AI, used judiciously. Quizzes, the final exam, and the final project ban AI, and any AI help on the final project is treated as cheating. The syllabus refers students to the SCI Academic Integrity Policy.

unit: Office of the Provost (University Academic Regulations, Bulletin 2026-2027)
title: Code of Academic Integrity (University Academic Regulations, Bulletin 2026-2027)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UP's university Code of Academic Integrity, which adds 'Misuse of AI' as a violation comparable to cheating or plagiarism. It says what counts as misuse depends on context and discipline and lists examples (submitting AI output as one's own, unauthorized AI use, not acknowledging AI contributions); the rest of the code sets violation levels and reporting procedures.

unit: Teaching and Learning Centre / Generative AI Task Force (GAIT)
title: Guidance on Using Generative AI in Teaching and Learning (Provisional Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI)
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Provisional guidelines from UPEI's Generative AI Task Force, adapted from McMaster's, hosted on the Teaching and Learning Centre's resource site. Instructors decide whether to use AI, must communicate expectations and disclose their own use, provide equitable access and opt-outs, and may not use AI detectors to substantiate misconduct; privacy and student consent rules apply. A short student section covers verification, responsibility, and transparency.

unit: Junta de Gobierno, Universidad de Puerto Rico (system-wide policy applying to the Mayagüez campus)
title: Política de Uso de Inteligencia Artificial en la Universidad de Puerto Rico (Certificación 66, 2024-2025)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Spanish-language system-wide AI regulation of the University of Puerto Rico, which governs all campuses including Mayagüez; no UPRM-specific or CIIC/ICOM AI policy was found. Its academic section lets faculty use AI for content, assessment and feedback (respecting FERPA), allows students to use AI only when their professors authorize it, treats unauthorized AI use during assessments as academic dishonesty, and requires every syllabus to state AI rules.

university: University of Puerto Rico, Rio Piedras
unit: Decanato de Asuntos Académicos (Deanship of Academic Affairs)
title: Circular 8 (2024-2025) Lineamientos y guías para la integración y uso de la Inteligencia Artificial (IA) en los proyectos académicos y de investigación del Recinto de Río Piedras
analyst_summary: Spanish-language campus circular from the Rio Piedras academic affairs dean. It requires every syllabus and every assignment to state the permitted level of AI use, defines five levels adapted from the AI Assessment Scale (prohibited through open use) with sample syllabus text and disclosure requirements for each, and asks faculty to discuss the levels with students at course start. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Generative AI Hub (Office of the Associate Vice-President Academic)
title: Instructor Resources (Generative AI Hub)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. University-wide instructor guidance that leaves AI decisions to each instructor but asks for a syllabus statement, assignment-level rules, a stated rationale, and student disclosure through a transparency framework. It gives sample statements (prohibited, writing assistance only, allowed for some tasks) and sample assignments. One sample is a computer coding assignment that maps which programming learning objectives AI supports or undermines. It also warns that AI detectors are only supplementary.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Statistics
title: CSC 212: Data Structures (Fall 2026)
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus that lets students use generative AI freely on condition of disclosure. A table compares ways of using a model and what each does for learning, a team project is built with AI on purpose and must report what the team fixed or rejected, and some assignments carry oral check-ins.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Statistics
title: CSC 411 Machine Organization (Prof. Noah M. Daniels, syllabus)
analyst_summary: Systems course syllabus (no term stated) that allows generative AI only 'in a tutorial fashion' for general questions. Students may not paste assignments or code into the tool or paste its results into their work, must document any prompts and outputs, and risk a zero for violations.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Statistics
title: CSC 461: Machine Learning (Fall 2024)
analyst_summary: Machine learning syllabus that welcomes ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Copilot as learning aids for brainstorming, code analysis and problem solving. Any AI-generated content must be cited with the tool named, AI-suggested code must be understood before it is used, and uncredited AI content counts as plagiarism.

title: CSC 171 - Introduction To Computer Science
analyst_summary: Intro course page that weighs AI's educational risks and benefits, prohibits using AI to complete homework in whole or part, and requires students to be able to explain their submitted work. It also commits that AI will not be used for grading or feedback.

unit: Shiley-Marcos School of Engineering, MS Applied Data Science (Online) program
title: Shiley-Marcos School of Engineering MS Applied Data Science (Online) Graduate Student Handbook 2023-2024
analyst_summary: Program handbook for USD's online MS in Applied Data Science, which contains a three-point 'Generative AI Guidelines' section. Students may use ChatGPT-like tools to support their learning but must disclose AI-generated content through citation, verify its accuracy, and keep developing their own critical thinking; the handbook also restates the engineering school's academic integrity procedure. Tier 2 (data science program; no CS-specific AI policy found).

unit: Office of the Provost (Joint University Curriculum Committee)
title: Syllabus Statement Options for Generative AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Provost-approved set of three syllabus statements instructors choose from: comprehensive AI use with attribution, use only within instructor parameters, or AI strongly discouraged / not permitted. A note warns that prohibition may be unenforceable and raises equity concerns.

title: CMPT 434-02 Term 2, 2024-25 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Upper-year networking syllabus with a single 'Use of Generative AI Tools' rule: any GenAI use on assignments or the project is banned and counts as academic misconduct.

title: CMPT 815-01 Term 1, 2024-25 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Graduate course syllabus, same instructor as CMPT 434 but a different rule: any GenAI use for paper summaries, assignments or the project needs the instructor's approval in advance.

title: Computer Science Graduate Student Generative AI Policy
analyst_summary: Department-level GenAI policy for Computer Science graduate students. Course use is left to each instructor, who must state the rules. Using GenAI in a thesis requires written permission from the supervisor and a transparency statement. The policy also covers bias, privacy, publishing and peer-review rules, and calls violations academic misconduct.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Usage for Faculty and Student Use in Academic Coursework
analyst_summary: Academic Affairs policy covering faculty use of GenAI for course materials and grading (licensed tools only, for FERPA) and requiring one of two syllabus options (prohibited, or permitted as specified). It lists default allowed and prohibited student uses, including submitting AI-generated code as original work, and routes violations through the Student Academic Conduct Policy. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CSCE 491: Capstone Computer Engineering Project Spring 2026
analyst_summary: Capstone syllabus that allows generative AI as a development tool. Students must explain their project code in demos, and some lab code is tested on closed-book written exams.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: Tentative Syllabus CSCE 763: Digital Image Processing (Spring 2026)
analyst_summary: Graduate image processing syllabus requiring credit for any AI use. Students must add an appendix with the full exchange, the exact tools, how they were used and why. AI is barred from quizzes, exams and homework unless permitted, and students are urged to use it reflectively.

unit: University of South Dakota (Artificial Intelligence information hub, Faculty)
title: Generative AI Information: Faculty
analyst_summary: USD's faculty guidance on generative AI. Faculty must state in each syllabus whether AI is allowed, limited or prohibited and explain why, design process-focused assignments, keep sensitive data out of unapproved tools (Copilot is the approved platform), avoid using AI to replace grading judgment, and handle suspected misuse through conversation and evidence such as oral explanation or drafts rather than relying on detector scores. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing
title: CAP 4111 Introduction to Augmented & Virtual Reality (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for a Bellini College computing course (instructor Zhao Han) with a full 'Acceptable Use of Generative AI Tools' policy. GenAI is allowed for all submissions, as in the workplace, but students must verify output, cite all AI content and use AI only as a supplement. Copying AI code or writing is not allowed, misuse brings penalties up to program dismissal under USF and Bellini integrity policy, and assignments where AI is inappropriate will be marked. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing
title: CDA 4621 Control of Mobile Robots (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for a Bellini College robotics programming course (instructor Alfredo Weitzenfeld). Its lab policy treats unacknowledged AI use as plagiarism unless verifiable references are given, and requires exact prompts and results whenever AI generates code. Identical code from the same AI prompt also counts as plagiarism, and any plagiarism brings an F for the lab and possibly the course. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Bellini College of Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Computing
title: CIS 4219 Human Aspects of Cybersecurity (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for a Bellini College cybersecurity course (instructor Yili Ren). Noting that tools like ChatGPT can produce text and code, it lets students use AI as a supplemental editor but requires citing and describing all AI content, bans AI on quizzes and exams, and lets the professor require students to show deep understanding. Students are responsible for checking AI output for accuracy. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Thomas Lord Department of Computer Science, Viterbi School of Engineering
title: CSCI 103L Introduction to Programming (Syllabus)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus banning AI for any purpose on homework, projects and exams, with an exercise analogy as rationale. Projects are paired with exams of equal weight so that outsourcing coding to an LLM shows up in exam scores; violations are reported to the integrity office.

title: Artificial Intelligence (USM AI Syllabus Policy; Artificial Intelligence Usage Policy for Instruction)
date_or_term: Implemented Spring 2024; policy as of May 6, 2025
analyst_summary: Provost page requiring every course syllabus to state whether AI is permitted and how to cite it, motivated by a rise in AI-related integrity violations. It supplies mandatory syllabus language with three usage options (encouraged, permissible for specified assignments, human-generated work only), including a note that instructors may use AI detection software. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Min H. Kao Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science
course: COSC 202 Data Structures and Algorithms I
title: COSC 202 Data Structures and Algorithms I Spring 2024 Syllabus (Draft)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for UTK's first data-structures course (C++). Its honor-code section bars copying complete solutions or code for the key topic being assessed, but lets students use outside resources, including generative AI or Copilot, for non-critical parts of labs, provided they cite the tool in code comments and take responsibility for the code passing tests. Retrieved from an Internet Archive snapshot because web.eecs.utk.edu returns 403 to automated requests.

university: University of Texas at El Paso
title: UTEP Department of Computer Science CS 1310 – Introduction to Computational Thinking
analyst_summary: Introductory syllabus that limits AI tools such as ChatGPT to learning and reinforcement outside graded work. AI is banned on every assessment unless an assignment explicitly allows it, and noncompliance is treated as an academic integrity violation.

university: University of Texas at El Paso
course: CS 2401 Elementary Data Structures and Algorithms
title: Spring 2026 CS 2401 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Second-course CS syllabus with a short 'Using generative AI' paragraph. It allows tools like ChatGPT to complement learning but restricts them on exams and quizzes, requires proper citation, and refers violations to the student conduct office.

university: University of Texas at El Paso
title: CS-4379/5375: Software Reverse Engineering Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Security course syllabus with an OK / NOT OK collaboration list and a 'Guidance on Artificial Intelligence' paragraph. AI may be used for brainstorming and as a cited source, students must share a link to their AI chat history, and copying AI solutions or submitting AI work as one's own counts as plagiarism.

university: University of Texas at San Antonio
unit: Department of Computer Science (College of AI, Cyber and Computing)
title: CS 1063 901 Introduction to Computer Programming I (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Public Simple Syllabus page for a Fall 2026 section of UTSA's intro programming course (instructor Byron Long). Its GenAI guidelines section is a flat ban: GenAI is not authorized, and programs created with AI earn a zero on the assignment or exam. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

university: University of Texas at San Antonio
unit: Department of Computer Science (College of AI, Cyber and Computing)
title: CS 1083 901 Programming I for Computer Scientists (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for UTSA's first programming course for CS majors (instructor Mauricio Alejandro Gomez Morales). Its GenAI Use Policy bans GenAI for all work before the first exam, then allows it only as a learning and debugging aid, with lists of permitted and banned uses. Students must be able to explain and demonstrate any submitted work, and failing to do so may count as an integrity violation. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

university: University of Texas at San Antonio
unit: Department of Computer Science (College of AI, Cyber and Computing)
title: CS 2113 901 Fundamentals of Object-Oriented Programming (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for UTSA's object-oriented programming course (instructor John Heaps). The instructor does not restrict GenAI and encourages experimenting with it as a real-world coding skill, but advises against using it to write code or full solutions in an introductory course. Students are told to use it to learn, because over-reliance will leave them unprepared. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Center for Excellence in Teaching and Learning (Office of the Provost)
title: Assignments, AI Tool and Policies
analyst_summary: CETL guidance for the Simple Syllabus template explaining that the AI Tool Usage section is required, so every instructor must state how generative AI may be used, limited or prohibited. Sample language is provided in the template's help text. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: Course Syllabus (CSC108H1F, Fall 2025)
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that prohibits using generative AI to produce code for for-credit work, with a learning rationale (false mastery, unprepared for supervised tests and CSC148). Students instead get a course-trained AI tool (LearnAid), and the instructors flag that the policy may be revised later in the term. Most recent public DCS outline found (Fall 2025); no Fall 2026 outline was posted.

title: Course Syllabus (CSC148H1F, Fall 2025)
analyst_summary: Second intro CS syllabus permitting generative AI (ChatGPT, Copilot) as a learning aid but banning it on the midterm and final. It warns about unvetted tools (privacy, IP, records), similarity of AI-generated code across students, and over-reliance, and places responsibility for learning and submitted work on the student.

title: INF2214 Streaming Data Analytics
analyst_summary: Graduate data-analytics syllabus from the Faculty of Information with a three-point 'Use of Generative AI' section. GenAI may be used to learn and practise concepts but not to complete assignments; using AI writing or coding assistants on any assessment may be treated as an academic offence.

title: Plagiarism & AI Policies - Electrical & Computer Engineering
analyst_summary: Tier 2. Department page of Utah's ECE department (home of the computer engineering degree; no Kahlert School of Computing AI policy was found). Its Artificial Intelligence Use Policy leaves coursework AI use to each instructor's syllabus, assigns research use to the supervisory committee chair, warns that unacknowledged AI use in writing can be plagiarism, and quotes IEEE disclosure guidance.

title: Syllabus: Introduction to Programming
analyst_summary: The intro programming syllabus classes using generative AI (ChatGPT, Claude) to complete coursework as academic dishonesty, alongside Chegg and Course Hero. It also bans submitting copyrighted course materials as prompts to generative AI.

title: Fall 2025 CSC 110: Fundamentals of Programming I
analyst_summary: The intro programming outline lists using generative AI as a tutor (explaining code, breaking down problems, making practice problems) among its learning outcomes. It forbids copying even partial solutions from ChatGPT. The JS-rendered outline was read with WebFetch.

title: Fall 2025 CSC 226: Algorithms and Data Structures II
analyst_summary: The outline discourages generative AI even as a study aid, since learners cannot verify its output. It bans GenAI for any graded work, including translation, formatting, typesetting and brainstorming. Students may not feed problem-set materials to AI tools. The JS-rendered outline was read with WebFetch.

title: CSC 361 Official Course Outline
analyst_summary: The instructor welcomes generative AI for assignments and class activities and points students to university-provided Microsoft Copilot. Use is optional, but students who use it must cite the tools and describe how they were used. The outline also warns that GenAI is biased, hallucinates and does not fact-check. The JS-rendered outline was read with WebFetch.

unit: Department of Computer Science, School of Engineering and Applied Science
title: DMT1 Syllabus | cs2120: Discrete Mathematics and Theory 1 (AI Tools)
analyst_summary: Discrete math course syllabus that encourages ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini on problem sets as tutors, provided use supports learning, and explains the risks of shortcuts and convincing but wrong output. It relies on in-class closed-resource tests and requires documenting AI use with links to transcripts.

course: DS 1001 (Foundations of Data Science / Think Like a Data Scientist)
title: DS 1001: Think Like a Data Scientist (TLaDS) (course README)
analyst_summary: In this intro data science course, using generative-AI tools is itself a learning objective, with labs built around AI tools. The short GenAI course policy treats AI as a study partner for clarifying, polishing wording, or feedback, but bans asking it assignment questions, copying large chunks of output, or presenting its ideas as one's own. It offers a 'would you do it with a friend' rule of thumb.

title: DS 4021 – Machine Learning (course README)
analyst_summary: The policy sets different rules by type of work. LLMs are acceptable and even encouraged for coding in labs and the final project, as long as generated code is checked. LLM use is discouraged for the writing parts because it may hinder learning, and prohibited for quizzes.

title: Policy Title: AI Policy (Policy on student use of AI tools in Data Science courses)
analyst_summary: School-wide policy requiring every Data Science syllabus to state allowable AI uses, listing rights and responsibilities of students and instructors, and supplying default rules (adapted from Temple University) that apply when a syllabus is silent. Defaults permit brainstorming, outlining and grammar help, prohibit drafting and impersonation, require citation, and set a zero for violations.

unit: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
title: Syllabus - CSE 121
analyst_summary: Intro programming syllabus that adopts the Allen School 'AI for Support and Growth' policy with projects as the only AI-authorized graded work. AI is free on projects and ungraded practice but barred from proctored computer and paper quizzes, which carry most of the assessment weight; violations cap the course grade.

unit: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
title: Generative AI - CSE 122
analyst_summary: Course page on generative AI adapted from the 2023 ITiCSE working group on GenAI in computing education. It explains risks (accuracy, quality, learning, over-reliance, motivation) and harms to others, lists permitted learning-oriented uses and inappropriate uses with examples, asks for a usage statement, and states sanctions.

unit: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
title: AI Policy - CSE 312, Autumn 2026
analyst_summary: Theory course policy built on the Allen School's shared policy template at its most restrictive level: AI is allowed for studying and ungraded exploration but not on any graded work. It shares the template's broad AI definition (explicitly covering autonomous agents), data-privacy expectations and group-responsibility sanctions.

unit: Information School (course in the MHCI+D program, taught by iSchool faculty)
title: ARCHIVED: HCID 520: User Interface Software And Technology (Winter 2024)
analyst_summary: A note on generative AI in this public Canvas syllabus lets students use AI to generate the course's essays, provided they credit the tools and the people whose writing trained them. The instructor predicts the results will fall short of the course's standards and recommends only narrow uses: spell checking, first-draft translations for English learners, and superficial writing feedback.

unit: Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering
title: AI for Support and Growth
analyst_summary: One of the Allen School's named, reusable course AI policies (adopted by CSE 121 and CSE 123; CSE 312 uses a stricter sibling). It allows AI for general learning and ungraded work and only on graded work the instructor lists as authorized, with a broad AI definition covering IDE features and coding agents, required attribution, data-privacy rules for agents and course materials, a preference for university-provided tools, and standard sanctions.

unit: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science (Faculty of Mathematics)
title: CS114: Course Outline
analyst_summary: Generative-AI section of the CS 114 (Principles of Computing for Science) outline. GenAI is allowed only under conditions stated per assessment, and most components do not permit it. Students are pointed to the university's licensed Copilot for privacy, warned about copyright, and asked to keep notes, drafts and prompts as evidence of their learning.

unit: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science (Faculty of Mathematics)
title: Course Outline - Elementary Algorithm Design and Data Abstraction (Fall 2024)
analyst_summary: Generative-AI section of the CS 136 outline: GenAI is allowed with documentation, citation and acknowledgement, and specific permitted uses are set per assignment. It warns about fabrication, bias and unclear copyright and makes students accountable for all submitted work.
