The wording follows Waterloo's university outline template; this was the most recent public CS 136 outline found, and no public CS 135 outline with AI text turned up.

unit: David R. Cheriton School of Computer Science (Faculty of Mathematics)
title: CS349 Winter 2026 : Policies
analyst_summary: Course policy page for CS 349 (User Interfaces) that treats AI-generated code like code from any other external source. Every source must be cited in a code comment, no single source may exceed 15% of an assignment, and students may be asked to explain their code to staff.

title: COMP-1410-01 Introduction to Algorithms & Programming II, Fall 2024 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Syllabus for the second introductory programming course. It bans all generative AI tools, explicitly naming ChatGPT, Claude and GitHub Copilot, as an unauthorized aid in graded work, treats such use as academic misconduct under Bylaw 31, and withholds bonus marks from students who use generative AI.

title: ACS-1903-001 Course Outline, Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Intro programming course outline whose academic-integrity section bans all AI tools, including chatbots and AI writing/paraphrasing tools. Students are told to ask the instructor before using any uncertain technology, and suspected misuse may be reported to the Senate misconduct committee.

title: ACS-1904-002 Course Outline, Winter 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Second intro programming course outline using the department's prohibitive AI boilerplate: generative AI and AI writing/paraphrasing tools are banned. Students must check with the instructor before using uncertain tools, and suspected misuse may be referred to the Senate misconduct committee.

title: ACS-3931-001 Course Outline, Winter 2025
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Operating-systems course outline that reproduces the earlier ACS boilerplate (prohibited use is misconduct; permitted use must be cited per MLA, explicitly including code) and then permits AI only in assignment labs. Each lab part must carry an MLA citation or an explicit 'No AI tool used' declaration.

title: CS220 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Intro data programming syllabus that bans generative AI on projects and on all assignments and assessments, framing it as contrary to the learning objectives and as academic misconduct under university rules. It lists using AI to write code as unacceptable, notes automated similarity detection across roughly 1000 students, and mentions a course-run AI feedback server for some project questions.

title: CS540 Introduction to Artificial Intelligence (Fall 2025): Use of AI Tools
analyst_summary: Course information page for the intro AI course that allows AI tools only in the ways a student might consult a peer: brainstorming, clarifying instructions, reviewing concepts, syntax and debugging help while remaining the primary problem-solver. Generating or copying solutions, code or written work is forbidden, with a 'would a friend do this' test and a warning that plagiarism detection is itself an AI application.

title: Syllabus Statements: Guiding Student Generative AI Usage in Your Class
analyst_summary: Tier 4. UWM teaching-center guidance asking instructors to state their generative AI expectations in the syllabus and on each assignment, and to explain how AI use should be cited. It gives three sample statements: full use with citations and prompts, specific permitted uses, and a ban under which AI-assisted work counts as academic misconduct under UWS 14.

title: University of Wyoming syllabus template with sample language (AI Technology section)
analyst_summary: UW's official syllabus template recommends that every syllabus include a section on permitted and unpermitted AI use next to the academic dishonesty statement, and offers four draft options adapted from the University of Delaware: prohibited, use only with prior permission, use with acknowledgement (with a sample ChatGPT citation), and freely permitted. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: AI Guidelines: Generative AI and UFV: Guiding Considerations
analyst_summary: Tier 4: Teaching and Learning Centre guidance mapping each of the seven UFV AI Principles to instructor practice. It leaves the extent of AI use to instructors, requires mutual disclosure when AI is permitted, advises against AI detectors, stresses privacy and consent, and supplies sample syllabus use statements (unrestricted, some use, prohibited), disclosure/citation formats, and an honour pledge.

unit: Vice-rectorat aux études et aux affaires étudiantes (Enseigner à l'Université Laval)
title: Principes directeurs concernant l'intelligence artificielle dans l'enseignement et l'apprentissage
analyst_summary: Tier 4. French-language university guiding principles for AI in teaching and learning, organized around five principles: primacy of the human relationship, openness and training, informed and responsible use, integrity and transparency, and collaboration. Instructors decide on AI use and must spell it out in the course plan; students must follow course rules and declare use when asked; equity, bias, environmental footprint and assessment validity are addressed.

title: inf1420 — Utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle générative (IAG)
analyst_summary: Tier 1 (informatique course): Public course site for a TÉLUQ computing course on human-computer interfaces, which includes Java prototype development. Under the TÉLUQ institutional statement, AI use is optional but allowed; it is banned in oral and supervised exams. Students must document and describe their use, include interaction traces where relevant, and explain results in their own words. Undeclared use may count as an academic-integrity breach.

course: INF 1901 Initiation à l’intelligence artificielle : concepts et réflexions
title: Usage de l'IA (pour ce cours) — INF1901
analyst_summary: Tier 1 (informatique course): The AI-use page of an introductory AI course (the current version of the course site) openly encourages assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for graded work and all course content. It asks students to understand the answers deeply and to talk with the assistant to clear up gaps, since the course aims to build mental models of AI. A v2 of the site (cjauvin.github.io/inf1901-teluq-v2) is in preparation.

unit: Intégrité intellectuelle (site Intégrité, ressources pour le corps professoral)
title: IA et vos plans de cours
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): University-wide guidance for instructors offering three ready-made course-outline statements: AI tools banned in all assessments (treated as plagiarism under regulation 10.9.3), allowed in some assessments, or allowed in assessments, with the permissive options requiring an explanatory note from students. No computing-specific AI document was found for the Département d'informatique, so this is the university-wide fallback.

unit: École de bibliothéconomie et des sciences de l'information (EBSI)
title: Intelligence artificielle (IA) générative (2e et 3e cycles)
analyst_summary: French-language guide page of the iSchool (EBSI) for graduate students stating that using AI in evaluations without explicit instructor authorization counts as plagiarism or fraud under the university's graduate disciplinary regulation. Students are told to check permitted practices with instructors, which may appear in the course plan, and are pointed to library guidance when use is permitted.

title: Plan d’activité pédagogique – IFT 339 – Structures de données Automne 2026
analyst_summary: French-language course plan that assigns an AI-use level to each assessment; in this course every assessment (assignments, mini-tests, exams) is set to 'Interdite'. The plan appends the Faculty of Science's five-level framework (0 forbidden to 4 free), which covers instructor reporting duties at level 0, disclosure requirements, student responsibility for AI output, and how to declare use.

title: Plan d’activité pédagogique – IFT 615 – Intelligence artificielle Hiver 2026
analyst_summary: French-language AI course plan using the same faculty level framework as IFT 339 (shared boilerplate not re-excerpted here): the two-part AI project is set to 'Balisée' (level 3), while the midterm and final are 'Interdite'. The instructor adds that generative AI is not documentation and its answers must be checked against real sources.

unit: Service de la bibliothèque — Guide de présentation des travaux écrits (UQAT)
title: Guide de présentation des travaux écrits — Normes pour les citations: Intelligence artificielle dans les travaux
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): The official UQAT guide for written work tells students to check each course outline and assessment instructions to see whether generative AI is allowed. It lists conditions instructors may impose, such as restricted uses, describing AI use, giving prompts and outputs in an appendix, and signing an intellectual-integrity declaration. Passing off AI output as one's own or having AI do the work counts as a sanctionable fraudulent practice. No computing-specific AI document was public for UQAT's computing-track programs (création numérique profil informatique, jeux vidéo programmation).

course: CYB6023 Forensique numérique avancée et réponse aux incidents
title: Plan de cours CYB6023-01 — Automne 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1 (Département d'informatique et d'ingénierie course): Graduate cybersecurity course outline from the department's public course-plan pages. It warns that lab work and exams are poorly suited to generative tools and requires students to treat generated output as a citation in text and bibliography. All Fall 2026 and Winter 2026 DII course plans were scanned; only this instructor's plans (CYB6023, CYB6063) contained an AI-use clause.

course: 8INF972 Atelier pratique en intelligence artificielle I (plan posted as 8INF934.pdf)
title: PLAN DE COURS Été 2024 — Atelier Pratique en Intelligence Artificielle I. (8INF972)

It allows AI tools such as ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot only for code, and requires a source-code comment marking any AI-generated code. Of the roughly 60 public DIM course plans scanned, this was the only one with an AI-use clause; note the PDF file name (8INF934) differs from the course code in its content (8INF972).

title: INF1120 — Programmation I (UQAM) - Plan de cours
analyst_summary: French-language course plan for the intro programming course. External generative AI tools such as ChatGPT are banned unless stated otherwise, for both writing and code. The instructor may ask students to explain their work, and the reproduced Règlement no 18 counts unauthorized AI use as an academic offence.

course: INF2050 Outils et pratiques de développement logiciel
title: INF2050 — Outils et pratiques de développement logiciel (UQAM) - Plan de cours
analyst_summary: French-language course plan for a software development tools course that bans all generative AI use and says detection tools will be used. Any detected use on an assessment is treated as attempted plagiarism and reported. Ungraded team labs are meant to be done without AI to prepare for the exams.

course: INF3105 Structures de données et algorithmes
title: INF3105 — Structures de données et algorithmes (UQAM) - Plan de cours
analyst_summary: French-language course plan with a dedicated generative AI section. It recommends avoiding AI so students master data structures, but does not formally ban it because use is hard to detect and prove. Students must be able to explain their code, and paper exams test similar programming.

unit: Secrétariat général (adopted by the Conseil d’administration)
title: C3-D117 Politique encadrant l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): Institution-wide AI policy focused on governance, privacy, confidentiality, copyright, security, and automated decision-making. It explicitly leaves teaching- and study-specific rules unspecified, but it covers AI-only grading as an automated decision and adds bias and digital-sobriety duties. No computing-specific AI document was public for UQAR's informatique programs, so this is the university-wide fallback.

unit: Comité institutionnel sur l’intelligence artificielle (with the Vice-rectorat aux études et à la formation)
title: Principes d’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle générative dans les activités d’enseignement et de recherche réalisées dans le cadre des programmes d’études de l’UQTR — Pour les membres du personnel
analyst_summary: Tier 4 (university-wide; tiers 1-3 searched, none found): Institutional principles for teaching staff, built on CEST and UNESCO guidance. They list cautionary considerations (errors, explainability, IP, unknown cognitive effects) and require staff who use generative AI to verify outputs, protect personal data, and keep pedagogical alignment. Staff must also state their AI expectations in the course outline and disclose their own AI use in course materials. A parallel version exists for students; no computing-specific document was public for UQTR's Département de mathématiques et d'informatique.

unit: USU Teach (Center for Empowering Teaching Excellence / Center for Instructional Design and Innovation)
title: AI in Teaching: Communicate about AI
analyst_summary: Tier 4. USU teaching guidance requiring instructors to define AI guidelines in the syllabus and enforce them under Article VI of the Student Code. It describes three broad categories of course policy, from prohibited (which explicitly covers coding assistants) to encouraged, with template statements on detection, sanctions, citation and acknowledgement. It also asks instructors to disclose their own AI use, such as for grading feedback.

unit: B.S. Software Development / Computing Technology and Software Development
title: CEN 3024C 13038 Software Development I (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for Valencia's Software Development I (instructor Lisa Macon). It allows AI chatbots for research and debugging on marked assignments but bans GitHub Copilot and other coding copilots, arguing that developers must be able to write their own code. It sets six ethical practices: verify accuracy, use AI as a tool not a crutch, watch for bias, protect privacy, disclose use, and follow no-AI instructions. The college's template 'Academic Integrity and Use of AI' block is also included. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

unit: Computer Programming and Analysis (Engineering, Computer Programming and Technology)
title: COP 1000C 14088 Intro to Programming Concepts (Fall 2026 syllabus)
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for Valencia's intro programming course (instructor Jenny Hu). Its 'Academic Integrity and Use of AI' section allows GenAI only for limited purposes (brainstorming and outlining essays, grammar and style checks on the student's own drafts), forbids submitting AI-generated work, and requires a note naming the tool, prompts and purpose. The wording, which refers to essay assignments, appears to be a shared template; the same block appears in other Valencia computing syllabi. Text retrieved via the Simple Syllabus platform's public JSON endpoint for this public syllabus page.

title: CSCI159 Fall 2025 Course Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Intro programming (C++) syllabus with a course policy on LLMs and generative AI. It forbids entering instructor or other students' material into AI tools on intellectual-property grounds, requires citation of any AI help in submitted work, and cautions students against bypassing learning.

title: CSCI 159 Course Outline (Fall 2026, sections N01/N02)
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Intro programming (C++) course outline from a different instructor than the Carruthers section. Its individual-work rule bars outside help, naming AI tools such as Copilot and ChatGPT, for all quizzes, labs, assignments and exams unless stated otherwise.

title: CSCI 161 - Computing Science II Outline
analyst_summary: Tier 1: Second programming course outline that permits generative AI as a learning aid and for producing assignments, provided students document tools, usage, and how outputs were incorporated, including exact prompts and responses, in an appendix. Failure to document is treated as an integrity breach.

unit: Vanderbilt Generative AI site (Center for Teaching / Academic Affairs)
title: Sample Syllabi Statements for Generative AI and ChatGPT Usage
analyst_summary: Tier 1. A university collection of sample AI syllabus statements, linked from Vanderbilt's 'Academic Integrity and Generative AI' page. It opens with Professor Alan Peters' AI policy for his Electrical and Computer Engineering courses, the only computing-specific and only Vanderbilt-authored section; the rest reproduces samples from other universities. Under that policy students may use generative AI, but they must cite AI-generated text and code with the prompt used, test and explain any generated code, and comment every part of it. Breaking these rules is an Honor Code violation. Excerpts come only from the ECE section.

title: CMPU-224: Computer Organization — Policy on the Use of AI and Large Language Models (LLMs)
analyst_summary: The policy discourages but does not forbid LLMs: cited use for conceptual questions, syntax/tooling help and cautious debugging is allowed (with example prompts), while generating assignment code or any written prose (comments, READMEs, analyses) is forbidden. A specific acknowledgement block at the top of each submission is mandatory.

title: Proposed AI Guidelines
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Villanova's university-wide (proposed) AI guidelines for students, faculty and staff. They cover confidentiality and data classification, bias (including in integrity detectors), disclosure, accountability, equity, intellectual property and over-reliance on AI for writing or coding. On teaching, Villanova does not restrict AI: instructors may prohibit, allow with attribution, or encourage it, and must say which in the syllabus.

unit: Department of Computer Science, College of Engineering
title: CMSC 210 Computers and Programming — Syllabus Fall 2026
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for VCU's introductory Python programming course, posted on the CS department's public syllabi page. It treats AI tools as a normal programming aid to be used like a TA or textbook for explanations and error help, applies the ordinary plagiarism line to AI output (no solving assignments, no submitting output one cannot explain), and bans AI on quizzes and exams under the device policy.

unit: Department of Computer Science, College of Engineering
title: CMSC 357: Computer Systems — Fall 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for VCU's computer systems course from the CS department's public syllabi page. Its collaboration lists allow AI for understanding bugs but not for writing programs, and a dedicated AI policy lists permitted uses (concept help, debugging, refactoring after a working solution), requires instructor permission for anything else, and keeps students fully responsible for and able to explain submitted code.

unit: Department of Computer Science, College of Engineering
title: CMSC 413: Introduction to Cybersecurity — Fall 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 1. Fall 2026 syllabus for VCU's introductory cybersecurity course from the CS department's public syllabi page. It allows AI for learning support, writing polish and debugging, labels individual assignments as AI-required or AI-prohibited, forbids using AI for hands-on system and lab tasks (noting AI output for such tasks is often wrong), and keeps students responsible for everything they submit.

title: AI & Academic Integrity - Artificial Intelligence & Information Literacy
analyst_summary: Short library guide page stating that using AI without permission or citation may be plagiarism or a conduct violation, with tips to ask instructors about their AI policies, treat AI as a source, and cite it. It is the only AI guidance found on VSU's own domain. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

title: CS 3214: Computer Systems, Fall 2026 Syllabus (AI Considerations; Use of Generative AI)
analyst_summary: Systems course syllabus that explains how coding agents changed assessment and sets a fourfold response: keep projects designed for humans, allow but not require AI assistants, grade projects on functionality, and add more proctored, closed-AI tests. There are no restrictions on AI for generating or debugging code, but students must be able to explain AI-assisted work and may not use AI to impersonate themselves in discussion posts without attribution.

unit: AI at Wake Forest (AI Working Group for Academics)
title: Guidelines for Academic Use
date_or_term: Adapted from AI Working Group for Academics Final Report (March 2025)
analyst_summary: Tier 4. University guidelines adapted from the March 2025 AI Working Group report. Every syllabus must state GAI expectations, which can differ by course and assignment. Misconduct is defined as GAI use without permission, instructors and students share responsibility for communication, AI detectors cannot be the only evidence, and instructors who require GAI must make sure every student has access.

unit: School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
title: CptS 317: Automata and Formal Languages Syllabus, Fall 2024
analyst_summary: Brief syllabus statement allowing generative AI for learning course material but not for producing solutions to graded homework, which must be the student's own work.

title: AI Best Practices - CSE330 Wiki
analyst_summary: Course wiki page that permits AI tools for brainstorming, debugging and scaffolding but makes students responsible for verification, security and style. Every assignment carries a graded AI reflection (before, during and after coding) and an AI interaction log of copied prompts and responses.

title: CSE 4202: Operating Systems Organization
analyst_summary: OS course collaboration policy that allows ChatGPT or GitHub Copilot output in studios and labs only with in-code attribution: marking the generated lines, giving the exact prompts, and explaining the code in the student's own words.

unit: Academic Senate, Ad hoc Subcommittee on Artificial Intelligence
title: Ad hoc Subcommittee on Artificial Intelligence (AI) Running Report – Winter 2024
analyst_summary: Tier 4. Academic Senate subcommittee report giving Wayne State's recommended AI syllabus language. Faculty decide whether to allow AI, must communicate expectations (including on AI editing tools such as Grammarly), and get two model statements: a prohibition and a conditional-use version with undergraduate and graduate variants that require prior consultation, disclosure of prompts, accuracy checks, and awareness of bias and copyright. It also says AI detectors remain unreliable.

course: CS 111: Computer Programming and Problem Solving
title: AI-powered Tools Policy for CS 111
analyst_summary: A standalone, extensively argued policy banning all AI use in the intro course, equating AI help with consulting a former student, backed by in-house tools that screen submissions for AI-generated code and possible Honor Code charges. It gives research-based and ethical rationales (hallucinations, novice harm, licensing, labor, bias, energy), restricts students to course IDEs, and requires students to read and present an AI paper.

unit: Department of Mathematics and Computer Science
title: COMP 211: Computer Science 1 — Policies
analyst_summary: AI tools are prohibited for idea generation, problem-solving and coding, leaving only use to improve understanding of class topics; the rationale stresses that students must be able to write and debug code themselves and be aware of security risks of unvetted AI code. Any AI use on homework, labs or exams is an Honor Code violation.

unit: Information Services & Technology and Teaching & Learning Center
title: Generative AI @ WCU – A Guiding Framework
analyst_summary: WCU's cross-university framework (a living document, not a policy) with recommendations on following academic integrity policies, protecting data and student work, equity of access, verifying accuracy and bias, and transparency. For teaching it asks faculty to give a clear syllabus statement on student AI use, be transparent about their own AI use for grading and materials, and not submit student work to AI tools without permission. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Teaching and Learning Commons (Faculty Senate-adopted syllabus statements)
title: Syllabus Policies and Statements: Artificial Intelligence Syllabus Statement and Additional Sample AI Statements
analyst_summary: WVU's official syllabus-statement page carries the Faculty Senate general AI statement, which bars content-generating AI tools unless the instructor permits them, plus four sample statements instructors can adopt instead. One permissive sample explicitly covers AI coding and problem-solving help, with documentation, citation and a requirement to explain submitted work. Tier 4 (university-general fallback; no Tier 2 or Tier 3 document found).

unit: Office of Faculty Development / Center for Teaching, Learning, and Development
title: AI in the Syllabus
analyst_summary: Tier 4. WMU teaching-center guidance on writing syllabus AI statements. It warns that outright bans are hard to enforce because detectors are unreliable and biased, recommends clear, flexible, process-focused policies discussed on day one, and suggests co-creating policies with students. Sample statements range from open use with an AI acknowledgement to authorized-only use, including language under Faculty Senate review.

title: CS1026A Fall 2026: Computer Science Fundamentals I - Course Outline
analyst_summary: Intro programming outline that bans generative AI and any code- or comment-generating tools (a long list of named products) on assignments, quizzes and tests. Violations mean a zero and referral to the department's integrity committee; some labs and in-class activities may allow limited use, but only when stated explicitly.

title: CS 1027A Fall 2026 Course Outline - Computer Science Fundamentals II
analyst_summary: Second intro course outline that bans outside GenAI on assignments and labs, comment generation included, while offering an optional vendor AI tutor in VS Code (Kritik Coding Authorship) that guides without giving full solutions. Its general GenAI statement makes 'not permitted unless stated' the default for all assessments, and the outline notes that tools beyond MOSS may be used to detect AI-generated code.

title: CS 2120 Fall 2026 Course Outline
analyst_summary: Programming course outline that generally forbids GenAI because it hinders novice programmers' learning. Assignments are screened with similarity software and AI use on them gets a zero plus integrity-committee referral; some tutorials and in-class activities may allow limited, explicitly stated use.

title: CSCI 141 - Computer Programming I
analyst_summary: Intro programming course page with a one-line AI policy banning AI for all assigned work, followed by a 'regret policy' that lets students who made a bad decision self-report within 48 hours for a zero instead of the department's standard integrity penalty.

title: CSCI 241 - Data Structures
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus section 'On the Use of AI Tools' that argues fundamentals still matter (calculator analogy) and allows AI only when the same help from a human would pass the collaboration policy. Code completion tools are therefore ruled out.

title: CSCI 301 - Formal Languages and Functional Programming
analyst_summary: Course page allowing generative AI under two conditions: genuine use as a learning tool and submission of the interaction transcript with the assignment. Exams are closed-book without AI, and the policy is flagged as subject to change.

title: CP164: Syllabus
analyst_summary: Data structures syllabus with a 'Generative AI/Academic Integrity Statement' prohibiting generative AI entirely and treating its use for coursework as academic misconduct under Senate Policy 12.2.

title: Computer Science 304 Computer Organization Spring 2026 Syllabus
analyst_summary: Syllabus whose 'Independent Work' rule defines cheating to include looking at, copying or discussing problems or code from the internet, explicitly including AI such as ChatGPT. Students are directed to the instructor and TAs for help.

title: CS 334: Syllabus
analyst_summary: An allow-list policy: AI may be used only for tooling/setup questions, lecture clarifications, and study aids; any other use, especially submitting AI-written code or answers, is academic dishonesty and grounds for course failure. Students are told to stop using AI on an assignment once they start it.

course: CSCI 104: Data Science and Computing for All
title: Syllabus — CSCI 104
analyst_summary: An introductory data-science/computing course that asks students not to use ChatGPT to produce, refine, or check coursework answers, while allowing AI assistants for understanding course material; instructors promise to discuss effective AI use later in the term and help students navigate the boundary.

title: Operating Systems - CS 3013
analyst_summary: The course encourages GenAI coding assistants, citing employer demand, and teaches a 'Using Generative AI for Learning' process. Assessment moves to in-person quizzes where AI and all other resources are banned. A table spells out that AI tools are allowed on projects but not quizzes, and that students must be able to explain all submitted work.

unit: Department of Computer Science and Engineering
title: CEG4350/CEG5350 - Operating Systems (syllabus)
analyst_summary: Operating systems syllabus that forbids all generative AI tools, explicitly including ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, for any coursework. It justifies the ban by the instructor's need to evaluate unassisted work and treats use as an academic integrity violation. Tier 1 (CS course).

title: CPSC 2010 - Introduction to Computer Science
analyst_summary: Course home page note pointing students to the university-provided LLMs (via Yale's Clarity platform) and suggesting their use as a study aid, such as generating practice exam questions. It contains no further rules on assignment use.

title: Academic Integrity Policy: Resources (Syllabus Language)
analyst_summary: Yeshiva's academic integrity resources page. It tells students to assume generative AI is not allowed without explicit permission, and gives faculty four AI syllabus templates distinguishing generative from assistive AI (none, assistive only, select generative plus assistive, all allowed with citation), plus integrity practices such as Turnitin AI screening and drafting in Google Docs for provenance. Tier 4 (university-general fallback).

unit: Lassonde School of Engineering, Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS)
title: EECS4414 Information Networks (Cross-listed as EECS5414)
analyst_summary: Upper-year EECS syllabus allowing generative AI for learning, programming, experimentation and project work provided all use is fully disclosed. It frames AI as an accelerator that must not replace understanding: students own everything they submit and must be able to explain and defend it without AI.

unit: Département de génie logiciel et des TI
title: LOG430 Plan de cours (Version PDF), Automne 2026
analyst_summary: French-language software-architecture course plan. It carries the school-wide SIAG clause (generative AI in assessments is an academic offence unless the instructor authorizes it) and an evaluation table with an 'Utilisation de l'IA' column marking each assessment as 'Utilisation libre' (free use) or 'Utilisation interdite' (forbidden): free on projects and team lab reports, forbidden on the final exam, peer evaluations and orals.
